documents.text:
The Ponmi system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth the
trouble. It has 5 vashumbs, two operations, and one relation, and nothing else.

The vashumbs are written korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri. The first
operation is written ?. The second is written & and binds more tightly, so x ? y & z
means x ? (y & z). The relation is written %%; where it holds between two vashumbs we
say the left one governs the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x ? x ? x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

We turn to the Ponmi signature, the Ponmi combination tables and closure under the first operation. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about vashumbs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for ?. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | korrvex keldclo glimsib hobtez korrdri ------------------------------------------------------- korrvex | korrvex korrvex korrvex korrvex korrvex keldclo | korrvex keldclo glimsib hobtez korrdri glimsib | korrvex glimsib korrdri keldclo hobtez hobtez | korrvex hobtez keldclo korrdri glimsib korrdri | korrvex korrdri hobtez glimsib keldclo The table for &. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | korrvex keldclo glimsib hobtez korrdri ------------------------------------------------------- korrvex | korrvex keldclo glimsib hobtez korrdri keldclo | keldclo glimsib hobtez korrdri korrvex glimsib | glimsib hobtez korrdri korrvex keldclo hobtez | hobtez korrdri korrvex keldclo glimsib korrdri | korrdri korrvex keldclo glimsib hobtez Every pair standing in the %% relation, grouped by left argument. korrvex %% korrvex keldclo %% korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri glimsib %% korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri hobtez %% korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri korrdri %% korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all vashumbs x and y, x ? y is again a vashumb. A2. Association of the first operation. For all vashumbs x, y, z: (x ? y) ? z = x ? (y ? z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all vashumbs x and y: x ? y = y ? x.

Two questions sort the vashumbs quickly. Does combining a vashumb with itself change it? For korrvex and keldclo it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri it does not. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Ponmi combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Ponmi combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take korrdri ? korrvex & glimsib and work it out one step at a time. korrvex & glimsib = glimsib (the table for &) korrdri ? glimsib = hobtez (the table for ?) The expression comes to hobtez. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is korrvex ? (glimsib ? korrdri) for contrast. glimsib ? korrdri = hobtez (the table for ?) korrvex ? hobtez = korrvex (the table for ?) The value is korrvex, not hobtez. Test hobtez %% keldclo. The zammorn of hobtez is korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri, and keldclo lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R2. It is not the case that: For every vashumb x: x ? x = x. The case that settles it: x = glimsib, value = korrdri. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all vashumbs x, y, z: if x ? y = x ? z then y = z. It fails at x = korrvex, y = korrvex, z = keldclo. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (closure under the second operation) and A7 (association of the second operation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every vashumb x: x ? x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimsib, value = korrdri, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all vashumbs x, y, z: if x ? y = x ? z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = korrvex, y = korrvex, z = keldclo, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R2 and R3. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation, and each claim can be checked by hand. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about vashumbs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a vashumb keldclo with keldclo ? x = x ? keldclo = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a vashumb korrvex with korrvex ? x = x ? korrvex = korrvex for every x.

The neutral vashumb keldclo is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Ponmi combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate (korrdri ? korrvex) ? (keldclo ? glimsib). Each line below is one lookup in a table. korrdri ? korrvex = korrvex (the table for ?) keldclo ? glimsib = glimsib (the table for ?) korrvex ? glimsib = korrvex (the table for ?) So (korrdri ? korrvex) ? (keldclo ? glimsib) is korrvex. A companion case, korrvex ? (keldclo ? korrdri), to show what the brackets are doing. keldclo ? korrdri = korrdri (the table for ?) korrvex ? korrdri = korrvex (the table for ?) That gives korrvex, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does hobtez %% glimsib hold? Read off what hobtez stands over: korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri. glimsib is among them, so it holds.
R1. Some vashumb x admits no vashumb y for which x ? y and y ? x both land on a neutral object. It fails at x = korrvex. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
Read alongside S2 (the Ponmi combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the zamtez) and T1 (the zamtez is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some vashumb x admits no vashumb y for which x ? y and y ? x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = korrvex, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The results collected here were not found in this order. Reflexivity of the relation, transitivity of the relation and comparability of every pair came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A10. Reflexivity of the relation. For every vashumb x: x %% x. A11. Transitivity of the relation. For all vashumbs x, y, z: if x %% y and y %% z then x %% z. A12. Comparability of every pair. For all vashumbs x and y, at least one of x %% y and y %% x holds. A13. Agreement of the relation with the first operation. For all vashumbs x, y, z: if x %% y then (z ? x) %% (z ? y) and (x ? z) %% (y ? z). D4. The zammorn of a vashumb. The zammorn of a vashumb x is the collection of vashumbs y for which x %% y holds. Worked out for each vashumb: korrvex to korrvex; keldclo to korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri; glimsib to korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri; hobtez to korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri; korrdri to korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri.

The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. documents.text: Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through tarnqen vashumbs, vashumbs that quilnak and the zamtez. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about vashumbs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D1. Tarnqen vashumbs. A vashumb x is called tarnqen when x ? x = x. In this system that picks out korrvex and keldclo, which is 2 of the 5 vashumbs. D2. Vashumbs that quilnak. Two vashumbs x and y are said to quilnak when x ? y = y ? x. D5. The zamtez. The vashumb keldclo is called the zamtez of the system. It is the unique vashumb that leaves every vashumb unchanged under ?. Here that is keldclo.

A useful mental split: some vashumbs are inert under the operation and some are not. korrvex and keldclo come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri commute with everything. The neutral vashumb keldclo is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 vashumbs the table is short enough to consult every time.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Evaluate hobtez ? glimsib & korrvex. Each line below is one lookup in a table. glimsib & korrvex = glimsib (the table for &) hobtez ? glimsib = keldclo (the table for ?) So hobtez ? glimsib & korrvex is keldclo. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take glimsib ? (korrvex ? hobtez). korrvex ? hobtez = korrvex (the table for ?) glimsib ? korrvex = korrvex (the table for ?) That gives korrvex, against keldclo above. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does keldclo %% korrdri hold? Read off what keldclo stands over: korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri. korrdri is among them, so it holds.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of vashumbs that come back unchanged from themselves: korrvex and keldclo. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

Read alongside A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). What is built on it later: D6 (the fexsib), D7 (the opalvex), D10 (hobkeld vashumbs) and T1 (the zamtez is the only one of its kind).
No proofs are needed here. Everything asserted is a definition or a table entry.

documents.text: D13. Iskbra pairs. Two distinct vashumbs x and y form a iskbra pair when x %% y and y %% x both hold, that is, when each lies in the zammorn of the other. Running the definition over every vashumb leaves keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri. D3. Yukzam collections. A collection S of vashumbs is yukzam when x ? y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A thrarast. A vashumb f is a thrarast when f %% y holds for every vashumb y, that is, when the zammorn of f is the whole system. Running the definition over every vashumb leaves keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri.

documents.text: Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is hobkeld vashumbs, the fexsib and the opalvex. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 2 and 5, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about vashumbs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

D10. Hobkeld vashumbs. A vashumb x is hobkeld when x ? x equals the zamtez. In this system that picks out keldclo and korrdri, which is 2 of the 5 vashumbs. D6. The fexsib. The fexsib of the system is the collection of vashumbs that quilnak with every vashumb. In this system that picks out korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri, that is, all of them. D7. The opalvex. The opalvex is the collection of all tarnqen vashumbs. Running the definition over every vashumb leaves korrvex and keldclo.

Two questions sort the vashumbs quickly. Does combining a vashumb with itself change it? For korrvex and keldclo it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single vashumb and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R13 rests on D5 (the zamtez). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T1 rests on D5 (the zamtez) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is keldclo ? glimsib & hobtez, reduced without skipping anything. glimsib & hobtez = korrvex (the table for &) keldclo ? korrvex = korrvex (the table for ?) So keldclo ? glimsib & hobtez is korrvex. A companion case, glimsib ? (hobtez ? keldclo), to show what the brackets are doing. hobtez ? keldclo = hobtez (the table for ?) glimsib ? hobtez = keldclo (the table for ?) The value is keldclo, not korrvex. Test keldclo %% hobtez. The zammorn of keldclo is korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri, and hobtez lies inside it, so the relation holds.
R13. It is not the case that: e ? x equals the zamtez for every vashumb x. It fails at anchor = keldclo, x = korrvex, value = korrvex. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (tarnqen vashumbs), D2 (vashumbs that quilnak) and D5 (the zamtez). What is built on it later: T2 (the zamtez lies in the fexsib), T3 (the fexsib is yukzam), T7 (the umbgrix of a fexsib vashumb stays in the fexsib) and T8 (the opalvex is yukzam).

R13. It is not the case that: e ? x equals the zamtez for every vashumb x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = keldclo, x = korrvex, value = korrvex, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one vashumb e with e ? x = x ? e = x for every vashumb x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every vashumb unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e ? f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e ? f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 25 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: hobkeld vashumbs, the fexsib and the opalvex. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. The results now available are T1, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Do not carry forward R13. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, the umbgrix of a vashumb, the system has a thrarast and where every vashumb is tarnqen breaks down, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1, 3, 5, 6 and 7, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about vashumbs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D8. The umbgrix of a vashumb. The umbgrix of a vashumb x, written [x], is the smallest yukzam collection that contains x. Worked out for each vashumb: korrvex to korrvex; keldclo to keldclo; glimsib to keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri; hobtez to keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri; korrdri to keldclo and korrdri.

The right picture for umbgrix is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one vashumb in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1, 2 and 4 vashumbs depending on where it started. Think of %% as pointing downhill. The zammorn of a vashumb is everything downhill of it, and those shadows here have sizes 1 and 5. Two questions sort the vashumbs quickly. Does combining a vashumb with itself change it? For korrvex and keldclo it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri it does not. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

T10. Some vashumb thrarasts the whole system. (1) [A12] Every pair is comparable, so the relation orders the objects into a line. (2) [D9] The claim is that the line has a bottom. (3) The carrier is finite, so the search over candidates terminates. Checked over 25 cases: every candidate against every object. pair of vashumbs quilnaks. (1) [D6] The fexsib is defined by quilnaking with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x ? y = y ? x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The zamtez quilnaks with every vashumb. (1) [D5] Let e be the zamtez and x any vashumb. (2) [D5] Then e ? x = x and x ? e = x. (3) [D2] So e ? x = x ? e, which is what it means to quilnak. (4) [D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the fexsib. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both quilnak with every vashumb, then so does x ? y. (1)

[D6] Let x and y lie in the fexsib and let z be any vashumb. (2) [A2] Then (x ? y) ? z = x ? (y ? z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each quilnaks with everything. (4) [D3] So x ? y quilnaks with z, and the fexsib is yukzam. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x and y are both tarnqen then so is x ? y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be tarnqen. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x ? y) ? (x ? y) returns x ? y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

D11. The grixumb of a vashumb. The grixumb of a vashumb x is the number of vashumbs in its umbgrix [x]. Worked out for each vashumb: korrvex to 1; keldclo to 1; glimsib to 4; hobtez to 4; korrdri to 2.

Picture the umbgrix as what happens when you start with one vashumb and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 vashumbs, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. A useful mental split: some vashumbs are inert under the operation and some are not. korrvex and keldclo come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and korrvex, keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri commute with everything. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

That gives glimsib, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test korrvex %% hobtez. The zammorn of korrvex is korrvex, and hobtez lies outside it, so the relation fails. Now compute [hobtez]. Fold hobtez against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is keldclo, glimsib, hobtez and korrdri, of size 4.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of vashumbs that come back unchanged from themselves: korrvex and keldclo. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

T4. For every vashumb x, the collection [x] is yukzam. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under ?. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 125 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the fexsib then every vashumb of [x] lies in the fexsib. (1) [T3] The fexsib is yukzam. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest yukzam collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the fexsib is one. Checked over 25 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text:
The Umbtu system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth the
trouble. It has 5 drigrixs, two operations, and one relation, and nothing else.

The drigrixs are written solvex, umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex. The first
operation is written @. The second is written + and binds more tightly, so x @ y + z
means x @ (y + z). The relation is written ::; where it holds between two drigrixs we
say the left one covers the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x @ x @ x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is the Umbtu signature, the Umbtu combination tables and closure under the first operation. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over drigrixs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for @. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | solvex umbazt glimmux vashtez qenvex ------------------------------------------------------- solvex | solvex solvex solvex solvex solvex umbazt | solvex umbazt glimmux vashtez qenvex glimmux | solvex glimmux qenvex umbazt vashtez vashtez | solvex vashtez umbazt qenvex glimmux qenvex | solvex qenvex vashtez glimmux umbazt The table for +. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | solvex umbazt glimmux vashtez qenvex ------------------------------------------------------- solvex | solvex umbazt glimmux vashtez qenvex umbazt | umbazt glimmux vashtez qenvex solvex glimmux | glimmux vashtez qenvex solvex umbazt vashtez | vashtez qenvex solvex umbazt glimmux qenvex | qenvex solvex umbazt glimmux vashtez Every pair standing in the :: relation, grouped by left argument. solvex :: solvex, umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex umbazt :: umbazt glimmux :: umbazt vashtez :: umbazt qenvex :: umbazt

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all drigrixs x and y, x @ y is again a drigrix. A2. Association of the first operation. For all drigrixs x, y, z: (x @ y) @ z = x @ (y @ z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all drigrixs x and y: x @ y = y @ x.

A useful mental split: some drigrixs are inert under the operation and some are not. solvex and umbazt come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and solvex, umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex commute with everything. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 drigrixs the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Umbtu combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Umbtu combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is umbazt @ qenvex + solvex, reduced without skipping anything. qenvex + solvex = qenvex (the table for +) umbazt @ qenvex = qenvex (the table for @) The expression comes to qenvex. A companion case, qenvex @ (solvex @ umbazt), to show what the brackets are doing. solvex @ umbazt = solvex (the table for @) qenvex @ solvex = solvex (the table for @) That gives solvex, against qenvex above. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does qenvex :: solvex hold? Read off what qenvex stands over: umbazt. solvex is not among them, so it fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every drigrix x: x @ x = x. The case that settles it: x = glimmux, value = qenvex. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all drigrixs x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then y = z. It fails at x = solvex, y = solvex, z = umbazt. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (closure under the second operation) and A7 (association of the second operation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every drigrix x: x @ x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimmux, value = qenvex, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all drigrixs x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = solvex, y = solvex, z = umbazt, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R2 and R3. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over drigrixs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a drigrix umbazt with umbazt @ x = x @ umbazt = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a drigrix solvex with solvex @ x = x @ solvex = solvex for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single drigrix and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Umbtu combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (solvex @ vashtez) @ (glimmux @ umbazt), reduced without skipping anything. solvex @ vashtez = solvex (the table for @) glimmux @ umbazt = glimmux (the table for @) solvex @ glimmux = solvex (the table for @) So (solvex @ vashtez) @ (glimmux @ umbazt) is solvex. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take vashtez @ (glimmux @ solvex). glimmux @ solvex = solvex (the table for @) vashtez @ solvex = solvex (the table for @) The value is solvex. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test vashtez :: umbazt. The muxqen of vashtez is umbazt, and umbazt lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R1. Some drigrix x admits no drigrix y for which x @ y and y @ x both land on a neutral object. The case that settles it: x = solvex. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
Read alongside S2 (the Umbtu combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the thrasib) and T1 (the thrasib is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some drigrix x admits no drigrix y for which x @ y and y @ x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = solvex, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet antisymmetry of the relation, transitivity of the relation and the muxqen of a drigrix early, whether or not they go looking. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about drigrixs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The muxqen of a drigrix x is the collection of drigrixs y for which x :: y holds. Worked out for each drigrix: solvex to solvex, umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex; umbazt to umbazt; glimmux to umbazt; vashtez to umbazt; qenvex to umbazt.

documents.text: We turn to rastka drigrixs, drigrixs that iskopal and the thrasib. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about drigrixs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D1. Rastka drigrixs. A drigrix x is called rastka when x @ x = x. In this system that picks out solvex and umbazt, which is 2 of the 5 drigrixs. D2. Drigrixs that iskopal. Two drigrixs x and y are said to iskopal when x @ y = y @ x. D5. The thrasib. The drigrix umbazt is called the thrasib of the system. It is the unique drigrix that leaves every drigrix unchanged under @. Here that is umbazt.

Two questions sort the drigrixs quickly. Does combining a drigrix with itself change it? For solvex and umbazt it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For solvex, umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single drigrix and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 drigrixs the table is short enough to consult every time.
Nothing is derived in this chapter. It lays down material that later chapters draw on.

Take vashtez @ qenvex + solvex and work it out one step at a time. qenvex + solvex = qenvex (the table for +) vashtez @ qenvex = glimmux (the table for @) The expression comes to glimmux. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take qenvex @ (solvex @ vashtez). solvex @ vashtez = solvex (the table for @) qenvex @ solvex = solvex (the table for @) The value is solvex, not glimmux. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does umbazt :: solvex hold? Read off what umbazt stands over: umbazt. solvex is not among them, so it fails.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

The material this chapter borrows from: A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). These results are used again in D6 (the brazam), D7 (the geljen), D10 (korrtu drigrixs) and T1 (the thrasib is the only one of its kind).
No proofs are needed here. Everything asserted is a definition or a table entry.
New vocabulary from this chapter: rastka drigrixs, drigrixs that iskopal and the thrasib. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over drigrixs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. documents.text: D13. Zamtarn pairs. Two distinct drigrixs x and y form a zamtarn pair when x :: y and y :: x both hold, that is, when each lies in the muxqen of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Ponclo collections. A collection S of drigrixs is ponclo when x @ y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A vintzam. A drigrix f is a vintzam when f :: y holds for every drigrix y, that is, when the muxqen of f is the whole system. In this system that picks out solvex, which is 1 of the 5 drigrixs.

documents.text: What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, korrtu drigrixs, the brazam and the geljen, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D10. Korrtu drigrixs. A drigrix x is korrtu when x @ x equals the thrasib. In this system that picks out umbazt and qenvex, which is 2 of the 5 drigrixs. D6. The brazam. The brazam of the system is the collection of drigrixs that iskopal with every drigrix. Running the definition over every drigrix leaves solvex, umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex. D7. The geljen. The geljen is the collection of all rastka drigrixs. In this system that picks out solvex and umbazt, which is 2 of the 5 drigrixs.

Two questions sort the drigrixs quickly. Does combining a drigrix with itself change it? For solvex and umbazt it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 drigrixs the table is short enough to consult every time.

Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T1 rests on D5 (the thrasib) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is vashtez @ (umbazt @ qenvex) for contrast. umbazt @ qenvex = qenvex (the table for @) vashtez @ qenvex = glimmux (the table for @) The value is glimmux, not umbazt. Read alongside A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (rastka drigrixs), D2 (drigrixs that iskopal) and D5 (the thrasib). These results are used again in T2 (the thrasib lies in the brazam), T3 (the brazam is ponclo), T7 (the fexyuk of a brazam drigrix stays in the brazam) and T8 (the geljen is ponclo).

R15. It is not the case that: e @ x equals the thrasib for every drigrix x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = umbazt, x = solvex, value = solvex, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one drigrix e with e @ x = x @ e = x for every drigrix x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every drigrix unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e @ f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e @ f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 25 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: korrtu drigrixs, the brazam and the geljen. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T1. Do not carry forward R15. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet the fexyuk of a drigrix, there is at most one vintzam and no zamtarn pairs exist early, whether or not they go looking. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 3 and 6 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 5 drigrixs that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

documents.text: D8. The fexyuk of a drigrix. The fexyuk of a drigrix x, written [x], is the smallest ponclo collection that contains x. Worked out for each drigrix: solvex to solvex; umbazt to umbazt; glimmux to umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex; vashtez to umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex; qenvex to umbazt and qenvex.

documents.text: Picture the fexyuk as what happens when you start with one drigrix and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 drigrixs, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. The relation is easiest to see as a height. Each drigrix casts a muxqen over what it covers, and the sizes of those shadows here are 1 and 5. Sizes repeat, so the objects do not line up in single file. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

documents.text: T10. No two distinct drigrixs can both be vintzams. (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors. (2) [D9] Then f :: h, since h is any object, and h :: f likewise. (3) [A10] Antisymmetry forces f = h. Checked over 25 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T11. No two distinct drigrixs lie in each other's muxqen. (1) [D13] Suppose x and y form a tight pair. (2) [A10] Antisymmetry then identifies x with y. (3) So a tight pair of distinct objects cannot arise. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text: Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through where every drigrix is rastka breaks down, every drigrix lies in the brazam and the thrasib lies in the brazam. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1, 5, 6 and 7 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over drigrixs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
This chapter introduces no new vocabulary. It works entirely with what has already been defined.

A useful mental split: some drigrixs are inert under the operation and some are not. solvex and umbazt come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and solvex, umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex commute with everything. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T12. Every pair of drigrixs iskopals. (1) [D6] The brazam is defined by iskopaling with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x @ y = y @ x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The thrasib iskopals with every drigrix. (1) [D5] Let e be the thrasib and x any drigrix. (2) [D5] Then e @ x = x and x @ e = x. (3) [D2] So e @ x = x @ e, which is what it means to iskopal. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the brazam. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both iskopal with every drigrix, then so does x @ y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the brazam and let z be any drigrix. (2) [A2] Then (x @ y) @ z = x @ (y @ z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each iskopals with everything. (4) [D3] So x @ y iskopals with z, and the brazam is ponclo. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x and y are both rastka then so is x @ y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be rastka. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x @ y) @ (x @ y) returns x @ y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D8 (the fexyuk of a drigrix), D6 (the brazam) and T3 (the brazam is ponclo). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (vashtez @ qenvex) @ (solvex @ umbazt). Each line below is one lookup in a table. vashtez @ qenvex = glimmux (the table for @) solvex @ umbazt = solvex (the table for @) glimmux @ solvex = solvex (the table for @) The expression comes to solvex. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take qenvex @ (solvex @ vashtez). solvex @ vashtez = solvex (the table for @) qenvex @ solvex = solvex (the table for @) That gives solvex, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does qenvex :: solvex hold? Read off what qenvex stands over: umbazt. solvex is not among them, so it fails. A second case, this time a fexyuk. Start from qenvex. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is umbazt and qenvex, so the duthgrix of qenvex is 2.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of drigrixs that come back unchanged from themselves: solvex and umbazt. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

T4. For every drigrix x, the collection [x] is ponclo. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under @. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 125 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the brazam then every drigrix of [x] lies in the brazam. (1) [T3] The brazam is ponclo. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest ponclo collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the brazam is one. Checked over 25 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
New vocabulary from this chapter: the duthgrix of a drigrix. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T4 and T7.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is the zamkorr, where the duthgrix divides the number of drigrixs breaks down and where some drigrix reaches every other breaks down. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 5, 8 and 10, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 5 drigrixs that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
D12. The zamkorr. The zamkorr of the system is the collection of drigrixs whose duthgrix is largest. In this system that picks out glimmux and vashtez, which is 2 of the 5 drigrixs.

Picture the fexyuk as what happens when you start with one drigrix and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 drigrixs, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 drigrixs the table is short enough to consult every time.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is glimmux @ (umbazt @ vashtez) for contrast. umbazt @ vashtez = vashtez (the table for @) glimmux @ vashtez = umbazt (the table for @) That gives umbazt, against qenvex above. Test solvex :: solvex. The muxqen of solvex is solvex, umbazt, glimmux, vashtez and qenvex, and solvex lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R11. It is not the case that: For every drigrix x, the duthgrix of x divides 5. It fails at x = glimmux, reach = 4, size = 5. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R13. It is not the case that: There is a drigrix whose fexyuk is the whole system. It fails at largest_span = 4, size = 5. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. R11. It is not the case that: For every drigrix x, the duthgrix of x divides 5. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimmux, reach = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R13. It is not the case that: There is a drigrix whose fexyuk is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is ponclo and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 35 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x @ x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x @ x = x then {x} is already closed under @. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the duthgrix is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x @ x, which is then x. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the zamkorr. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T5 and T6. Do not carry forward R11 and R13. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

documents.text:
The Bramorn system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth
the trouble. It has 4 zelbras, two operations, and one relation, and nothing else.

The zelbras are written tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi. The first operation is
written *. The second is written - and binds more tightly, so x * y - z means x * (y -
z). The relation is written <~; where it holds between two zelbras we say the left one
shadows the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written without
brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3 means x *
x * x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, the Bramorn signature, the Bramorn combination tables and closure under the first operation, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about zelbras covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for *. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | tarnnyr cloxil isktez iskmi ---------------------------------------------- tarnnyr | tarnnyr tarnnyr tarnnyr tarnnyr cloxil | tarnnyr cloxil isktez iskmi isktez | tarnnyr isktez tarnnyr isktez iskmi | tarnnyr iskmi isktez cloxil The table for -. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | tarnnyr cloxil isktez iskmi ---------------------------------------------- tarnnyr | tarnnyr cloxil isktez iskmi cloxil | cloxil isktez iskmi tarnnyr isktez | isktez iskmi tarnnyr cloxil iskmi | iskmi tarnnyr cloxil isktez Every pair standing in the <~ relation, grouped by left argument. tarnnyr <~ tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi cloxil <~ nothing isktez <~ nothing iskmi <~ nothing

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all zelbras x and y, x * y is again a zelbra. A2. Association of the first operation. For all zelbras x, y, z: (x * y) * z = x * (y * z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all zelbras x and y: x * y = y * x.

A useful mental split: some zelbras are inert under the operation and some are not. tarnnyr and cloxil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi commute with everything. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 4 zelbras the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Bramorn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. R3 rests on S2 (the Bramorn combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is cloxil * isktez - tarnnyr, reduced without skipping anything. isktez - tarnnyr = isktez (the table for -) cloxil * isktez = isktez (the table for *) The expression comes to isktez. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take isktez * (tarnnyr * cloxil). tarnnyr * cloxil = tarnnyr (the table for *) isktez * tarnnyr = tarnnyr (the table for *) The value is tarnnyr, not isktez. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does isktez <~ iskmi hold? Read off what isktez stands over: nothing at all. iskmi is not among them, so it fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every zelbra x: x * x = x. It fails at x = isktez, value = tarnnyr. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all zelbras x, y, z: if x * y = x * z then y = z. It fails at x = tarnnyr, y = tarnnyr, z = cloxil. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (closure under the second operation) and A7 (association of the second operation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every zelbra x: x * x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = isktez, value = tarnnyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all zelbras x, y, z: if x * y = x * z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = tarnnyr, y = tarnnyr, z = cloxil, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The practical content of this chapter is a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. It is the part that shows up in use. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about zelbras covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a zelbra cloxil with cloxil * x = x * cloxil = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a zelbra tarnnyr with tarnnyr * x = x * tarnnyr = tarnnyr for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single zelbra and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Bramorn combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (isktez * cloxil) * (tarnnyr * iskmi) and work it out one step at a time. isktez * cloxil = isktez (the table for *) tarnnyr * iskmi = tarnnyr (the table for *) isktez * tarnnyr = tarnnyr (the table for *) So (isktez * cloxil) * (tarnnyr * iskmi) is tarnnyr. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take cloxil * (tarnnyr * isktez). tarnnyr * isktez = tarnnyr (the table for *) cloxil * tarnnyr = tarnnyr (the table for *) The value is tarnnyr. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does cloxil <~ iskmi hold? Read off what cloxil stands over: nothing at all. iskmi is not among them, so it fails.
R1. Some zelbra x admits no zelbra y for which x * y and y * x both land on a neutral object. It fails at x = tarnnyr. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside S2 (the Bramorn combination tables). What is built on it later: D5 (the umblorn) and T1 (the umblorn is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some zelbra x admits no zelbra y for which x * y and y * x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = tarnnyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R1. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through antisymmetry of the relation, transitivity of the relation and agreement of the relation with the first operation. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about zelbras covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

documents.text: These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A10. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all zelbras x and y: if x <~ y and y <~ x then x = y. A11. Transitivity of the relation. For all zelbras x, y, z: if x <~ y and y <~ z then x <~ z. A12. Agreement of the relation with the first operation. For all zelbras x, y, z: if x <~ y then (z * x) <~ (z * y) and (x * z) <~ (y * z). D4. The xilquil of a zelbra. The xilquil of a zelbra x is the collection of zelbras y for which x <~ y holds. Worked out for each zelbra: tarnnyr to tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi; cloxil to nothing; isktez to nothing; iskmi to nothing.

documents.text: The relation is easiest to see as a height. Each zelbra casts a xilquil over what it shadows, and the sizes of those shadows here are 0 and 4. documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A6. Closure under the second operation. For all zelbras x and y, x - y is again a zelbra. A7. Association of the second operation. For all zelbras x, y, z: (x - y) - z = x - (y - z). A8. Commutation of the second operation. For all zelbras x and y: x - y = y - x. A9. A neutral object for the second operation. There is a zelbra tarnnyr with tarnnyr - x = x for every x.

documents.text: Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers vashgrix zelbras, zelbras that xilgrix and the umblorn, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about zelbras covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D1. Vashgrix zelbras. A zelbra x is called vashgrix when x * x = x. In this system that picks out tarnnyr and cloxil, which is 2 of the 4 zelbras. D2. Zelbras that xilgrix. Two zelbras x and y are said to xilgrix when x * y = y * x. D5. The umblorn. The zelbra cloxil is called the umblorn of the system. It is the unique zelbra that leaves every zelbra unchanged under *. Here that is cloxil.

Two questions sort the zelbras quickly. Does combining a zelbra with itself change it? For tarnnyr and cloxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single zelbra and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 4 zelbras the table is short enough to consult every time.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Here is isktez * cloxil - tarnnyr, reduced without skipping anything. cloxil - tarnnyr = cloxil (the table for -) isktez * cloxil = isktez (the table for *) So isktez * cloxil - tarnnyr is isktez. A companion case, cloxil * (tarnnyr * isktez), to show what the brackets are doing. tarnnyr * isktez = tarnnyr (the table for *) cloxil * tarnnyr = tarnnyr (the table for *) The value is tarnnyr, not isktez. Test tarnnyr <~ tarnnyr. The xilquil of tarnnyr is tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi, and tarnnyr lies inside it, so the relation holds.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of zelbras that come back unchanged from themselves: tarnnyr and cloxil. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

Read alongside A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). What is built on it later: D6 (the jenzam), D7 (the soltu), D10 (vintyuk zelbras) and T1 (the umblorn is the only one of its kind).
No proofs are needed here. Everything asserted is a definition or a table entry.

documents.text: D13. Espaclo pairs. Two distinct zelbras x and y form a espaclo pair when x <~ y and y <~ x both hold, that is, when each lies in the xilquil of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Gelmorn collections. A collection S of zelbras is gelmorn when x * y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A jenpyr. A zelbra f is a jenpyr when f <~ y holds for every zelbra y, that is, when the xilquil of f is the whole system. Running the definition over every zelbra leaves tarnnyr.

documents.text: Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet vintyuk zelbras, the jenzam and the soltu early, whether or not they go looking. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 2 and 5 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 4 zelbras that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D10. Vintyuk zelbras. A zelbra x is vintyuk when x * x equals the umblorn. In this system that picks out cloxil and iskmi, which is 2 of the 4 zelbras. D6. The jenzam. The jenzam of the system is the collection of zelbras that xilgrix with every zelbra. Running the definition over every zelbra leaves tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi. D7. The soltu. The soltu is the collection of all vashgrix zelbras. In this system that picks out tarnnyr and cloxil, which is 2 of the 4 zelbras.

A useful mental split: some zelbras are inert under the operation and some are not. tarnnyr and cloxil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single zelbra and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 4 zelbras the table is short enough to consult every time.

One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does tarnnyr <~ iskmi hold? Read off what tarnnyr stands over: tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi. iskmi is among them, so it holds.

R13. It is not the case that: e * x equals the umblorn for every zelbra x. The case that settles it: anchor = cloxil, x = tarnnyr, value = tarnnyr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The material this chapter borrows from: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (vashgrix zelbras), D2 (zelbras that xilgrix) and D5 (the umblorn). What is built on it later: T2 (the umblorn lies in the jenzam), T3 (the jenzam is gelmorn), T8 (the grixhurn of a jenzam zelbra stays in the jenzam) and T9 (the soltu is gelmorn).

R13. It is not the case that: e * x equals the umblorn for every zelbra x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = cloxil, x = tarnnyr, value = tarnnyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 4 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one zelbra e with e * x = x * e = x for every zelbra x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every zelbra unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e * f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e * f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 16 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
