documents.text: We turn to where every zelbra is vashgrix breaks down, every zelbra lies in the jenzam and the umblorn lies in the jenzam. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1, 5, 6 and 7 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over zelbras, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.
Nothing new is named here. The chapter is about consequences of definitions already given.

A useful mental split: some zelbras are inert under the operation and some are not. tarnnyr and cloxil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi commute with everything. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R10 rests on D7 (the soltu). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T14 rests on D6 (the jenzam). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T2 rests on D5 (the umblorn) and D6 (the jenzam). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T3 rests on D6 (the jenzam), D3 (gelmorn collections) and A2 (association of the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T9 rests on D7 (the soltu) and D3 (gelmorn collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate isktez * cloxil - iskmi. Each line below is one lookup in a table. cloxil - iskmi = tarnnyr (the table for -) isktez * tarnnyr = tarnnyr (the table for *) So isktez * cloxil - iskmi is tarnnyr. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is cloxil * (iskmi * isktez) for contrast. iskmi * isktez = isktez (the table for *) cloxil * isktez = isktez (the table for *) The value is isktez, not tarnnyr. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does tarnnyr <~ tarnnyr hold? Read off what tarnnyr stands over: tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi. tarnnyr is among them, so it holds.

R10. It is not the case that: x * x = x for every zelbra x. The case that settles it: x = isktez, value = tarnnyr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A2 (association of the first operation), D3 (gelmorn collections), D5 (the umblorn) and D6 (the jenzam). What is built on it later: T8 (the grixhurn of a jenzam zelbra stays in the jenzam) and T15 (the second operation keeps the jenzam intact).

R10. It is not the case that: x * x = x for every zelbra x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = isktez, value = tarnnyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T14. Every pair of zelbras xilgrixs. (1) [D6] The jenzam is defined by xilgrixing with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x * y = y * x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The umblorn xilgrixs with every zelbra. (1) [D5] Let e be the umblorn and x any zelbra. (2) [D5] Then e * x = x and x * e = x. (3) [D2] So e * x = x * e, which is what it means to xilgrix. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the jenzam. Checked over 4 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both xilgrix with every zelbra, then so does x * y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the jenzam and let z be any zelbra. (2) [A2] Then (x * y) * z = x * (y * z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each xilgrixs with everything. (4) [D3] So x * y xilgrixs with z, and the jenzam is gelmorn. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. If x and y are both vashgrix then so is x * y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be vashgrix. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x * y) * (x * y) returns x * y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Established here and safe to use: T14, T2, T3 and T9. Explicitly not available: R10. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Prerequisites are real here: chapters 6, 7, 8 and 9 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.
D11. The jenmux of a zelbra. The jenmux of a zelbra x is the number of zelbras in its grixhurn [x]. Worked out for each zelbra: tarnnyr to 1; cloxil to 1; isktez to 2; iskmi to 2.

Picture the grixhurn as what happens when you start with one zelbra and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 4 zelbras, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. Two questions sort the zelbras quickly. Does combining a zelbra with itself change it? For tarnnyr and cloxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi it does not. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 4 zelbras the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. T4 rests on D8 (the grixhurn of a zelbra) and D3 (gelmorn collections). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T8 rests on D8 (the grixhurn of a zelbra), D6 (the jenzam) and T3 (the jenzam is gelmorn). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (cloxil * tarnnyr) * (iskmi * isktez) and work it out one step at a time. cloxil * tarnnyr = tarnnyr (the table for *) iskmi * isktez = isktez (the table for *) tarnnyr * isktez = tarnnyr (the table for *) That leaves tarnnyr, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take tarnnyr * (iskmi * cloxil). iskmi * cloxil = iskmi (the table for *) tarnnyr * iskmi = tarnnyr (the table for *) The value is tarnnyr. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test cloxil <~ tarnnyr. The xilquil of cloxil is empty, and tarnnyr lies outside it, so the relation fails. A second case, this time a grixhurn. Start from cloxil. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is cloxil, so the jenmux of cloxil is 1.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: D3 (gelmorn collections), D6 (the jenzam), D8 (the grixhurn of a zelbra) and T3 (the jenzam is gelmorn). These results are used again in D12 (the grixtarn), T5 (the grixhurn is contained in every gelmorn collection), T6 (a zelbra is vashgrix exactly when its jenmux is one) and T7 (the jenmux divides the number of zelbras).

T4. For every zelbra x, the collection [x] is gelmorn. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under *. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 64 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x lies in the jenzam then every zelbra of [x] lies in the jenzam. (1) [T3] The jenzam is gelmorn. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest gelmorn collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the jenzam is one. Checked over 16 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

The results collected here were not found in this order. The grixtarn, where some zelbra reaches every other breaks down and the grixhurn is contained in every gelmorn collection came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. D12. The grixtarn. The grixtarn of the system is the collection of zelbras whose jenmux is largest. In this system that picks out isktez and iskmi, which is 2 of the 4 zelbras.

Test tarnnyr <~ isktez. The xilquil of tarnnyr is tarnnyr, cloxil, isktez and iskmi, and isktez lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R11. It is not the case that: There is a zelbra whose grixhurn is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 2, size = 4. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

R11. It is not the case that: There is a zelbra whose grixhurn is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 4, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 4 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is gelmorn and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 32 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x * x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x * x = x then {x} is already closed under *. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the jenmux is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x * x, which is then x. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every zelbra x, the jenmux of x divides 4. (1) [T4] [x] is a gelmorn collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the jenmux of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 4. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text:
This book is about wrenhobs. A wrenhob is not a number and not a set; it is one of
exactly 6 objects, and everything said here is said about how those 6 objects combine.

The wrenhobs are written iskglim, lornhob, tuisk, kaglim, xilfal and ovipyr. The first
operation is written ;. The second is written |= and binds more tightly, so x ; y |= z
means x ; (y |= z). The relation is written >-; where it holds between two wrenhobs we
say the left one dominates the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x ; x ; x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

The practical content of this chapter is the Espadri signature, the Espadri combination tables and closure under the first operation. It is the part that shows up in use. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over wrenhobs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

Two wrenhobs x and y are said to espavor when x ; y = y ; x. D5. The korrhurn. The wrenhob lornhob is called the korrhurn of the system. It is the unique wrenhob that leaves every wrenhob unchanged under ;. Here that is lornhob.

Two questions sort the wrenhobs quickly. Does combining a wrenhob with itself change it? For iskglim, lornhob, kaglim and xilfal it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? documents.text: D13. Hurnbra pairs. Two distinct wrenhobs x and y form a hurnbra pair when x >- y and y >- x both hold, that is, when each lies in the umbvex of the other. A collection S of wrenhobs is nyrazt when x ; y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A gelkeld. A wrenhob f is a gelkeld when f >- y holds for every wrenhob y, that is, when the umbvex of f is the whole system. Running the definition over every wrenhob leaves iskglim.

documents.text: So far the wrenhobs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up iskgrix wrenhobs, the vexumb and the hobsib. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 2 and 5 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about wrenhobs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

D10. Iskgrix wrenhobs. A wrenhob x is iskgrix when x ; x equals the korrhurn. Running the definition over every wrenhob leaves lornhob and ovipyr. D6. The vexumb. The vexumb of the system is the collection of wrenhobs that espavor with every wrenhob. Running the definition over every wrenhob leaves iskglim, lornhob, tuisk, kaglim, xilfal and ovipyr. D7. The hobsib. The hobsib is the collection of all sibumb wrenhobs. Running the definition over every wrenhob leaves iskglim, lornhob, kaglim and xilfal.

A useful mental split: some wrenhobs are inert under the operation and some are not. iskglim, lornhob, kaglim and xilfal come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and iskglim, lornhob, tuisk, kaglim, xilfal and ovipyr commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single wrenhob and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R12 rests on D5 (the korrhurn). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T1 rests on D5 (the korrhurn) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Move the brackets and the work changes. Take tuisk ; (lornhob ; iskglim). lornhob ; iskglim = iskglim (the table for ;) tuisk ; iskglim = iskglim (the table for ;) The value is iskglim. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does lornhob >- iskglim hold? Read off what lornhob stands over: lornhob, tuisk, kaglim, xilfal and ovipyr. iskglim is not among them, so it fails.

(2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one wrenhob e with e ; x = x ; e = x for every wrenhob x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every wrenhob unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e ; f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e ; f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 36 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

(3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 156 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x ; x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x ; x = x then {x} is already closed under ;. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the glimlorn is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x ; x, which is then x. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every wrenhob x, the glimlorn of x divides 6. (1) [T4] [x] is a nyrazt collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the glimlorn of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 6. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text:
This book is about wrenclos. A wrenclo is not a number and not a set; it is one of
exactly 4 objects, and everything said here is said about how those 4 objects combine.

The wrenclos are written glimfex, bratu, vorkeld and falzam. The first operation is
written #. The relation is written <~; where it holds between two wrenclos we say the
left one covers the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written
without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3
means x # x # x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through the Qenshen signature, the Qenshen combination tables and closure under the first operation. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over wrenclos, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for #. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | glimfex bratu vorkeld falzam ---------------------------------------------- glimfex | glimfex glimfex glimfex glimfex bratu | glimfex bratu vorkeld falzam vorkeld | glimfex vorkeld glimfex vorkeld falzam | glimfex falzam vorkeld bratu Every pair standing in the <~ relation, grouped by left argument. glimfex <~ glimfex bratu <~ glimfex, bratu, vorkeld and falzam vorkeld <~ glimfex falzam <~ glimfex and vorkeld

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all wrenclos x and y, x # y is again a wrenclo. A2. Association of the first operation. For all wrenclos x, y, z: (x # y) # z = x # (y # z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all wrenclos x and y: x # y = y # x.

A useful mental split: some wrenclos are inert under the operation and some are not. glimfex and bratu come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and glimfex, bratu, vorkeld and falzam commute with everything. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Qenshen combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. R3 rests on S2 (the Qenshen combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (bratu # vorkeld) # glimfex and work it out one step at a time. bratu # vorkeld = vorkeld (the table for #) vorkeld # glimfex = glimfex (the table for #) So (bratu # vorkeld) # glimfex is glimfex. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is vorkeld # (glimfex # bratu) for contrast. glimfex # bratu = glimfex (the table for #) vorkeld # glimfex = glimfex (the table for #) The value is glimfex. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does falzam <~ falzam hold? Read off what falzam stands over: glimfex and vorkeld. falzam is not among them, so it fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every wrenclo x: x # x = x. The case that settles it: x = vorkeld, value = glimfex. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all wrenclos x, y, z: if x # y = x # z then y = z. It fails at x = glimfex, y = glimfex, z = bratu. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (antisymmetry of the relation) and A7 (transitivity of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every wrenclo x: x # x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = vorkeld, value = glimfex, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all wrenclos x, y, z: if x # y = x # z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimfex, y = glimfex, z = bratu, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

We turn to a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 4 wrenclos that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a wrenclo bratu with bratu # x = x # bratu = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a wrenclo glimfex with glimfex # x = x # glimfex = glimfex for every x.

The neutral wrenclo bratu is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Qenshen combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (vorkeld # glimfex) # (bratu # falzam). Each line below is one lookup in a table. vorkeld # glimfex = glimfex (the table for #) bratu # falzam = falzam (the table for #) glimfex # falzam = glimfex (the table for #) The expression comes to glimfex. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take glimfex # (bratu # vorkeld). bratu # vorkeld = vorkeld (the table for #) glimfex # vorkeld = glimfex (the table for #) That gives glimfex, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test falzam <~ glimfex. The espaazt of falzam is glimfex and vorkeld, and glimfex lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R1. Some wrenclo x admits no wrenclo y for which x # y and y # x both land on a neutral object. The case that settles it: x = glimfex. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside S2 (the Qenshen combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the opalglim) and T1 (the opalglim is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some wrenclo x admits no wrenclo y for which x # y and y # x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimfex, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is antisymmetry of the relation, transitivity of the relation and the espaazt of a wrenclo. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about wrenclos covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

For all wrenclos x and y: if x <~ y and y <~ x then x = y. A7. Transitivity of the relation. For all wrenclos x, y, z: if x <~ y and y <~ z then x <~ z. D4. The espaazt of a wrenclo. The espaazt of a wrenclo x is the collection of wrenclos y for which x <~ y holds. Worked out for each wrenclo: glimfex to glimfex; bratu to glimfex, bratu, vorkeld and falzam; vorkeld to glimfex; falzam to glimfex and vorkeld.

documents.text: The results collected here were not found in this order. Mornxil wrenclos, wrenclos that mornthra and the opalglim came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. Nothing here stands on its own. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 4 wrenclos that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

D1. Mornxil wrenclos. A wrenclo x is called mornxil when x # x = x. In this system that picks out glimfex and bratu, which is 2 of the 4 wrenclos. D2. Wrenclos that mornthra. Two wrenclos x and y are said to mornthra when x # y = y # x. D5. The opalglim. The wrenclo bratu is called the opalglim of the system. It is the unique wrenclo that leaves every wrenclo unchanged under #. Here that is bratu.

A useful mental split: some wrenclos are inert under the operation and some are not. glimfex and bratu come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and glimfex, bratu, vorkeld and falzam commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single wrenclo and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.
Nothing is derived in this chapter. It lays down material that later chapters draw on.

Take (bratu # glimfex) # (vorkeld # falzam) and work it out one step at a time. bratu # glimfex = glimfex (the table for #) vorkeld # falzam = vorkeld (the table for #) glimfex # vorkeld = glimfex (the table for #) That leaves glimfex, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take glimfex # (vorkeld # bratu). vorkeld # bratu = vorkeld (the table for #) glimfex # vorkeld = glimfex (the table for #) The value is glimfex. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test falzam <~ glimfex. The espaazt of falzam is glimfex and vorkeld, and glimfex lies inside it, so the relation holds.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of wrenclos that come back unchanged from themselves: glimfex and bratu. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. documents.text: So far the wrenclos have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up faltez wrenclos, the fexka and the oviumb. D10. Faltez wrenclos. A wrenclo x is faltez when x # x equals the opalglim. Running the definition over every wrenclo leaves bratu and falzam. D6. The fexka. The fexka of the system is the collection of wrenclos that mornthra with every wrenclo. In this system that picks out glimfex, bratu, vorkeld and falzam, that is, all of them. D7. The oviumb. The oviumb is the collection of all mornxil wrenclos. Running the definition over every wrenclo leaves glimfex and bratu.

Two questions sort the wrenclos quickly. Does combining a wrenclo with itself change it? For glimfex and bratu it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For glimfex, bratu, vorkeld and falzam it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. R8. It is not the case that: There is a wrenclo whose xillorn is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 4, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 32 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. documents.text:
What follows is a complete account of the Tarnsib system. It is complete in a strong
sense: the system has 3 jenxils and finitely many facts, and every one of those facts is
settled here by inspection rather than left to argument.

The jenxils are written reldvint, wrenmux and zellum. The first operation is written %.
The relation is written =<; where it holds between two jenxils we say the left one
shadows the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written without
brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3 means x %
x % x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

We turn to the Tarnsib signature, the Tarnsib combination tables and closure under the first operation. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over jenxils, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for %. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | reldvint wrenmux zellum ----------------------------------------- reldvint | reldvint reldvint reldvint wrenmux | reldvint wrenmux zellum zellum | reldvint zellum wrenmux Every pair standing in the =< relation, grouped by left argument. reldvint =< reldvint, wrenmux and zellum wrenmux =< wrenmux and zellum zellum =< zellum

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all jenxils x and y, x % y is again a jenxil. A2. Association of the first operation. For all jenxils x, y, z: (x % y) % z = x % (y % z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all jenxils x and y: x % y = y % x.

Two questions sort the jenxils quickly. Does combining a jenxil with itself change it? For reldvint and wrenmux it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For reldvint, wrenmux and zellum it does not. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 3 jenxils the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Tarnsib combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Tarnsib combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (reldvint % wrenmux) % zellum, reduced without skipping anything. reldvint % wrenmux = reldvint (the table for %) reldvint % zellum = reldvint (the table for %) That leaves reldvint, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, wrenmux % (zellum % reldvint), to show what the brackets are doing. zellum % reldvint = reldvint (the table for %) wrenmux % reldvint = reldvint (the table for %) That gives reldvint, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test zellum =< reldvint. The tezyuk of zellum is zellum, and reldvint lies outside it, so the relation fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every jenxil x: x % x = x. It fails at x = zellum, value = wrenmux. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all jenxils x, y, z: if x % y = x % z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = reldvint, y = reldvint, z = wrenmux. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (reflexivity of the relation) and A7 (antisymmetry of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every jenxil x: x % x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = zellum, value = wrenmux, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all jenxils x, y, z: if x % y = x % z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = reldvint, y = reldvint, z = wrenmux, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation, and each claim can be checked by hand. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 3 jenxils that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a jenxil wrenmux with wrenmux % x = x % wrenmux = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a jenxil reldvint with reldvint % x = x % reldvint = reldvint for every x.

The neutral jenxil wrenmux is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 3 jenxils the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R1 rests on S2 (the Tarnsib combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take (reldvint % reldvint) % (reldvint % wrenmux) and work it out one step at a time. reldvint % reldvint = reldvint (the table for %) reldvint % wrenmux = reldvint (the table for %) reldvint % reldvint = reldvint (the table for %) That leaves reldvint, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take reldvint % (reldvint % reldvint). reldvint % reldvint = reldvint (the table for %) reldvint % reldvint = reldvint (the table for %) That gives reldvint, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test reldvint =< reldvint. The tezyuk of reldvint is reldvint, wrenmux and zellum, and reldvint lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R1. Some jenxil x admits no jenxil y for which x % y and y % x both land on a neutral object. The case that settles it: x = reldvint. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside S2 (the Tarnsib combination tables). What is built on it later: D5 (the iskkeld) and T1 (the iskkeld is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some jenxil x admits no jenxil y for which x % y and y % x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = reldvint, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, reflexivity of the relation, antisymmetry of the relation and transitivity of the relation, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. documents.text: These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A6. Reflexivity of the relation. For every jenxil x: x =< x. A7. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all jenxils x and y: if x =< y and y =< x then x = y. A8. Transitivity of the relation. For all jenxils x, y, z: if x =< y and y =< z then x =< z. A9. Comparability of every pair. For all jenxils x and y, at least one of x =< y and y =< x holds. D4. The tezyuk of a jenxil. The tezyuk of a jenxil x is the collection of jenxils y for which x =< y holds. Worked out for each jenxil: reldvint to reldvint, wrenmux and zellum; wrenmux to wrenmux and zellum; zellum to zellum.

documents.text: The practical content of this chapter is lornthra jenxils, jenxils that keldwren and the iskkeld. It is the part that shows up in use. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1 and 2 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about jenxils covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D1. Lornthra jenxils. A jenxil x is called lornthra when x % x = x. In this system that picks out reldvint and wrenmux, which is 2 of the 3 jenxils. D2. Jenxils that keldwren. Two jenxils x and y are said to keldwren when x % y = y % x. D5. The iskkeld. The jenxil wrenmux is called the iskkeld of the system. It is the unique jenxil that leaves every jenxil unchanged under %. Here that is wrenmux.

A useful mental split: some jenxils are inert under the operation and some are not. reldvint and wrenmux come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and reldvint, wrenmux and zellum commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single jenxil and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 3 jenxils the table is short enough to consult every time.
Nothing is derived in this chapter. It lays down material that later chapters draw on.

Test wrenmux =< wrenmux. The tezyuk of wrenmux is wrenmux and zellum, and wrenmux lies inside it, so the relation holds.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

documents.text: D13. Brapyr pairs. Two distinct jenxils x and y form a brapyr pair when x =< y and y =< x both hold, that is, when each lies in the tezyuk of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Aztquil collections. A collection S of jenxils is aztquil when x % y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A keldrast. A jenxil f is a keldrast when f =< y holds for every jenxil y, that is, when the tezyuk of f is the whole system. In this system that picks out reldvint, which is 1 of the 3 jenxils.

The stain here reaches 1 and 2 jenxils depending on where it started. The relation is easiest to see as a height. Each jenxil casts a tezyuk over what it shadows, and the sizes of those shadows here are 1, 2 and 3. No two are the same size, so the objects line up in a single file. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 3, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 3 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is aztquil and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 15 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x % x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x % x = x then {x} is already closed under %. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the mornlum is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x % x, which is then x. Checked over 3 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

The results now available are T5 and T6, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Do not carry forward R5 and R7. This book is about grixbras. A grixbra is not a number and not a set; it is one of
exactly 5 objects, and everything said here is said about how those 5 objects combine.

The grixbras are written mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra. The first
operation is written @. The second is written ! and binds more tightly, so x @ y ! z
means x @ (y ! z). The relation is written %%; where it holds between two grixbras we
say the left one shadows the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x @ x @ x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers the Vexumb signature, the Vexumb combination tables and closure under the first operation, and each claim can be checked by hand. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 5 grixbras that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for @. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | mika fexnyr hobglim umbtarn mornthra ------------------------------------------------------------- mika | mika mika mika mika mika fexnyr | mika fexnyr hobglim umbtarn mornthra hobglim | mika hobglim mornthra fexnyr umbtarn umbtarn | mika umbtarn fexnyr mornthra hobglim mornthra | mika mornthra umbtarn hobglim fexnyr The table for !. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | mika fexnyr hobglim umbtarn mornthra ------------------------------------------------------------- mika | mika fexnyr hobglim umbtarn mornthra fexnyr | fexnyr hobglim umbtarn mornthra mika hobglim | hobglim umbtarn mornthra mika fexnyr umbtarn | umbtarn mornthra mika fexnyr hobglim mornthra | mornthra mika fexnyr hobglim umbtarn Every pair standing in the %% relation, grouped by left argument. mika %% mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra fexnyr %% mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra hobglim %% mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra umbtarn %% mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra mornthra %% mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all grixbras x and y, x @ y is again a grixbra. A2. Association of the first operation. For all grixbras x, y, z: (x @ y) @ z = x @ (y @ z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all grixbras x and y: x @ y = y @ x.

A useful mental split: some grixbras are inert under the operation and some are not. mika and fexnyr come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra commute with everything. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 grixbras the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Vexumb combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Vexumb combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take mika @ mornthra ! umbtarn and work it out one step at a time. mornthra ! umbtarn = hobglim (the table for !) mika @ hobglim = mika (the table for @) The expression comes to mika. A companion case, mornthra @ (umbtarn @ mika), to show what the brackets are doing. umbtarn @ mika = mika (the table for @) mornthra @ mika = mika (the table for @) That gives mika, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test mika %% mika. The aztnak of mika is mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra, and mika lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R2. It is not the case that: For every grixbra x: x @ x = x. The case that settles it: x = hobglim, value = mornthra. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all grixbras x, y, z: if x @ y = x @ z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = mika, y = mika, z = fexnyr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (closure under the second operation) and A7 (association of the second operation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every grixbra x: x @ x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = hobglim, value = mornthra, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. (1) [S2] Take the case x = mika, y = mika, z = fexnyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R2 and R3. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a grixbra fexnyr with fexnyr @ x = x @ fexnyr = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a grixbra mika with mika @ x = x @ mika = mika for every x.

The neutral grixbra fexnyr is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 grixbras the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R1 rests on S2 (the Vexumb combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (mika @ hobglim) @ (mornthra @ fexnyr) and work it out one step at a time. mika @ hobglim = mika (the table for @) mornthra @ fexnyr = mornthra (the table for @) mika @ mornthra = mika (the table for @) So (mika @ hobglim) @ (mornthra @ fexnyr) is mika. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is hobglim @ (mornthra @ mika) for contrast. mornthra @ mika = mika (the table for @) hobglim @ mika = mika (the table for @) That gives mika, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does fexnyr %% umbtarn hold? Read off what fexnyr stands over: mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra. umbtarn is among them, so it holds.
R1. Some grixbra x admits no grixbra y for which x @ y and y @ x both land on a neutral object. It fails at x = mika. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

documents.text: The present chapter develops vorzam grixbras, grixbras that falhob and the keldvint. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over grixbras, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

D1. Vorzam grixbras. A grixbra x is called vorzam when x @ x = x. In this system that picks out mika and fexnyr, which is 2 of the 5 grixbras. D2. Grixbras that falhob. Two grixbras x and y are said to falhob when x @ y = y @ x. D5. The keldvint. The grixbra fexnyr is called the keldvint of the system. It is the unique grixbra that leaves every grixbra unchanged under @. Here that is fexnyr.

Two questions sort the grixbras quickly. Does combining a grixbra with itself change it? For mika and fexnyr it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For mika, fexnyr, hobglim, umbtarn and mornthra it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single grixbra and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is drithra and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 35 cases: every sealed collection against every object. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the tuvint is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x @ x, which is then x. Checked over 5 cases: every object. documents.text:
This book is about thrafexs. A thrafex is not a number and not a set; it is one of
exactly 3 objects, and everything said here is said about how those 3 objects combine.

The thrafexs are written tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel. The first operation is written =|.
The second is written ~ and binds more tightly, so x =| y ~ z means x =| (y ~ z). The
relation is written =<; where it holds between two thrafexs we say the left one supports
the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written without brackets, and
brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3 means x =| x =| x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, the Keldmux signature, the Keldmux combination tables and closure under the first operation, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over thrafexs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for =|. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | tuespa qenmorn hobzel ------------------------------------- tuespa | tuespa tuespa tuespa qenmorn | tuespa qenmorn hobzel hobzel | tuespa hobzel qenmorn The table for ~. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | tuespa qenmorn hobzel ------------------------------------- tuespa | tuespa tuespa tuespa qenmorn | tuespa qenmorn qenmorn hobzel | tuespa qenmorn hobzel Every pair standing in the =< relation, grouped by left argument. tuespa =< tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel qenmorn =< tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel hobzel =< tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all thrafexs x and y, x =| y is again a thrafex. A2. Association of the first operation. For all thrafexs x, y, z: (x =| y) =| z = x =| (y =| z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all thrafexs x and y: x =| y = y =| x.

Two questions sort the thrafexs quickly. Does combining a thrafex with itself change it? For tuespa and qenmorn it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel it does not. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Keldmux combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Keldmux combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is tuespa =| qenmorn ~ hobzel, reduced without skipping anything. qenmorn ~ hobzel = qenmorn (the table for ~) tuespa =| qenmorn = tuespa (the table for =|) The expression comes to tuespa. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is qenmorn =| (hobzel =| tuespa) for contrast. hobzel =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) qenmorn =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) That gives tuespa, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test hobzel =< tuespa. The qenglim of hobzel is tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel, and tuespa lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R2. It is not the case that: For every thrafex x: x =| x = x. It fails at x = hobzel, value = qenmorn. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all thrafexs x, y, z: if x =| y = x =| z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = tuespa, y = tuespa, z = qenmorn. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (closure under the second operation) and A7 (association of the second operation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every thrafex x: x =| x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = hobzel, value = qenmorn, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all thrafexs x, y, z: if x =| y = x =| z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = tuespa, y = tuespa, z = qenmorn, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The practical content of this chapter is a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. It is the part that shows up in use. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over thrafexs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a thrafex qenmorn with qenmorn =| x = x =| qenmorn = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a thrafex tuespa with tuespa =| x = x =| tuespa = tuespa for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single thrafex and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 3 thrafexs the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Keldmux combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate (tuespa =| hobzel) =| (hobzel =| qenmorn). Each line below is one lookup in a table. tuespa =| hobzel = tuespa (the table for =|) hobzel =| qenmorn = hobzel (the table for =|) tuespa =| hobzel = tuespa (the table for =|) That leaves tuespa, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, hobzel =| (hobzel =| tuespa), to show what the brackets are doing. hobzel =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) hobzel =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) That gives tuespa, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does qenmorn =< qenmorn hold? Read off what qenmorn stands over: tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel. qenmorn is among them, so it holds.

R1. Some thrafex x admits no thrafex y for which x =| y and y =| x both land on a neutral object. The case that settles it: x = tuespa. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

Read alongside S2 (the Keldmux combination tables). What is built on it later: D5 (the lornespa), T1 (the lornespa is the only one of its kind) and T14 (the absorbing object survives the second operation).

R1. Some thrafex x admits no thrafex y for which x =| y and y =| x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = tuespa, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

So far the thrafexs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up reflexivity of the relation, transitivity of the relation and comparability of every pair. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 3 thrafexs that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

documents.text: Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is solmi thrafexs, thrafexs that driduth and the lornespa. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1 and 2 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about thrafexs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D1. Solmi thrafexs. A thrafex x is called solmi when x =| x = x. In this system that picks out tuespa and qenmorn, which is 2 of the 3 thrafexs. D2. Thrafexs that driduth. Two thrafexs x and y are said to driduth when x =| y = y =| x. D5. The lornespa. The thrafex qenmorn is called the lornespa of the system. It is the unique thrafex that leaves every thrafex unchanged under =|. Here that is qenmorn.

A useful mental split: some thrafexs are inert under the operation and some are not. tuespa and qenmorn come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel commute with everything. The neutral thrafex qenmorn is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Test hobzel =< qenmorn. The qenglim of hobzel is tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel, and qenmorn lies inside it, so the relation holds.

documents.text: D13. Qengrix pairs. Two distinct thrafexs x and y form a qengrix pair when x =< y and y =< x both hold, that is, when each lies in the qenglim of the other. Running the definition over every thrafex leaves tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel. D3. Duthvash collections. A collection S of thrafexs is duthvash when x =| y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A thraazt. A thrafex f is a thraazt when f =< y holds for every thrafex y, that is, when the qenglim of f is the whole system. Running the definition over every thrafex leaves tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel.

documents.text: T11. If x =< y then (x =| z) =< (y =| z) for every thrafex z. (1) [D4] Let y lie in the qenglim of x. (2) [A15] Compatibility applies the operation to both sides at once. (1) [D4] Symmetry would mean y lies in the qenglim of x exactly when x lies in that of y. (2) The listed pairs settle it directly. Checked over 9 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. If y lies in the qenglim of x, then the qenglim of y is contained in the qenglim of x. (1) [D4] Let y satisfy x =< y and let z satisfy y =< z. (2) [A13] Transitivity gives x =< z. (3) [D4] So every member of the qenglim of y is a member of that of x. Checked over 27 cases: every ordered triple. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
