The right picture for yuklorn is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one thrafex in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1 and 2 thrafexs depending on where it started. A useful mental split: some thrafexs are inert under the operation and some are not. tuespa and qenmorn come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel commute with everything. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. T4 rests on D8 (the yuklorn of a thrafex) and D3 (duthvash collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D8 (the yuklorn of a thrafex), D6 (the tunak) and T3 (the tunak is duthvash). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (tuespa =| tuespa) =| (qenmorn =| qenmorn) and work it out one step at a time. tuespa =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) qenmorn =| qenmorn = qenmorn (the table for =|) tuespa =| qenmorn = tuespa (the table for =|) That leaves tuespa, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take tuespa =| (qenmorn =| tuespa). qenmorn =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) tuespa =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) The value is tuespa. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does qenmorn =< qenmorn hold? Read off what qenmorn stands over: tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel. qenmorn is among them, so it holds. A second case, this time a yuklorn. Start from qenmorn. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is qenmorn, so the reldbra of qenmorn is 1.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

Read alongside D3 (duthvash collections), D6 (the tunak), D8 (the yuklorn of a thrafex) and T3 (the tunak is duthvash). These results are used again in D12 (the ovifex), T5 (the yuklorn is contained in every duthvash collection), T6 (a thrafex is solmi exactly when its reldbra is one) and R6 (where the reldbra divides the number of thrafexs breaks down).

T4. For every thrafex x, the collection [x] is duthvash. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under =|. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 27 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the tunak then every thrafex of [x] lies in the tunak. (1) [T3] The tunak is duthvash. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest duthvash collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the tunak is one. Checked over 9 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Carry forward the reldbra of a thrafex. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T4 and T7.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, the ovifex, where the reldbra divides the number of thrafexs breaks down and where some thrafex reaches every other breaks down, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 5, 9 and 10 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over thrafexs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.
D12. The ovifex. The ovifex of the system is the collection of thrafexs whose reldbra is largest. In this system that picks out hobzel, which is 1 of the 3 thrafexs.

The right picture for yuklorn is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one thrafex in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1 and 2 thrafexs depending on where it started. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R6 rests on D11 (the reldbra of a thrafex) and T4 (the yuklorn of a thrafex is duthvash). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R8 rests on D8 (the yuklorn of a thrafex) and D11 (the reldbra of a thrafex). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T5 rests on D8 (the yuklorn of a thrafex) and T4 (the yuklorn of a thrafex is duthvash). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T6 rests on D1 (solmi thrafexs), D11 (the reldbra of a thrafex) and T4 (the yuklorn of a thrafex is duthvash). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take hobzel =| hobzel ~ tuespa and work it out one step at a time. hobzel ~ tuespa = tuespa (the table for ~) hobzel =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) That leaves tuespa, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is hobzel =| (tuespa =| hobzel) for contrast. tuespa =| hobzel = tuespa (the table for =|) hobzel =| tuespa = tuespa (the table for =|) That gives tuespa, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test hobzel =< qenmorn. The qenglim of hobzel is tuespa, qenmorn and hobzel, and qenmorn lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R6. It is not the case that: For every thrafex x, the reldbra of x divides 3. The case that settles it: x = hobzel, reach = 2, size = 3. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R8. It is not the case that: There is a thrafex whose yuklorn is the whole system. It fails at largest_span = 2, size = 3. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
The material this chapter borrows from: D1 (solmi thrafexs), D11 (the reldbra of a thrafex), D8 (the yuklorn of a thrafex) and T4 (the yuklorn of a thrafex is duthvash).

R6. It is not the case that: For every thrafex x, the reldbra of x divides 3. (1) [S2] Take the case x = hobzel, reach = 2, size = 3, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 3 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R8. It is not the case that: There is a thrafex whose yuklorn is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 3, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 3 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is duthvash and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 15 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x =| x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x =| x = x then {x} is already closed under =|. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the reldbra is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x =| x, which is then x. Checked over 3 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the ovifex. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T5 and T6. Explicitly not available: R6 and R8. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The practical content of this chapter is the second operation keeps the tunak intact. It is the part that shows up in use. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 4, 7 and 9, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 3 thrafexs that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

documents.text:
What follows is a complete account of the Vashdri system. It is complete in a strong
sense: the system has 5 ovimorns and finitely many facts, and every one of those facts
is settled here by inspection rather than left to argument.

The ovimorns are written rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor. The first
operation is written :. The relation is written ::; where it holds between two ovimorns
we say the left one governs the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x : x : x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet the Vashdri signature, the Vashdri combination tables and closure under the first operation early, whether or not they go looking. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over ovimorns, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The table for :. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | rastmi bradri wrenkorr tezkeld muxvor ------------------------------------------------------------- rastmi | rastmi bradri wrenkorr tezkeld muxvor bradri | bradri wrenkorr tezkeld muxvor muxvor wrenkorr | wrenkorr tezkeld muxvor muxvor muxvor tezkeld | tezkeld muxvor muxvor muxvor muxvor muxvor | muxvor muxvor muxvor muxvor muxvor Every pair standing in the :: relation, grouped by left argument. rastmi :: rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor bradri :: rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor wrenkorr :: rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor tezkeld :: rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor muxvor :: rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all ovimorns x and y, x : y is again a ovimorn. A2. Association of the first operation. For all ovimorns x, y, z: (x : y) : z = x : (y : z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all ovimorns x and y: x : y = y : x.

Two questions sort the ovimorns quickly. Does combining a ovimorn with itself change it? For rastmi and muxvor it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor it does not. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 ovimorns the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Vashdri combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Vashdri combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate (rastmi : wrenkorr) : tezkeld. Each line below is one lookup in a table. rastmi : wrenkorr = wrenkorr (the table for :) wrenkorr : tezkeld = muxvor (the table for :) The expression comes to muxvor. A companion case, wrenkorr : (tezkeld : rastmi), to show what the brackets are doing. tezkeld : rastmi = tezkeld (the table for :) wrenkorr : tezkeld = muxvor (the table for :) That gives muxvor, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does wrenkorr :: rastmi hold? Read off what wrenkorr stands over: rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor. rastmi is among them, so it holds.

R2. It is not the case that: For every ovimorn x: x : x = x. The case that settles it: x = bradri, value = wrenkorr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all ovimorns x, y, z: if x : y = x : z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = bradri, y = tezkeld, z = muxvor. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (reflexivity of the relation) and A7 (transitivity of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every ovimorn x: x : x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = bradri, value = wrenkorr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all ovimorns x, y, z: if x : y = x : z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = bradri, y = tezkeld, z = muxvor, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R2 and R3. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over ovimorns, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a ovimorn rastmi with rastmi : x = x : rastmi = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a ovimorn muxvor with muxvor : x = x : muxvor = muxvor for every x.

The neutral ovimorn rastmi is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Vashdri combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate (bradri : muxvor) : (wrenkorr : rastmi). Each line below is one lookup in a table. bradri : muxvor = muxvor (the table for :) wrenkorr : rastmi = wrenkorr (the table for :) muxvor : wrenkorr = muxvor (the table for :) So (bradri : muxvor) : (wrenkorr : rastmi) is muxvor. A companion case, muxvor : (wrenkorr : bradri), to show what the brackets are doing. wrenkorr : bradri = tezkeld (the table for :) muxvor : tezkeld = muxvor (the table for :) That gives muxvor, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does bradri :: bradri hold? Read off what bradri stands over: rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor. bradri is among them, so it holds.
R1. Some ovimorn x admits no ovimorn y for which x : y and y : x both land on a neutral object. It fails at x = bradri. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside S2 (the Vashdri combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the pyrkeld) and T1 (the pyrkeld is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some ovimorn x admits no ovimorn y for which x : y and y : x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = bradri, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R1. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

We turn to reflexivity of the relation, transitivity of the relation and comparability of every pair. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about ovimorns covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

documents.text: These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A6. Reflexivity of the relation. For every ovimorn x: x :: x. A7. Transitivity of the relation. For all ovimorns x, y, z: if x :: y and y :: z then x :: z. A8. Comparability of every pair. For all ovimorns x and y, at least one of x :: y and y :: x holds. A9. Agreement of the relation with the first operation. For all ovimorns x, y, z: if x :: y then (z : x) :: (z : y) and (x : z) :: (y : z). D4. The yukhurn of a ovimorn. The yukhurn of a ovimorn x is the collection of ovimorns y for which x :: y holds. Worked out for each ovimorn: rastmi to rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor; bradri to rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor; wrenkorr to rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor; tezkeld to rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor; muxvor to rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor.

D10. Sibsol ovimorns. A ovimorn x is sibsol when x : x equals the pyrkeld. In this system that picks out rastmi, which is 1 of the 5 ovimorns. D6. The brareld. T4. For every ovimorn x, the collection [x] is vexjen. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under :. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 125 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the brareld then every ovimorn of [x] lies in the brareld. (1) [T3] The brareld is vexjen. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest vexjen collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the brareld is one. Checked over 25 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
New vocabulary from this chapter: the rastopal of a ovimorn. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T4 and T7.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is the hurnnak, where the rastopal divides the number of ovimorns breaks down and where some ovimorn reaches every other breaks down. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 4, 7 and 8 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 5 ovimorns that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
D12. The hurnnak. The hurnnak of the system is the collection of ovimorns whose rastopal is largest. In this system that picks out bradri, which is 1 of the 5 ovimorns.

Picture the espapyr as what happens when you start with one ovimorn and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 ovimorns, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R5 rests on D11 (the rastopal of a ovimorn) and T4 (the espapyr of a ovimorn is vexjen). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R7 rests on D8 (the espapyr of a ovimorn) and D11 (the rastopal of a ovimorn). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T5 rests on D8 (the espapyr of a ovimorn) and T4 (the espapyr of a ovimorn is vexjen). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T6 rests on D1 (hurnxil ovimorns), D11 (the rastopal of a ovimorn) and T4 (the espapyr of a ovimorn is vexjen). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (tezkeld : rastmi) : muxvor, reduced without skipping anything. tezkeld : rastmi = tezkeld (the table for :) tezkeld : muxvor = muxvor (the table for :) The expression comes to muxvor. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take rastmi : (muxvor : tezkeld). muxvor : tezkeld = muxvor (the table for :) rastmi : muxvor = muxvor (the table for :) The value is muxvor. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test bradri :: wrenkorr. The yukhurn of bradri is rastmi, bradri, wrenkorr, tezkeld and muxvor, and wrenkorr lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R5. It is not the case that: For every ovimorn x, the rastopal of x divides 5. It fails at x = bradri, reach = 4, size = 5. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R7. It is not the case that: There is a ovimorn whose espapyr is the whole system. It fails at largest_span = 4, size = 5. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
The material this chapter borrows from: D1 (hurnxil ovimorns), D11 (the rastopal of a ovimorn), D8 (the espapyr of a ovimorn) and T4 (the espapyr of a ovimorn is vexjen).

R5. It is not the case that: For every ovimorn x, the rastopal of x divides 5. (1) [S2] Take the case x = bradri, reach = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R7. It is not the case that: There is a ovimorn whose espapyr is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is vexjen and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 55 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x : x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x : x = x then {x} is already closed under :. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the rastopal is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x : x, which is then x. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the hurnnak. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. The results now available are T5 and T6, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Explicitly not available: R5 and R7. documents.text:
The Mornyuk system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth
the trouble. It has 4 reldjens, two operations, and one relation, and nothing else.

The reldjens are written nakopal, kagel, korrreld and iskbra. The first operation is
written <>. The second is written # and binds more tightly, so x <> y # z means x <> (y
# z). The relation is written ::; where it holds between two reldjens we say the left
one yields to the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written without
brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3 means x
<> x <> x. A trailing mark reverses: x' is the reldjen that combines with x to give the
neutral one.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through the Mornyuk signature, the Mornyuk combination tables and closure under the first operation. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about reldjens covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The table for <>. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | nakopal kagel korrreld iskbra --------------------------------------------------- nakopal | nakopal kagel korrreld iskbra kagel | kagel korrreld iskbra nakopal korrreld | korrreld iskbra nakopal kagel iskbra | iskbra nakopal kagel korrreld The table for #. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | nakopal kagel korrreld iskbra --------------------------------------------------- nakopal | nakopal kagel korrreld iskbra kagel | kagel kagel korrreld iskbra korrreld | korrreld korrreld korrreld iskbra iskbra | iskbra iskbra iskbra iskbra Every pair standing in the :: relation, grouped by left argument. nakopal :: nakopal, kagel, korrreld and iskbra kagel :: kagel, korrreld and iskbra korrreld :: korrreld and iskbra iskbra :: iskbra

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all reldjens x and y, x <> y is again a reldjen. A2. Association of the first operation. For all reldjens x, y, z: (x <> y) <> z = x <> (y <> z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all reldjens x and y: x <> y = y <> x. A6. Cancellation in the first operation. For all reldjens x, y, z: if x <> y = x <> z then y = z.

A useful mental split: some reldjens are inert under the operation and some are not. nakopal come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and nakopal, kagel, korrreld and iskbra commute with everything. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R1 rests on S2 (the Mornyuk combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate kagel <> iskbra # korrreld. Each line below is one lookup in a table. iskbra # korrreld = iskbra (the table for #) kagel <> iskbra = nakopal (the table for <>) That leaves nakopal, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take iskbra <> (korrreld <> kagel). korrreld <> kagel = iskbra (the table for <>) iskbra <> iskbra = korrreld (the table for <>) That gives korrreld, against nakopal above. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does kagel :: nakopal hold? Read off what kagel stands over: kagel, korrreld and iskbra. nakopal is not among them, so it fails.
R1. It is not the case that: For every reldjen x: x <> x = x. It fails at x = kagel, value = korrreld. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (reversal under the first operation), A7 (closure under the second operation) and A8 (association of the second operation).

R1. It is not the case that: For every reldjen x: x <> x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = kagel, value = korrreld, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R1. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

We turn to a neutral object for the first operation, reversal under the first operation and the system does not have an absorbing object for the first operation. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about reldjens covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a reldjen nakopal with nakopal <> x = x <> nakopal = x for every x. A5. Reversal under the first operation. For every reldjen x there is a reldjen y with x <> y = y <> x = nakopal.

The neutral reldjen nakopal is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Mornyuk combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (korrreld <> iskbra) <> (kagel <> nakopal) and work it out one step at a time. korrreld <> iskbra = kagel (the table for <>) kagel <> nakopal = kagel (the table for <>) kagel <> kagel = korrreld (the table for <>) That leaves korrreld, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, iskbra <> (kagel <> korrreld), to show what the brackets are doing. kagel <> korrreld = iskbra (the table for <>) iskbra <> iskbra = korrreld (the table for <>) That gives korrreld, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test kagel :: kagel. The tezqen of kagel is kagel, korrreld and iskbra, and kagel lies inside it, so the relation holds.
R2. There is no reldjen z with z <> x = x <> z = z for every reldjen x. It fails at reason = no absorbing element. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
Read alongside S2 (the Mornyuk combination tables). What is built on it later: D5 (the hobazt), D11 (the nakquil of a reldjen) and T1 (the hobazt is the only one of its kind).

R2. There is no reldjen z with z <> x = x <> z = z for every reldjen x. (1) [S2] Take the case reason = no absorbing element, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is reflexivity of the relation, antisymmetry of the relation and transitivity of the relation. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over reldjens, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

documents.text: These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A12. Reflexivity of the relation. For every reldjen x: x :: x. A13. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all reldjens x and y: if x :: y and y :: x then x = y. A14. Transitivity of the relation. For all reldjens x, y, z: if x :: y and y :: z then x :: z. A15. Comparability of every pair. For all reldjens x and y, at least one of x :: y and y :: x holds. A16. Agreement of the relation with the second operation. For all reldjens x, y, z: if x :: y then (z # x) :: (z # y) and (x # z) :: (y # z). D4. The tezqen of a reldjen. The tezqen of a reldjen x is the collection of reldjens y for which x :: y holds. Worked out for each reldjen: nakopal to nakopal, kagel, korrreld and iskbra; kagel to kagel, korrreld and iskbra; korrreld to korrreld and iskbra; iskbra to iskbra.

documents.text: Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet rastyuk reldjens, reldjens that duthquil and the hobazt early, whether or not they go looking. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over reldjens, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

D1. Rastyuk reldjens. A reldjen x is called rastyuk when x <> x = x. In this system that picks out nakopal, which is 1 of the 4 reldjens. D2. Reldjens that duthquil. Two reldjens x and y are said to duthquil when x <> y = y <> x. D5. The hobazt. The reldjen nakopal is called the hobazt of the system. It is the unique reldjen that leaves every reldjen unchanged under <>. Here that is nakopal.

A useful mental split: some reldjens are inert under the operation and some are not. nakopal come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and nakopal, kagel, korrreld and iskbra commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single reldjen and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.
Nothing is derived in this chapter. It lays down material that later chapters draw on.

Here is iskbra <> korrreld # kagel, reduced without skipping anything. korrreld # kagel = korrreld (the table for #) iskbra <> korrreld = kagel (the table for <>) So iskbra <> korrreld # kagel is kagel. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take korrreld <> (kagel <> iskbra). kagel <> iskbra = nakopal (the table for <>) korrreld <> nakopal = korrreld (the table for <>) The value is korrreld, not kagel. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does iskbra :: nakopal hold? Read off what iskbra stands over: iskbra. nakopal is not among them, so it fails.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of reldjens that come back unchanged from themselves: nakopal. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). These results are used again in D6 (the solthra), D7 (the hurnlum), D10 (zeltu reldjens) and D11 (the nakquil of a reldjen).
No proofs are needed here. Everything asserted is a definition or a table entry.
New vocabulary from this chapter: rastyuk reldjens, reldjens that duthquil and the hobazt. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through brapon pairs, iskyuk collections and a grixhob. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1 and 3 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about reldjens covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

documents.text: D14. Brapon pairs. Two distinct reldjens x and y form a brapon pair when x :: y and y :: x both hold, that is, when each lies in the tezqen of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Iskyuk collections. A collection S of reldjens is iskyuk when x <> y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A grixhob. A reldjen f is a grixhob when f :: y holds for every reldjen y, that is, when the tezqen of f is the whole system. Running the definition over every reldjen leaves nakopal.

documents.text: Picture the quilpon as what happens when you start with one reldjen and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Each reldjen casts a tezqen over what it yields to, and the sizes of those shadows here are 1, 2, 3 and 4. No two are the same size, so the objects line up in a single file. (3) So the assignment is injective, and being injective on a finite carrier it is onto. Checked over 16 cases: every object translated by every object. D10. Zeltu reldjens. A reldjen x is zeltu when x <> x equals the hobazt. In this system that picks out nakopal and korrreld, which is 2 of the 4 reldjens. D11. The nakquil of a reldjen. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every reldjen unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e <> f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e <> f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

The material this chapter borrows from: A2 (association of the first operation), D3 (iskyuk collections), D5 (the hobazt) and D6 (the solthra). These results are used again in T10 (the quilpon of a solthra reldjen stays in the solthra) and T19 (the second operation keeps the solthra intact).

R6. It is not the case that: x <> x = x for every reldjen x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = kagel, value = korrreld, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T11. If x and y are both rastyuk then so is x <> y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be rastyuk. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x <> y) <> (x <> y) returns x <> y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T17. Every pair of reldjens duthquils. (1) [D6] The solthra is defined by duthquiling with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x <> y = y <> x for every pair. (3) That is settled by

scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The hobazt duthquils with every reldjen. (1) [D5] Let e be the hobazt and x any reldjen. (2) [D5] Then e <> x = x and x <> e = x. (3) [D2] So e <> x = x <> e, which is what it means to duthquil. (4) [D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the solthra. Checked over 4 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If x and y both duthquil with every reldjen, then so does x <> y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the solthra and let z be any reldjen. (2) [A2] Then (x <> y) <> z = x <> (y <> z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each duthquils with everything. (4) [D3] So x <> y duthquils with z, and the solthra is iskyuk. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Established here and safe to use: T11, T17, T2 and T5. Do not carry forward R6. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through the gelgrix of a reldjen, a reldjen has only one nakquil and the quilpon of a reldjen is iskyuk. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1, 6, 8 and 9, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about reldjens covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.
D12. The gelgrix of a reldjen. The gelgrix of a reldjen x is the number of reldjens in its quilpon [x]. Worked out for each reldjen: nakopal to 1; kagel to 4; korrreld to 2; iskbra to 4.

Picture the quilpon as what happens when you start with one reldjen and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 4 reldjens, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. The neutral reldjen nakopal is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. T3 rests on D11 (the nakquil of a reldjen), A2 (association of the first operation) and T1 (the hobazt is the only one of its kind). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T6 rests on D8 (the quilpon of a reldjen) and D3 (iskyuk collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate korrreld <> nakopal # iskbra. Each line below is one lookup in a table. nakopal # iskbra = iskbra (the table for #) korrreld <> iskbra = kagel (the table for <>) So korrreld <> nakopal # iskbra is kagel. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take nakopal <> (iskbra <> korrreld). iskbra <> korrreld = kagel (the table for <>) nakopal <> kagel = kagel (the table for <>) That gives kagel, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test nakopal :: kagel. The tezqen of nakopal is nakopal, kagel, korrreld and iskbra, and kagel lies inside it, so the relation holds. A second case, this time a quilpon. Start from iskbra. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is nakopal, kagel, korrreld and iskbra, so the gelgrix of iskbra is 4.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of reldjens that come back unchanged from themselves: nakopal. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation, closure under the first operation and reversal under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

The material this chapter borrows from: A2 (association of the first operation), D11 (the nakquil of a reldjen), D3 (iskyuk collections) and D8 (the quilpon of a reldjen). These results are used again in D13 (the duthfex), T4 (a zeltu reldjen is its own nakquil), T7 (the quilpon is contained in every iskyuk collection) and T8 (a reldjen is rastyuk exactly when its gelgrix is one).

T3. For every reldjen x there is exactly one nakquil of x. (1) [D11] Let y and z both be partners of x. (2) [A2] Then y = y <> (x <> z) = (y <> x) <> z. (3) [D11] Both bracketed products collapse to the neutral object. (4) So y = z. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. For every reldjen x, the collection [x] is iskyuk. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under <>. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 64 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Carry forward the gelgrix of a reldjen. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T3 and T6.

We turn to the duthfex, the quilpon of a solthra reldjen stays in the solthra and some reldjen reaches every other. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over reldjens, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.
D13. The duthfex. The duthfex of the system is the collection of reldjens whose gelgrix is largest. In this system that picks out kagel and iskbra, which is 2 of the 4 reldjens.

The right picture for quilpon is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one reldjen in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1, 2 and 4 reldjens depending on where it started. Two questions sort the reldjens quickly. Does combining a reldjen with itself change it? For nakopal it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For nakopal, kagel, korrreld and iskbra it does not. The neutral reldjen nakopal is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. T10 rests on D8 (the quilpon of a reldjen), D6 (the solthra) and T5 (the solthra is iskyuk). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T18 rests on D8 (the quilpon of a reldjen) and D12 (the gelgrix of a reldjen). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T4 rests on D10 (zeltu reldjens), D11 (the nakquil of a reldjen) and T3 (a reldjen has only one nakquil). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D8 (the quilpon of a reldjen) and T6 (the quilpon of a reldjen is iskyuk). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T8 rests on D1 (rastyuk reldjens), D12 (the gelgrix of a reldjen) and T6 (the quilpon of a reldjen is iskyuk). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T9 rests on D12 (the gelgrix of a reldjen) and T6 (the quilpon of a reldjen is iskyuk). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take (iskbra <> kagel) <> (korrreld <> nakopal) and work it out one step at a time. iskbra <> kagel = nakopal (the table for <>) korrreld <> nakopal = korrreld (the table for <>) nakopal <> korrreld = korrreld (the table for <>) That leaves korrreld, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take kagel <> (korrreld <> iskbra). korrreld <> iskbra = kagel (the table for <>) kagel <> kagel = korrreld (the table for <>) That gives korrreld, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does korrreld :: kagel hold? Read off what korrreld stands over: korrreld and iskbra. kagel is not among them, so it fails.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of reldjens that come back unchanged from themselves: nakopal. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation, closure under the first operation and reversal under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. To see how little the notation guarantees: rebuild the system with the same names over different tables and T18 fail outright.
Read alongside D1 (rastyuk reldjens), D10 (zeltu reldjens), D11 (the nakquil of a reldjen) and D12 (the gelgrix of a reldjen).

T10. If x lies in the solthra then every reldjen of [x] lies in the solthra. (1) [T5] The solthra is iskyuk. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest iskyuk collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the solthra is one. Checked over 16 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T18. There is a reldjen whose quilpon is the whole system. (1) [D8] Compute [x] for each reldjen in turn. (2) [D12] The claim is that some gelgrix equals 4. (3) The search runs over finitely many objects, so it settles. Checked over 4 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T4. If x <> x is the hobazt then the nakquil of x is x itself. (1) [D10] Let x be zeltu, so x <> x is the hobazt. (2) [D11] That is exactly the condition for x to be a partner of x. (3) [T3] Partners are unique, so no other object can be one. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If S is

iskyuk and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 12 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. x <> x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x <> x = x then {x} is already closed under <>. (2) [T6] So [x] = {x} and the gelgrix is one. (3) [D12] Conversely a span of one object must contain x <> x, which is then x. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. For every reldjen x, the gelgrix of x divides 4. (1) [T6] [x] is a iskyuk collection. (2) [D12] Its size is the gelgrix of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 4. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the duthfex. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T10, T18, T4, T7, T8 and T9.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers the second operation keeps the solthra intact, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 4, 7 and 10, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about reldjens covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

documents.text:
The Hurnglim system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth
the trouble. It has 3 grixmis, one operation, and one relation, and nothing else.

The grixmis are written tezreld, vexyuk and muxlum. The first operation is written #.
The relation is written |>; where it holds between two grixmis we say the left one
refines the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written without
brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3 means x #
x # x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

We turn to the Hurnglim signature, the Hurnglim combination tables and closure under the first operation. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over grixmis, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for #. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | tezreld vexyuk muxlum ------------------------------------- tezreld | tezreld vexyuk muxlum vexyuk | vexyuk muxlum muxlum muxlum | muxlum muxlum muxlum Every pair standing in the |> relation, grouped by left argument. tezreld |> tezreld, vexyuk and muxlum vexyuk |> vexyuk and muxlum muxlum |> muxlum

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all grixmis x and y, x # y is again a grixmi. A2. Association of the first operation. For all grixmis x, y, z: (x # y) # z = x # (y # z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all grixmis x and y: x # y = y # x.

Two questions sort the grixmis quickly. Does combining a grixmi with itself change it? For tezreld and muxlum it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For tezreld, vexyuk and muxlum it does not. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 3 grixmis the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Hurnglim combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Hurnglim combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is (muxlum # tezreld) # vexyuk, reduced without skipping anything. muxlum # tezreld = muxlum (the table for #) muxlum # vexyuk = muxlum (the table for #) The expression comes to muxlum. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take tezreld # (vexyuk # muxlum). vexyuk # muxlum = muxlum (the table for #) tezreld # muxlum = muxlum (the table for #) The value is muxlum. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does vexyuk |> tezreld hold? Read off what vexyuk stands over: vexyuk and muxlum. tezreld is not among them, so it fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every grixmi x: x # x = x. It fails at x = vexyuk, value = muxlum. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all grixmis x, y, z: if x # y = x # z then y = z. It fails at x = vexyuk, y = vexyuk, z = muxlum. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (reflexivity of the relation) and A7 (antisymmetry of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every grixmi x: x # x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = vexyuk, value = muxlum, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all grixmis x, y, z: if x # y = x # z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = vexyuk, y = vexyuk, z = muxlum, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R2 and R3. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about grixmis covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a grixmi tezreld with tezreld # x = x # tezreld = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a grixmi muxlum with muxlum # x = x # muxlum = muxlum for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single grixmi and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is vexhurn and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. This book is about aztfals. A aztfal is not a number and not a set; it is one of exactly
6 objects, and everything said here is said about how those 6 objects combine.

The aztfals are written korrhob, pyrnak, korrglim, lornjen, nakqen and aztclo. The first
operation is written &. The relation is written <<; where it holds between two aztfals
we say the left one yields to the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x & x & x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is the Vintreld signature, the Vintreld combination tables and closure under the first operation. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over aztfals, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for &. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | korrhob pyrnak korrglim lornjen nakqen aztclo ----------------------------------------------------------------------- korrhob | korrhob korrhob korrhob korrhob korrhob korrhob pyrnak | korrhob pyrnak korrglim lornjen nakqen aztclo korrglim | korrhob korrglim nakqen korrhob korrglim nakqen lornjen | korrhob lornjen korrhob lornjen korrhob lornjen nakqen | korrhob nakqen korrglim korrhob nakqen korrglim aztclo | korrhob aztclo nakqen lornjen korrglim pyrnak Every pair standing in the << relation, grouped by left argument. korrhob << korrhob, pyrnak, korrglim, lornjen, nakqen and aztclo pyrnak << pyrnak korrglim << pyrnak and nakqen lornjen << pyrnak, lornjen and aztclo nakqen << pyrnak and nakqen aztclo << pyrnak

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all aztfals x and y, x & y is again a aztfal. A2. Association of the first operation. For all aztfals x, y, z: (x & y) & z = x & (y & z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all aztfals x and y: x & y = y & x.

Two questions sort the aztfals quickly. Does combining a aztfal with itself change it? For korrhob, pyrnak, lornjen and nakqen it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For korrhob, pyrnak, korrglim, lornjen, nakqen and aztclo it does not. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Vintreld combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is aztclo & (korrglim & korrhob) for contrast. korrglim & korrhob = korrhob (the table for &) aztclo & korrhob = korrhob (the table for &) That gives korrhob, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does pyrnak << korrglim hold? Read off what pyrnak stands over: pyrnak. korrglim is not among them, so it fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every aztfal x: x & x = x. It fails at x = korrglim, value = nakqen. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all aztfals x, y, z: if x & y = x & z then y = z. It fails at x = korrhob, y = korrhob, z = pyrnak. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

documents.text: So far the aztfals have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up korrtu aztfals, aztfals that mornjen and the tuovi. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 aztfals that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

D1. Korrtu aztfals. A aztfal x is called korrtu when x & x = x. In this system that picks out korrhob, pyrnak, lornjen and nakqen, which is 4 of the 6 aztfals. D2. Aztfals that mornjen. Two aztfals x and y are said to mornjen when x & y = y & x. D5. The tuovi. The aztfal pyrnak is called the tuovi of the system. It is the unique aztfal that leaves every aztfal unchanged under &. Here that is pyrnak.

A useful mental split: some aztfals are inert under the operation and some are not. korrhob, pyrnak, lornjen and nakqen come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and korrhob, pyrnak, korrglim, lornjen, nakqen and aztclo commute with everything. The neutral aztfal pyrnak is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.
Nothing is derived in this chapter. It lays down material that later chapters draw on.
