R7. It is not the case that: x & x = x for every aztfal x. The case that settles it: x = korrglim, value = nakqen. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

The material this chapter borrows from: A2 (association of the first operation), D3 (espaxil collections), D5 (the tuovi) and D6 (the sibtu). What is built on it later: T8 (the isktez of a sibtu aztfal stays in the sibtu).

R7. It is not the case that: x & x = x for every aztfal x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = korrglim, value = nakqen, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T13. Every pair of aztfals mornjens. (1) [D6] The sibtu is defined by mornjening with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x & y = y & x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The tuovi mornjens with every aztfal. (1) [D5] Let e be the tuovi and x any aztfal. (2) [D5] Then e & x = x and x & e = x. (3) [D2] So e & x = x & e, which is what it means to mornjen. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the sibtu. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both mornjen with every aztfal, then so does x & y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the sibtu and let z be any aztfal. (2) [A2] Then (x & y) & z = x & (y & z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each mornjens with everything. (4) [D3] So x & y mornjens with z, and the sibtu is espaxil. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. If x and y are both korrtu then so is x & y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be korrtu. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x & y) & (x & y) returns x & y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Established here and safe to use: T13, T2, T3 and T9. Do not carry forward R7. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through the lornhob of a aztfal, the isktez of a aztfal is espaxil and the isktez of a sibtu aztfal stays in the sibtu. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 5, 6, 7 and 8, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over aztfals, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

D11. The lornhob of a aztfal. The lornhob of a aztfal x is the number of aztfals in its isktez [x]. Worked out for each aztfal: korrhob to 1; pyrnak to 1; korrglim to 2; lornjen to 1; nakqen to 1; aztclo to 2.

Picture the isktez as what happens when you start with one aztfal and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 6 aztfals, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. A useful mental split: some aztfals are inert under the operation and some are not. korrhob, pyrnak, lornjen and nakqen come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and korrhob, pyrnak, korrglim, lornjen, nakqen and aztclo commute with everything. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 aztfals the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. T4 rests on D8 (the isktez of a aztfal) and D3 (espaxil collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T8 rests on D8 (the isktez of a aztfal), D6 (the sibtu) and T3 (the sibtu is espaxil). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (korrglim & nakqen) & pyrnak. Each line below is one lookup in a table. korrglim & nakqen = korrglim (the table for &) korrglim & pyrnak = korrglim (the table for &) So (korrglim & nakqen) & pyrnak is korrglim. A companion case, nakqen & (pyrnak & korrglim), to show what the brackets are doing. pyrnak & korrglim = korrglim (the table for &) nakqen & korrglim = korrglim (the table for &) The value is korrglim. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does aztclo << pyrnak hold? Read off what aztclo stands over: pyrnak. pyrnak is among them, so it holds. Now compute [korrglim]. Fold korrglim against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is korrglim and nakqen, of size 2.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of aztfals that come back unchanged from themselves: korrhob, pyrnak, lornjen and nakqen. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Every result in this chapter is downstream of association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

The material this chapter borrows from: D3 (espaxil collections), D6 (the sibtu), D8 (the isktez of a aztfal) and T3 (the sibtu is espaxil). What is built on it later: D12 (the jensib), T5 (the isktez is contained in every espaxil collection), T6 (a aztfal is korrtu exactly when its lornhob is one) and T7 (the lornhob divides the number of aztfals).

T4. For every aztfal x, the collection [x] is espaxil. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under &. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 216 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x lies in the sibtu then every aztfal of [x] lies in the sibtu. (1) [T3] The sibtu is espaxil. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest espaxil collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the sibtu is one. Checked over 36 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Carry forward the lornhob of a aztfal. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T4 and T8.

The present chapter develops the jensib, where some aztfal reaches every other breaks down and the isktez is contained in every espaxil collection. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 4, 7 and 9, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about aztfals covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.
D12. The jensib. The jensib of the system is the collection of aztfals whose lornhob is largest. Running the definition over every aztfal leaves korrglim and aztclo.

Picture the isktez as what happens when you start with one aztfal and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 6 aztfals, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R8 rests on D8 (the isktez of a aztfal) and D11 (the lornhob of a aztfal). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T5 rests on D8 (the isktez of a aztfal) and T4 (the isktez of a aztfal is espaxil). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T6 rests on D1 (korrtu aztfals), D11 (the lornhob of a aztfal) and T4 (the isktez of a aztfal is espaxil). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D11 (the lornhob of a aztfal) and T4 (the isktez of a aztfal is espaxil). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (nakqen & pyrnak) & (lornjen & korrglim), reduced without skipping anything. nakqen & pyrnak = nakqen (the table for &) lornjen & korrglim = korrhob (the table for &) nakqen & korrhob = korrhob (the table for &) The expression comes to korrhob. A companion case, pyrnak & (lornjen & nakqen), to show what the brackets are doing. lornjen & nakqen = korrhob (the table for &) pyrnak & korrhob = korrhob (the table for &) That gives korrhob, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test korrhob << aztclo. The lornthra of korrhob is korrhob, pyrnak, korrglim, lornjen, nakqen and aztclo, and aztclo lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R8. It is not the case that: There is a aztfal whose isktez is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 2, size = 6. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. That is not a rhetorical caution. Take the same 6 objects, the same symbols, and a different table, and T7 stop holding. The notation survives the substitution and the mathematics does not.
Read alongside D1 (korrtu aztfals), D11 (the lornhob of a aztfal), D8 (the isktez of a aztfal) and T4 (the isktez of a aztfal is espaxil).

R8. It is not the case that: There is a aztfal whose isktez is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is espaxil and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 156 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x & x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x & x = x then {x} is already closed under &. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the lornhob is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x & x, which is then x. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every aztfal x, the lornhob of x divides 6. (1) [T4] [x] is a espaxil collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the lornhob of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 6. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the jensib. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T5, T6 and T7. Do not carry forward R8. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

documents.text:
The Nyrduth system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth
the trouble. It has 6 glimyuks, two operations, and one relation, and nothing else.

The glimyuks are written fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr. The first
operation is written &. The second is written : and binds more tightly, so x & y : z
means x & (y : z). The relation is written >-; where it holds between two glimyuks we
say the left one precedes the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x & x & x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

The results collected here were not found in this order. The Nyrduth signature, the Nyrduth combination tables and closure under the first operation came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over glimyuks, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The table for &. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | fexvash kamorn muxreld quilisk ovifal kanyr ---------------------------------------------------------------- fexvash | fexvash fexvash fexvash fexvash fexvash fexvash kamorn | fexvash kamorn muxreld quilisk ovifal kanyr muxreld | fexvash muxreld ovifal fexvash muxreld ovifal quilisk | fexvash quilisk fexvash quilisk fexvash quilisk ovifal | fexvash ovifal muxreld fexvash ovifal muxreld kanyr | fexvash kanyr ovifal quilisk muxreld kamorn The table for :. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | fexvash kamorn muxreld quilisk ovifal kanyr ---------------------------------------------------------------- fexvash | fexvash kamorn muxreld quilisk ovifal kanyr kamorn | kamorn muxreld quilisk ovifal kanyr fexvash muxreld | muxreld quilisk ovifal kanyr fexvash kamorn quilisk | quilisk ovifal kanyr fexvash kamorn muxreld ovifal | ovifal kanyr fexvash kamorn muxreld quilisk kanyr | kanyr fexvash kamorn muxreld quilisk ovifal Every pair standing in the >- relation, grouped by left argument. fexvash >- fexvash kamorn >- fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr muxreld >- fexvash, muxreld and ovifal quilisk >- fexvash and quilisk ovifal >- fexvash, muxreld and ovifal kanyr >- fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all glimyuks x and y, x & y is again a glimyuk. A2. Association of the first operation. For all glimyuks x, y, z: (x & y) & z = x & (y & z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all glimyuks x and y: x & y = y & x.

Two questions sort the glimyuks quickly. Does combining a glimyuk with itself change it? For fexvash, kamorn, quilisk and ovifal it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr it does not. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Nyrduth combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. R3 rests on S2 (the Nyrduth combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate quilisk & kanyr : kamorn. Each line below is one lookup in a table. kanyr : kamorn = fexvash (the table for :) quilisk & fexvash = fexvash (the table for &) That leaves fexvash, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is kanyr & (kamorn & quilisk) for contrast. kamorn & quilisk = quilisk (the table for &) kanyr & quilisk = quilisk (the table for &) The value is quilisk, not fexvash. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does fexvash >- quilisk hold? Read off what fexvash stands over: fexvash. quilisk is not among them, so it fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every glimyuk x: x & x = x. It fails at x = muxreld, value = ovifal. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all glimyuks x, y, z: if x & y = x & z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = fexvash, y = fexvash, z = kamorn. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (closure under the second operation) and A7 (association of the second operation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every glimyuk x: x & x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = muxreld, value = ovifal, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all glimyuks x, y, z: if x & y = x & z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = fexvash, y = fexvash, z = kamorn, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation early, whether or not they go looking. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimyuks covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a glimyuk kamorn with kamorn & x = x & kamorn = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a glimyuk fexvash with fexvash & x = x & fexvash = fexvash for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single glimyuk and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R1 rests on S2 (the Nyrduth combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (ovifal & quilisk) & (kamorn & kanyr) and work it out one step at a time. ovifal & quilisk = fexvash (the table for &) kamorn & kanyr = kanyr (the table for &) fexvash & kanyr = fexvash (the table for &) That leaves fexvash, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take quilisk & (kamorn & ovifal). kamorn & ovifal = ovifal (the table for &) quilisk & ovifal = fexvash (the table for &) The value is fexvash. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does quilisk >- quilisk hold? Read off what quilisk stands over: fexvash and quilisk. quilisk is among them, so it holds.
R1. Some glimyuk x admits no glimyuk y for which x & y and y & x both land on a neutral object. It fails at x = fexvash. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside S2 (the Nyrduth combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the quilkeld) and T1 (the quilkeld is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some glimyuk x admits no glimyuk y for which x & y and y & x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = fexvash, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 glimyuks that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

D1. Ovika glimyuks. A glimyuk x is called ovika when x & x = x. In this system that picks out fexvash, kamorn, quilisk and ovifal, which is 4 of the 6 glimyuks. D2. Glimyuks that clokeld. Two glimyuks x and y are said to clokeld when x & y = y & x. D5. The quilkeld. The glimyuk kamorn is called the quilkeld of the system. It is the unique glimyuk that leaves every glimyuk unchanged under &. Here that is kamorn.

Two questions sort the glimyuks quickly. Does combining a glimyuk with itself change it? For fexvash, kamorn, quilisk and ovifal it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr it does not. The neutral glimyuk kamorn is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Test quilisk >- fexvash. The morngel of quilisk is fexvash and quilisk, and fexvash lies inside it, so the relation holds.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of glimyuks that come back unchanged from themselves: fexvash, kamorn, quilisk and ovifal. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

documents.text: D13. Hobshen pairs. Two distinct glimyuks x and y form a hobshen pair when x >- y and y >- x both hold, that is, when each lies in the morngel of the other. A collection S of glimyuks is fexvex when x & y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A thravex. A glimyuk f is a thravex when f >- y holds for every glimyuk y, that is, when the morngel of f is the whole system. In this system that picks out kamorn and kanyr, which is 2 of the 6 glimyuks.

The aztmux of the system is the collection of glimyuks that clokeld with every glimyuk. In this system that picks out fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr, that is, all of them. D7. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single glimyuk and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one glimyuk e with e & x = x & e = x for every glimyuk x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every glimyuk unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e & f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e & f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 36 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: duthvint glimyuks, the aztmux and the hurnzam. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T1. Do not carry forward R13. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through the umbtarn of a glimyuk, where every glimyuk is ovika breaks down and every glimyuk lies in the aztmux. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1, 5, 6 and 7, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimyuks covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

D8. The umbtarn of a glimyuk. The umbtarn of a glimyuk x, written [x], is the smallest fexvex collection that contains x. Worked out for each glimyuk: fexvash to fexvash; kamorn to kamorn; muxreld to muxreld and ovifal; quilisk to quilisk; ovifal to ovifal; kanyr to kamorn and kanyr.

Picture the umbtarn as what happens when you start with one glimyuk and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 6 glimyuks, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. A useful mental split: some glimyuks are inert under the operation and some are not. fexvash, kamorn, quilisk and ovifal come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr commute with everything. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R10 rests on D7 (the hurnzam). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T12 rests on D6 (the aztmux). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T2 rests on D5 (the quilkeld) and D6 (the aztmux). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T3 rests on D6 (the aztmux), D3 (fexvex collections) and A2 (association of the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T9 rests on D7 (the hurnzam) and D3 (fexvex collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take (kanyr & fexvash) & (quilisk & ovifal) and work it out one step at a time. kanyr & fexvash = fexvash (the table for &) quilisk & ovifal = fexvash (the table for &) fexvash & fexvash = fexvash (the table for &) The expression comes to fexvash. A companion case, fexvash & (quilisk & kanyr), to show what the brackets are doing. quilisk & kanyr = quilisk (the table for &) fexvash & quilisk = fexvash (the table for &) The value is fexvash. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test fexvash >- muxreld. The morngel of fexvash is fexvash, and muxreld lies outside it, so the relation fails. Now compute [kamorn]. Fold kamorn against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is kamorn, of size 1.

R10. It is not the case that: x & x = x for every glimyuk x. The case that settles it: x = muxreld, value = ovifal. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A2 (association of the first operation), D3 (fexvex collections), D5 (the quilkeld) and D6 (the aztmux). These results are used again in D11 (the glimdri of a glimyuk), T4 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk is fexvex), T5 (the umbtarn is contained in every fexvex collection) and T8 (the umbtarn of a aztmux glimyuk stays in the aztmux).

R10. It is not the case that: x & x = x for every glimyuk x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = muxreld, value = ovifal, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T12. Every pair of glimyuks clokelds. (1) [D6] The aztmux is defined by clokelding with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x & y = y & x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The quilkeld clokelds with every glimyuk. (1) [D5] Let e be the quilkeld and x any glimyuk. (2) [D5] Then e & x = x and x & e = x. (3) [D2] So e & x = x & e, which is what it means to clokeld. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the aztmux. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both clokeld with every glimyuk, then so does x & y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the aztmux and let z be any glimyuk. (2) [A2] Then (x & y) & z = x & (y & z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each clokelds with everything. (4) [D3] So x & y clokelds with z, and the aztmux is fexvex. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. If x and y are both ovika then so is x & y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be ovika. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x & y) & (x & y) returns x & y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the umbtarn of a glimyuk. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T12, T2, T3 and T9. Explicitly not available: R10. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The present chapter develops the glimdri of a glimyuk, the umbtarn of a glimyuk is fexvex and the umbtarn of a aztmux glimyuk stays in the aztmux. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 6, 7 and 8 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over glimyuks, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

D11. The glimdri of a glimyuk. The glimdri of a glimyuk x is the number of glimyuks in its umbtarn [x]. Worked out for each glimyuk: fexvash to 1; kamorn to 1; muxreld to 2; quilisk to 1; ovifal to 1; kanyr to 2.

The right picture for umbtarn is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one glimyuk in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1 and 2 glimyuks depending on where it started. A useful mental split: some glimyuks are inert under the operation and some are not. fexvash, kamorn, quilisk and ovifal come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr commute with everything. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 glimyuks the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. T4 rests on D8 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk) and D3 (fexvex collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T8 rests on D8 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk), D6 (the aztmux) and T3 (the aztmux is fexvex). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is kanyr & fexvash : kamorn, reduced without skipping anything. fexvash : kamorn = kamorn (the table for :) kanyr & kamorn = kanyr (the table for &) So kanyr & fexvash : kamorn is kanyr. A companion case, fexvash & (kamorn & kanyr), to show what the brackets are doing. kamorn & kanyr = kanyr (the table for &) fexvash & kanyr = fexvash (the table for &) The value is fexvash, not kanyr. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does fexvash >- kamorn hold? Read off what fexvash stands over: fexvash. kamorn is not among them, so it fails. A second case, this time a umbtarn. Start from ovifal. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is ovifal, so the glimdri of ovifal is 1.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of glimyuks that come back unchanged from themselves: fexvash, kamorn, quilisk and ovifal. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

Read alongside D3 (fexvex collections), D6 (the aztmux), D8 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk) and T3 (the aztmux is fexvex). These results are used again in D12 (the kasol), T5 (the umbtarn is contained in every fexvex collection), T6 (a glimyuk is ovika exactly when its glimdri is one) and T7 (the glimdri divides the number of glimyuks).

T4. For every glimyuk x, the collection [x] is fexvex. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under &. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 216 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x lies in the aztmux then every glimyuk of [x] lies in the aztmux. (1) [T3] The aztmux is fexvex. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest fexvex collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the aztmux is one. Checked over 36 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the glimdri of a glimyuk. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. The results now available are T4 and T8, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers the kasol, where some glimyuk reaches every other breaks down and the umbtarn is contained in every fexvex collection, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 5, 8 and 9, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 glimyuks that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
D12. The kasol. The kasol of the system is the collection of glimyuks whose glimdri is largest. In this system that picks out muxreld and kanyr, which is 2 of the 6 glimyuks.

Picture the umbtarn as what happens when you start with one glimyuk and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 6 glimyuks, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R11 rests on D8 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk) and D11 (the glimdri of a glimyuk). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T5 rests on D8 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk) and T4 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk is fexvex). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T6 rests on D1 (ovika glimyuks), D11 (the glimdri of a glimyuk) and T4 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk is fexvex). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T7 rests on D11 (the glimdri of a glimyuk) and T4 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk is fexvex). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is (muxreld & fexvash) & (ovifal & quilisk), reduced without skipping anything. muxreld & fexvash = fexvash (the table for &) ovifal & quilisk = fexvash (the table for &) fexvash & fexvash = fexvash (the table for &) So (muxreld & fexvash) & (ovifal & quilisk) is fexvash. A companion case, fexvash & (ovifal & muxreld), to show what the brackets are doing. ovifal & muxreld = muxreld (the table for &) fexvash & muxreld = fexvash (the table for &) That gives fexvash, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test kanyr >- kamorn. The morngel of kanyr is fexvash, kamorn, muxreld, quilisk, ovifal and kanyr, and kamorn lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R11. It is not the case that: There is a glimyuk whose umbtarn is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 2, size = 6. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside D1 (ovika glimyuks), D11 (the glimdri of a glimyuk), D8 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk) and T4 (the umbtarn of a glimyuk is fexvex).

R11. It is not the case that: There is a glimyuk whose umbtarn is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is fexvex and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 156 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x & x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x & x = x then {x} is already closed under &. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the glimdri is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x & x, which is then x. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every glimyuk x, the glimdri of x divides 6. (1) [T4] [x] is a fexvex collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the glimdri of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 6. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the kasol. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. The results now available are T5, T6 and T7, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Explicitly not available: R11. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The results collected here were not found in this order. The second operation keeps the aztmux intact came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 4, 7 and 8 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about glimyuks covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

documents.text:
The Opalopal system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth
the trouble. It has 4 xilzams, two operations, and one relation, and nothing else.

The xilzams are written muxovi, nyrfex, ovimux and shennak. The first operation is
written &. The second is written $ and binds more tightly, so x & y $ z means x & (y $
z). The relation is written <|; where it holds between two xilzams we say the left one
yields to the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written without
brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3 means x &
x & x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

The practical content of this chapter is the Opalopal signature, the Opalopal combination tables and closure under the first operation. It is the part that shows up in use. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 4 xilzams that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

documents.text: So far the xilzams have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up gelshen xilzams, the glimpyr and the qendri. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 2 and 5, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over xilzams, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D10. Gelshen xilzams. A xilzam x is gelshen when x & x equals the yuktarn. Running the definition over every xilzam leaves nyrfex and shennak. D6. The glimpyr. The glimpyr of the system is the collection of xilzams that solopal with every xilzam. Running the definition over every xilzam leaves muxovi, nyrfex, ovimux and shennak. D7. The qendri. The qendri is the collection of all drivint xilzams. Running the definition over every xilzam leaves muxovi and nyrfex.

Two questions sort the xilzams quickly. Does combining a xilzam with itself change it? For muxovi and nyrfex it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For muxovi, nyrfex, ovimux and shennak it does not. The neutral xilzam nyrfex is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 4 xilzams the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R12 rests on D5 (the yuktarn). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T1 rests on D5 (the yuktarn) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is ovimux & muxovi $ shennak, reduced without skipping anything. muxovi $ shennak = shennak (the table for $) ovimux & shennak = ovimux (the table for &) That leaves ovimux, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, muxovi & (shennak & ovimux), to show what the brackets are doing. shennak & ovimux = ovimux (the table for &) muxovi & ovimux = muxovi (the table for &) That gives muxovi, against ovimux above. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does shennak <| muxovi hold? Read off what shennak stands over: muxovi, nyrfex, ovimux and shennak. muxovi is among them, so it holds.

R12. It is not the case that: e & x equals the yuktarn for every xilzam x. The case that settles it: anchor = nyrfex, x = muxovi, value = muxovi. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

The material this chapter borrows from: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (drivint xilzams), D2 (xilzams that solopal) and D5 (the yuktarn). What is built on it later: T2 (the yuktarn lies in the glimpyr), T3 (the glimpyr is ponhurn), T8 (the ponjen of a glimpyr xilzam stays in the glimpyr) and T9 (the qendri is ponhurn).

R12. It is not the case that: e & x equals the yuktarn for every xilzam x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = nyrfex, x = muxovi, value = muxovi, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 4 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one xilzam e with e & x = x & e = x for every xilzam x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every xilzam unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e & f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e & f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 16 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward gelshen xilzams, the glimpyr and the qendri. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T1. Explicitly not available: R12. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The present chapter develops the ponjen of a xilzam, the system has a quilreld and where every xilzam is drivint breaks down. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1, 3, 5, 6 and 7, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over xilzams, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

D8. The ponjen of a xilzam. The ponjen of a xilzam x, written [x], is the smallest ponhurn collection that contains x. Worked out for each xilzam: muxovi to muxovi; nyrfex to nyrfex; ovimux to muxovi and ovimux; shennak to nyrfex and shennak.

Picture the ponjen as what happens when you start with one xilzam and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 4 xilzams, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. The relation is easiest to see as a height. Each xilzam casts a yukwren over what it yields to, and the sizes of those shadows here are 1, 2 and 4. Sizes repeat, so the objects do not line up in single file. A useful mental split: some xilzams are inert under the operation and some are not. muxovi and nyrfex come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and muxovi, nyrfex, ovimux and shennak commute with everything. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T9 rests on D7 (the qendri) and D3 (ponhurn collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is (ovimux & shennak) & (nyrfex & muxovi), reduced without skipping anything. ovimux & shennak = ovimux (the table for &) nyrfex & muxovi = muxovi (the table for &) ovimux & muxovi = muxovi (the table for &) So (ovimux & shennak) & (nyrfex & muxovi) is muxovi. A companion case, shennak & (nyrfex & ovimux), to show what the brackets are doing. nyrfex & ovimux = ovimux (the table for &) shennak & ovimux = ovimux (the table for &) That gives ovimux, against muxovi above. Test nyrfex <| muxovi. The yukwren of nyrfex is muxovi, nyrfex, ovimux and shennak, and muxovi lies inside it, so the relation holds. Now compute [shennak]. Fold shennak against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is nyrfex and shennak, of size 2.
R9. It is not the case that: x & x = x for every xilzam x. It fails at x = ovimux, value = muxovi. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

T11. Some xilzam quilrelds the whole system. (1) [A12] Every pair is comparable, so the relation orders the objects into a line. (2) [D9] The claim is that the line has a bottom. (3) The carrier is finite, so the search over candidates terminates. Checked over 16 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R9. It is not the case that: x & x = x for every xilzam x. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 4 cases: every object. pair of xilzams solopals. (1) [D6] The glimpyr is defined by solopaling with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x & y = y & x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The yuktarn solopals with every xilzam. (1) [D5] Let e be the yuktarn and x any xilzam. (2) [D5] Then e & x = x and x & e = x. (3) [D2] So e & x = x & e, which is what it means to solopal. (4) [D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the glimpyr. Checked over 4 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both solopal with every xilzam, then so does x & y. (1)

[D6] Let x and y lie in the glimpyr and let z be any xilzam. (2) [A2] Then (x & y) & z = x & (y & z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each solopals with everything. (4) [D3] So x & y solopals with z, and the glimpyr is ponhurn. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. If x and y are both drivint then so is x & y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be drivint. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x & y) & (x & y) returns x & y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers the vorumb of a xilzam, the ponjen of a xilzam is ponhurn and the ponjen of a glimpyr xilzam stays in the glimpyr, and each claim can be checked by hand. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 6, 7 and 8 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 4 xilzams that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.
D11. The vorumb of a xilzam. The vorumb of a xilzam x is the number of xilzams in its ponjen [x]. Worked out for each xilzam: muxovi to 1; nyrfex to 1; ovimux to 2; shennak to 2.

Take ovimux & shennak $ nyrfex and work it out one step at a time. shennak $ nyrfex = muxovi (the table for $) ovimux & muxovi = muxovi (the table for &) The expression comes to muxovi. Read off what nyrfex stands over: muxovi, nyrfex, ovimux and shennak. ovimux is among them, so it holds. A second case, this time a ponjen. Start from ovimux. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is muxovi and ovimux, so the vorumb of ovimux is 2.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

T4. For every xilzam x, the collection [x] is ponhurn. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under &. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 64 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x lies in the glimpyr then every xilzam of [x] lies in the glimpyr. (1) [T3] The glimpyr is ponhurn. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest ponhurn collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the glimpyr is one. Checked over 16 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

R10. It is not the case that: There is a xilzam whose ponjen is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 4, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 32 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x & x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x & x = x then {x} is already closed under &. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the vorumb is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x & x, which is then x. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every xilzam x, the vorumb of x divides 4. (1) [T4] [x] is a ponhurn collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the vorumb of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 4. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

documents.text:
This book is about qenjens. A qenjen is not a number and not a set; it is one of exactly
5 objects, and everything said here is said about how those 5 objects combine.

The qenjens are written yuktarn, xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld. The first operation
is written +. The second is written |= and binds more tightly, so x + y |= z means x +
(y |= z). The relation is written <~; where it holds between two qenjens we say the left
one answers to the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written without
brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3 means x +
x + x. A trailing mark reverses: x' is the qenjen that combines with x to give the
neutral one.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through the Quilumb signature, the Quilumb combination tables and closure under the first operation. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over qenjens, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The table for +. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | yuktarn xilzam shentu nyrazt cloreld ------------------------------------------------------- yuktarn | yuktarn xilzam shentu nyrazt cloreld xilzam | xilzam shentu nyrazt cloreld yuktarn shentu | shentu nyrazt cloreld yuktarn xilzam nyrazt | nyrazt cloreld yuktarn xilzam shentu cloreld | cloreld yuktarn xilzam shentu nyrazt The table for |=. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | yuktarn xilzam shentu nyrazt cloreld ------------------------------------------------------- yuktarn | yuktarn xilzam shentu nyrazt cloreld xilzam | xilzam xilzam shentu nyrazt cloreld shentu | shentu shentu shentu nyrazt cloreld nyrazt | nyrazt nyrazt nyrazt nyrazt cloreld cloreld | cloreld cloreld cloreld cloreld cloreld Every pair standing in the <~ relation, grouped by left argument. yuktarn <~ yuktarn, xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld xilzam <~ xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld shentu <~ shentu, nyrazt and cloreld nyrazt <~ nyrazt and cloreld cloreld <~ cloreld

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all qenjens x and y, x + y is again a qenjen. A2. Association of the first operation. For all qenjens x, y, z: (x + y) + z = x + (y + z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all qenjens x and y: x + y = y + x. A6. Cancellation in the first operation. For all qenjens x, y, z: if x + y = x + z then y = z.

Two questions sort the qenjens quickly. Does combining a qenjen with itself change it? For yuktarn it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For yuktarn, xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld it does not. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R1 rests on S2 (the Quilumb combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is cloreld + shentu |= nyrazt, reduced without skipping anything. shentu |= nyrazt = nyrazt (the table for |=) cloreld + nyrazt = shentu (the table for +) That leaves shentu, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take shentu + (nyrazt + cloreld). nyrazt + cloreld = shentu (the table for +) shentu + shentu = cloreld (the table for +) The value is cloreld, not shentu. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does cloreld <~ nyrazt hold? Read off what cloreld stands over: cloreld. nyrazt is not among them, so it fails.

R1. It is not the case that: For every qenjen x: x + x = x. The case that settles it: x = xilzam, value = shentu. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (reversal under the first operation), A7 (closure under the second operation) and A8 (association of the second operation).

R1. It is not the case that: For every qenjen x: x + x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = xilzam, value = shentu, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The present chapter develops a neutral object for the first operation, reversal under the first operation and the system does not have an absorbing object for the first operation. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over qenjens, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a qenjen yuktarn with yuktarn + x = x + yuktarn = x for every x. A5. Reversal under the first operation. For every qenjen x there is a qenjen y with x + y = y + x = yuktarn.

The neutral qenjen yuktarn is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Quilumb combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is (nyrazt + shentu) + (xilzam + cloreld), reduced without skipping anything. nyrazt + shentu = yuktarn (the table for +) xilzam + cloreld = yuktarn (the table for +) yuktarn + yuktarn = yuktarn (the table for +) The expression comes to yuktarn. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is shentu + (xilzam + nyrazt) for contrast. xilzam + nyrazt = cloreld (the table for +) shentu + cloreld = xilzam (the table for +) That gives xilzam, against yuktarn above. Test shentu <~ xilzam. The lumumb of shentu is shentu, nyrazt and cloreld, and xilzam lies outside it, so the relation fails.

R2. There is no qenjen z with z + x = x + z = z for every qenjen x. The case that settles it: reason = no absorbing element. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: S2 (the Quilumb combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the nyrvint), D11 (the braisk of a qenjen) and T1 (the nyrvint is the only one of its kind).

R2. There is no qenjen z with z + x = x + z = z for every qenjen x. (1) [S2] Take the case reason = no absorbing element, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R2. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is reflexivity of the relation, antisymmetry of the relation and transitivity of the relation. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about qenjens covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A12. Reflexivity of the relation. For every qenjen x: x <~ x. A13. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all qenjens x and y: if x <~ y and y <~ x then x = y. A14. Transitivity of the relation. For all qenjens x, y, z: if x <~ y and y <~ z then x <~ z. A15. Comparability of every pair. For all qenjens x and y, at least one of x <~ y and y <~ x holds. A16. Agreement of the relation with the second operation. For all qenjens x, y, z: if x <~ y then (z |= x) <~ (z |= y) and (x |= z) <~ (y |= z). D4. The lumumb of a qenjen. The lumumb of a qenjen x is the collection of qenjens y for which x <~ y holds. Worked out for each qenjen: yuktarn to yuktarn, xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld; xilzam to xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld; shentu to shentu, nyrazt and cloreld; nyrazt to nyrazt and cloreld; cloreld to cloreld.

documents.text: The practical content of this chapter is espapon qenjens, qenjens that qenmorn and the nyrvint. It is the part that shows up in use. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1 and 2 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about qenjens covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D1. Espapon qenjens. A qenjen x is called espapon when x + x = x. Running the definition over every qenjen leaves yuktarn. D2. Qenjens that qenmorn. Two qenjens x and y are said to qenmorn when x + y = y + x. D5. The nyrvint. The qenjen yuktarn is called the nyrvint of the system. It is the unique qenjen that leaves every qenjen unchanged under +. Here that is yuktarn.

A useful mental split: some qenjens are inert under the operation and some are not. yuktarn come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and yuktarn, xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single qenjen and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Evaluate xilzam + nyrazt |= shentu. Each line below is one lookup in a table. nyrazt |= shentu = nyrazt (the table for |=) xilzam + nyrazt = cloreld (the table for +) So xilzam + nyrazt |= shentu is cloreld. A companion case, nyrazt + (shentu + xilzam), to show what the brackets are doing. shentu + xilzam = nyrazt (the table for +) nyrazt + nyrazt = xilzam (the table for +) The value is xilzam, not cloreld. Test yuktarn <~ yuktarn. The lumumb of yuktarn is yuktarn, xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld, and yuktarn lies inside it, so the relation holds.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

documents.text: D14. Tezisk pairs. Two distinct qenjens x and y form a tezisk pair when x <~ y and y <~ x both hold, that is, when each lies in the lumumb of the other. A collection S of qenjens is vintshen when x + y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A drihurn. A qenjen f is a drihurn when f <~ y holds for every qenjen y, that is, when the lumumb of f is the whole system. Running the definition over every qenjen leaves yuktarn.
