Each line below is one lookup in a table. yuktarn |= shentu = shentu (the table for |=) cloreld + shentu = xilzam (the table for +) The expression comes to xilzam. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is yuktarn + (shentu + cloreld) for contrast. shentu + cloreld = xilzam (the table for +) yuktarn + xilzam = xilzam (the table for +) That gives xilzam, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test nyrazt <~ yuktarn. The lumumb of nyrazt is nyrazt and cloreld, and yuktarn lies outside it, so the relation fails. A second case, this time a zelsol. Start from shentu. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is yuktarn, xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld, so the espaovi of shentu is 5.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of qenjens that come back unchanged from themselves: yuktarn. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation, closure under the first operation and reversal under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

Read alongside A2 (association of the first operation), D11 (the braisk of a qenjen), D3 (vintshen collections) and D8 (the zelsol of a qenjen). What is built on it later: D13 (the fexmux), T4 (a duthka qenjen is its own braisk), T7 (the zelsol is contained in every vintshen collection) and T8 (a qenjen is espapon exactly when its espaovi is one).

T3. For every qenjen x there is exactly one braisk of x. (1) [D11] Let y and z both be partners of x. (2) [A2] Then y = y + (x + z) = (y + x) + z. (3) [D11] Both bracketed products collapse to the neutral object. (4) So y = z. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. For every qenjen x, the collection [x] is vintshen. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under +. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 125 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Carry forward the espaovi of a qenjen. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T3 and T6.

The present chapter develops the fexmux, the zelsol of a zelxil qenjen stays in the zelxil and some qenjen reaches every other. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 5 qenjens that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.
D13. The fexmux. The fexmux of the system is the collection of qenjens whose espaovi is largest. Running the definition over every qenjen leaves xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld.

Picture the zelsol as what happens when you start with one qenjen and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 qenjens, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 5. Two questions sort the qenjens quickly. Does combining a qenjen with itself change it? For yuktarn it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For yuktarn, xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld it does not. The neutral qenjen yuktarn is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 qenjens the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. T10 rests on D8 (the zelsol of a qenjen), D6 (the zelxil) and T5 (the zelxil is vintshen). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T18 rests on D8 (the zelsol of a qenjen) and D12 (the espaovi of a qenjen). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T4 rests on D10 (duthka qenjens), D11 (the braisk of a qenjen) and T3 (a qenjen has only one braisk). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making

sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D8 (the zelsol of a qenjen) and T6 (the zelsol of a qenjen is vintshen). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T8 rests on D1 (espapon qenjens), D12 (the espaovi of a qenjen) and T6 (the zelsol of a qenjen is vintshen). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T9 rests on D12 (the espaovi of a qenjen) and T6 (the zelsol of a qenjen is vintshen). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is (yuktarn + cloreld) + (shentu + xilzam), reduced without skipping anything. yuktarn + cloreld = cloreld (the table for +) shentu + xilzam = nyrazt (the table for +) cloreld + nyrazt = shentu (the table for +) The expression comes to shentu. A companion case, cloreld + (shentu + yuktarn), to show what the brackets are doing. shentu + yuktarn = shentu (the table for +) cloreld + shentu = xilzam (the table for +) The value is xilzam, not shentu. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does xilzam <~ yuktarn hold? Read off what xilzam stands over: xilzam, shentu, nyrazt and cloreld. yuktarn is not among them, so it fails.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of qenjens that come back unchanged from themselves: yuktarn. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation, closure under the first operation and reversal under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. That is not a rhetorical caution. Take the same 5 objects, the same symbols, and a different table, and T18 and T9 stop holding. The notation survives the substitution and the mathematics does not.
Read alongside D1 (espapon qenjens), D10 (duthka qenjens), D11 (the braisk of a qenjen) and D12 (the espaovi of a qenjen).

T10. If x lies in the zelxil then every qenjen of [x] lies in the zelxil. (1) [T5] The zelxil is vintshen. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest vintshen collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the zelxil is one. Checked over 25 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T18. There is a qenjen whose zelsol is the whole system. (1) [D8] Compute [x] for each qenjen in turn. (2) [D12] The claim is that some espaovi equals 5. (3) The search runs over finitely many objects, so it settles. Checked over 5 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T4. If x + x is the nyrvint then the braisk of x is x itself. (1) [D10] Let x be duthka, so x + x is the nyrvint. (2) [D11] That is exactly the condition for x to be a partner of x. (3) [T3] Partners are unique, so no other object can be one. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If S is

vintshen and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 10 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. x + x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x + x = x then {x} is already closed under +. (2) [T6] So [x] = {x} and the espaovi is one. (3) [D12] Conversely a span of one object must contain x + x, which is then x. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. For every qenjen x, the espaovi of x divides 5. (1) [T6] [x] is a vintshen collection. (2) [D12] Its size is the espaovi of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 5. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the fexmux. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. The results now available are T10, T18, T4, T7, T8 and T9, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is the second operation keeps the zelxil intact. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 4, 7 and 10, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over qenjens, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

documents.text:
This book is about tezkas. A tezka is not a number and not a set; it is one of exactly 3
objects, and everything said here is said about how those 3 objects combine.

The tezkas are written lumwren, vorzel and opalfex. The first operation is written ><.
The second is written | and binds more tightly, so x >< y | z means x >< (y | z). The
relation is written <~; where it holds between two tezkas we say the left one covers the
right one. Both operations associate to the left when written without brackets, and
brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3 means x >< x >< x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

The present chapter develops the Duthtarn signature, the Duthtarn combination tables and closure under the first operation. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over tezkas, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for ><. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | lumwren vorzel opalfex ------------------------------------- lumwren | lumwren lumwren lumwren vorzel | lumwren vorzel opalfex opalfex | lumwren opalfex vorzel The table for |. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | lumwren vorzel opalfex ------------------------------------- lumwren | lumwren lumwren lumwren vorzel | lumwren vorzel vorzel opalfex | lumwren vorzel opalfex Every pair standing in the <~ relation, grouped by left argument. lumwren <~ lumwren, vorzel and opalfex vorzel <~ lumwren, vorzel and opalfex opalfex <~ lumwren, vorzel and opalfex

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all tezkas x and y, x >< y is again a tezka. A2. Association of the first operation. For all tezkas x, y, z: (x >< y) >< z = x >< (y >< z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all tezkas x and y: x >< y = y >< x.

Two questions sort the tezkas quickly. Does combining a tezka with itself change it? For lumwren and vorzel it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For lumwren, vorzel and opalfex it does not. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Duthtarn combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Duthtarn combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate vorzel >< vorzel | lumwren. Each line below is one lookup in a table. vorzel | lumwren = lumwren (the table for |) vorzel >< lumwren = lumwren (the table for ><) So vorzel >< vorzel | lumwren is lumwren. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is vorzel >< (lumwren >< vorzel) for contrast. lumwren >< vorzel = lumwren (the table for ><) vorzel >< lumwren = lumwren (the table for ><) The value is lumwren. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does vorzel <~ vorzel hold? Read off what vorzel stands over: lumwren, vorzel and opalfex. vorzel is among them, so it holds.

R2. It is not the case that: For every tezka x: x >< x = x. It fails at x = opalfex, value = vorzel. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all tezkas x, y, z: if x >< y = x >< z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = lumwren, y = lumwren, z = vorzel. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (closure under the second operation) and A7 (association of the second operation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every tezka x: x >< x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = opalfex, value = vorzel, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all tezkas x, y, z: if x >< y = x >< z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = lumwren, y = lumwren, z = vorzel, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about tezkas covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a tezka vorzel with vorzel >< x = x >< vorzel = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a tezka lumwren with lumwren >< x = x >< lumwren = lumwren for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single tezka and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Duthtarn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is (opalfex >< opalfex) >< (vorzel >< vorzel), reduced without skipping anything. opalfex >< opalfex = vorzel (the table for ><) vorzel >< vorzel = vorzel (the table for ><) vorzel >< vorzel = vorzel (the table for ><) So (opalfex >< opalfex) >< (vorzel >< vorzel) is vorzel. A companion case, opalfex >< (vorzel >< opalfex), to show what the brackets are doing. vorzel >< opalfex = opalfex (the table for ><) opalfex >< opalfex = vorzel (the table for ><) That gives vorzel, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test opalfex <~ lumwren. The espakorr of opalfex is lumwren, vorzel and opalfex, and lumwren lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R1. Some tezka x admits no tezka y for which x >< y and y >< x both land on a neutral object. The case that settles it: x = lumwren. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

Read alongside S2 (the Duthtarn combination tables). What is built on it later: D5 (the tarnmi), T1 (the tarnmi is the only one of its kind) and T14 (the absorbing object survives the second operation).

R1. Some tezka x admits no tezka y for which x >< y and y >< x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = lumwren, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 27 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The results collected here were not found in this order. Reflexivity of the relation, transitivity of the relation and comparability of every pair came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 3 tezkas that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A12. Reflexivity of the relation. For every tezka x: x <~ x. A13. Transitivity of the relation. For all tezkas x, y, z: if x <~ y and y <~ z then x <~ z. A14. Comparability of every pair. For all tezkas x and y, at least one of x <~ y and y <~ x holds. A15. Agreement of the relation with the first operation. For all tezkas x, y, z: if x <~ y then (z >< x) <~ (z >< y) and (x >< z) <~ (y >< z). A16. Agreement of the relation with the second operation. For all tezkas x, y, z: if x <~ y then (z | x) <~ (z | y) and (x | z) <~ (y | z). D4. The espakorr of a tezka. The espakorr of a tezka x is the collection of tezkas y for which x <~ y holds. Worked out for each tezka: lumwren to lumwren, vorzel and opalfex; vorzel to lumwren, vorzel and opalfex; opalfex to lumwren, vorzel and opalfex.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A10. Self combination under the second operation. For every tezka x: x | x = x. A11. Spreading of the second operation over the first. For all tezkas x, y, z: x | (y >< z) = (x | y) >< (x | z), and the same on the right. A6. Closure under the second operation. For all tezkas x and y, x | y is again a tezka. A7. Association of the second operation. For all tezkas x, y, z: (x | y) | z = x | (y | z). A8. Commutation of the second operation. For all tezkas x and y: x | y = y | x. A9. A neutral object for the second operation. There is a tezka opalfex with opalfex | x = x for every x.

documents.text: Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through shendri tezkas, tezkas that zelnyr and the tarnmi. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1 and 2 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over tezkas, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

D1. Shendri tezkas. A tezka x is called shendri when x >< x = x. In this system that picks out lumwren and vorzel, which is 2 of the 3 tezkas. D2. Tezkas that zelnyr. Two tezkas x and y are said to zelnyr when x >< y = y >< x. D5. The tarnmi. The tezka vorzel is called the tarnmi of the system. It is the unique tezka that leaves every tezka unchanged under ><. Here that is vorzel.

Two questions sort the tezkas quickly. Does combining a tezka with itself change it? For lumwren and vorzel it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For lumwren, vorzel and opalfex it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single tezka and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 3 tezkas the table is short enough to consult every time.
Nothing is derived in this chapter. It lays down material that later chapters draw on.

Read off what lumwren stands over: lumwren, vorzel and opalfex. vorzel is among them, so it holds. A second case, this time a thrakorr. Start from opalfex. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is vorzel and opalfex, so the hobsib of opalfex is 2.

R7. It is not the case that: x >< x = x for every tezka x. The case that settles it: x = opalfex, value = vorzel. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation, closure under the first operation and comparability of every pair. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A14 (comparability of every pair), A2 (association of the first operation), D3 (qensib collections) and D5 (the tarnmi). What is built on it later: D11 (the hobsib of a tezka), T4 (the thrakorr of a tezka is qensib), T5 (the thrakorr is contained in every qensib collection) and T7 (the thrakorr of a zamkeld tezka stays in the zamkeld).

T10. Some tezka hobthras the whole system. (1) [A14] Every pair is comparable, so the relation orders the objects into a line. (2) [D9] The claim is that the line has a bottom. (3) The carrier is finite, so the search over candidates terminates. Checked over 9 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R7. It is not the case that: x >< x = x for every tezka x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = opalfex, value = vorzel, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 3 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T12. Every

pair of tezkas zelnyrs. (1) [D6] The zamkeld is defined by zelnyring with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x >< y = y >< x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 9 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The tarnmi zelnyrs with every tezka. (1) [D5] Let e be the tarnmi and x any tezka. (2) [D5] Then e >< x = x and x >< e = x. (3) [D2] So e >< x = x >< e, which is what it means to zelnyr. (4) [D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the zamkeld. Checked over 3 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both zelnyr with every tezka, then so does x >< y. (1)

[D6] Let x and y lie in the zamkeld and let z be any tezka. (2) [A2] Then (x >< y) >< z = x >< (y >< z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each zelnyrs with everything. (4) [D3] So x >< y zelnyrs with z, and the zamkeld is qensib. Checked over 9 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x and y are both shendri then so is x >< y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be shendri. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x >< y) >< (x >< y) returns x >< y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 9 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the thrakorr of a tezka. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. The results now available are T10, T12, T2, T3 and T8, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Do not carry forward R7. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

So far the tezkas have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up the hobsib of a tezka, the thrakorr of a tezka is qensib and the thrakorr of a zamkeld tezka stays in the zamkeld. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 6, 7 and 9, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about tezkas covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.
D11. The hobsib of a tezka. The hobsib of a tezka x is the number of tezkas in its thrakorr [x]. Worked out for each tezka: lumwren to 1; vorzel to 1; opalfex to 2.

The right picture for thrakorr is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one tezka in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1 and 2 tezkas depending on where it started. A useful mental split: some tezkas are inert under the operation and some are not. lumwren and vorzel come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and lumwren, vorzel and opalfex commute with everything. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. T4 rests on D8 (the thrakorr of a tezka) and D3 (qensib collections). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T7 rests on D8 (the thrakorr of a tezka), D6 (the zamkeld) and T3 (the zamkeld is qensib). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take (vorzel >< opalfex) >< (lumwren >< lumwren) and work it out one step at a time. vorzel >< opalfex = opalfex (the table for ><) lumwren >< lumwren = lumwren (the table for ><) opalfex >< lumwren = lumwren (the table for ><) So (vorzel >< opalfex) >< (lumwren >< lumwren) is lumwren. A companion case, opalfex >< (lumwren >< vorzel), to show what the brackets are doing. lumwren >< vorzel = lumwren (the table for ><) opalfex >< lumwren = lumwren (the table for ><) The value is lumwren. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test vorzel <~ opalfex. The espakorr of vorzel is lumwren, vorzel and opalfex, and opalfex lies inside it, so the relation holds. A second case, this time a thrakorr. Start from vorzel. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is vorzel, so the hobsib of vorzel is 1.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

Read alongside D3 (qensib collections), D6 (the zamkeld), D8 (the thrakorr of a tezka) and T3 (the zamkeld is qensib). What is built on it later: D12 (the tarnopal), T5 (the thrakorr is contained in every qensib collection), T6 (a tezka is shendri exactly when its hobsib is one) and R6 (where the hobsib divides the number of tezkas breaks down).

T4. For every tezka x, the collection [x] is qensib. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under ><. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 27 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the zamkeld then every tezka of [x] lies in the zamkeld. (1) [T3] The zamkeld is qensib. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest qensib collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the zamkeld is one. Checked over 9 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
New vocabulary from this chapter: the hobsib of a tezka. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T4 and T7.

The present chapter develops the tarnopal, where the hobsib divides the number of tezkas breaks down and where some tezka reaches every other breaks down. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 5, 9 and 10, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over tezkas, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
D12. The tarnopal. The tarnopal of the system is the collection of tezkas whose hobsib is largest. Running the definition over every tezka leaves opalfex.

The right picture for thrakorr is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one tezka in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1 and 2 tezkas depending on where it started. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R6 rests on D11 (the hobsib of a tezka) and T4 (the thrakorr of a tezka is qensib). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. R8 rests on D8 (the thrakorr of a tezka) and D11 (the hobsib of a tezka). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T5 rests on D8 (the thrakorr of a tezka) and T4 (the thrakorr of a tezka is qensib). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T6 rests on D1 (shendri tezkas), D11 (the hobsib of a tezka) and T4 (the thrakorr of a tezka is qensib). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is lumwren >< lumwren | vorzel, reduced without skipping anything. lumwren | vorzel = lumwren (the table for |) lumwren >< lumwren = lumwren (the table for ><) That leaves lumwren, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, lumwren >< (vorzel >< lumwren), to show what the brackets are doing. vorzel >< lumwren = lumwren (the table for ><) lumwren >< lumwren = lumwren (the table for ><) That gives lumwren, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does opalfex <~ opalfex hold? Read off what opalfex stands over: lumwren, vorzel and opalfex. opalfex is among them, so it holds.

R6. It is not the case that: For every tezka x, the hobsib of x divides 3. It fails at x = opalfex, reach = 2, size = 3. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R8. It is not the case that: There is a tezka whose thrakorr is the whole system. It fails at largest_span = 2, size = 3. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
The material this chapter borrows from: D1 (shendri tezkas), D11 (the hobsib of a tezka), D8 (the thrakorr of a tezka) and T4 (the thrakorr of a tezka is qensib).

R6. It is not the case that: For every tezka x, the hobsib of x divides 3. (1) [S2] Take the case x = opalfex, reach = 2, size = 3, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 3 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R8. It is not the case that: There is a tezka whose thrakorr is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 3, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 3 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is qensib and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 15 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x >< x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x >< x = x then {x} is already closed under ><. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the hobsib is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x >< x, which is then x. Checked over 3 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the tarnopal. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. The results now available are T5 and T6, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Explicitly not available: R6 and R8. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

documents.text:
What follows is a complete account of the Glimzam system. It is complete in a strong
sense: the system has 4 mornglims and finitely many facts, and every one of those facts
is settled here by inspection rather than left to argument.

The mornglims are written oviazt, kapon, nyrrast and xilwren. The first operation is
written |. The relation is written <~; where it holds between two mornglims we say the
left one dominates the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written
without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3
means x | x | x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers the Glimzam signature, the Glimzam combination tables and closure under the first operation, and each claim can be checked by hand. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about mornglims covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The table for |. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | oviazt kapon nyrrast xilwren ---------------------------------------------- oviazt | oviazt oviazt oviazt oviazt kapon | oviazt kapon nyrrast xilwren nyrrast | oviazt nyrrast oviazt nyrrast xilwren | oviazt xilwren nyrrast kapon Every pair standing in the <~ relation, grouped by left argument. oviazt <~ oviazt kapon <~ oviazt, kapon, nyrrast and xilwren nyrrast <~ oviazt and nyrrast xilwren <~ oviazt, kapon, nyrrast and xilwren

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all mornglims x and y, x | y is again a mornglim. A2. Association of the first operation. For all mornglims x, y, z: (x | y) | z = x | (y | z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all mornglims x and y: x | y = y | x.

A useful mental split: some mornglims are inert under the operation and some are not. oviazt and kapon come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and oviazt, kapon, nyrrast and xilwren commute with everything. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Glimzam combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Glimzam combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (xilwren | oviazt) | kapon, reduced without skipping anything. xilwren | oviazt = oviazt (the table for |) oviazt | kapon = oviazt (the table for |) That leaves oviazt, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take oviazt | (kapon | xilwren). kapon | xilwren = xilwren (the table for |) oviazt | xilwren = oviazt (the table for |) That gives oviazt, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test nyrrast <~ kapon. The korrlorn of nyrrast is oviazt and nyrrast, and kapon lies outside it, so the relation fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every mornglim x: x | x = x. It fails at x = nyrrast, value = oviazt. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all mornglims x, y, z: if x | y = x | z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = oviazt, y = oviazt, z = kapon. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (reflexivity of the relation) and A7 (transitivity of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every mornglim x: x | x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = nyrrast, value = oviazt, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all mornglims x, y, z: if x | y = x | z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = oviazt, y = oviazt, z = kapon, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 64 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about mornglims covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a mornglim kapon with kapon | x = x | kapon = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a mornglim oviazt with oviazt | x = x | oviazt = oviazt for every x.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A6. Reflexivity of the relation. For every mornglim x: x <~ x. A7. D1. Reldhurn mornglims. A mornglim x is called reldhurn when x | x = x. In this system that picks out oviazt and kapon, which is 2 of the 4 mornglims. D2. Mornglims that umbpyr. Two mornglims x and y are said to umbpyr when x | y = y | x. D5. The fexvex. The mornglim kapon is called the fexvex of the system. It is the unique mornglim that leaves every mornglim unchanged under |. Here that is kapon.

pair of mornglims umbpyrs. (1) [D6] The mornkeld is defined by umbpyring with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x | y = y | x for every pair. The fexvex umbpyrs with every mornglim. (1) [D5] Let e be the fexvex and x any mornglim. (2) [D5] Then e | x = x and x | e = x. (3) [D2] So e | x = x | e, which is what it means to umbpyr. (4) [D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the mornkeld. Checked over 4 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both umbpyr with every mornglim, then so does x | y. (1)

[D6] Let x and y lie in the mornkeld and let z be any mornglim. (2) [A2] Then (x | y) | z = x | (y | z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each umbpyrs with everything. (4) [D3] So x | y umbpyrs with z, and the mornkeld is ovipon. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. If x and y are both reldhurn then so is x | y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be reldhurn. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x | y) | (x | y) returns x | y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 16 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the tezsib of a mornglim. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T11, T13, T2, T3 and T9. Do not carry forward R5. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

The practical content of this chapter is the xilgel of a mornglim, the tezsib of a mornglim is ovipon and the tezsib of a mornkeld mornglim stays in the mornkeld. It is the part that shows up in use. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 5, 6 and 7, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about mornglims covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.
D11. The xilgel of a mornglim. The xilgel of a mornglim x is the number of mornglims in its tezsib [x]. Worked out for each mornglim: oviazt to 1; kapon to 1; nyrrast to 2; xilwren to 2.

Picture the tezsib as what happens when you start with one mornglim and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 4 mornglims, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. A useful mental split: some mornglims are inert under the operation and some are not. oviazt and kapon come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and oviazt, kapon, nyrrast and xilwren commute with everything. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. T4 rests on D8 (the tezsib of a mornglim) and D3 (ovipon collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T8 rests on D8 (the tezsib of a mornglim), D6 (the mornkeld) and T3 (the mornkeld is ovipon). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (oviazt | nyrrast) | (xilwren | kapon) and work it out one step at a time. oviazt | nyrrast = oviazt (the table for |) xilwren | kapon = xilwren (the table for |) oviazt | xilwren = oviazt (the table for |) That leaves oviazt, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take nyrrast | (xilwren | oviazt). xilwren | oviazt = oviazt (the table for |) nyrrast | oviazt = oviazt (the table for |) The value is oviazt. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does oviazt <~ nyrrast hold? Read off what oviazt stands over: oviazt. nyrrast is not among them, so it fails. Now compute [nyrrast]. Fold nyrrast against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is oviazt and nyrrast, of size 2.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of mornglims that come back unchanged from themselves: oviazt and kapon. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Every result in this chapter is downstream of association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: D3 (ovipon collections), D6 (the mornkeld), D8 (the tezsib of a mornglim) and T3 (the mornkeld is ovipon). What is built on it later: D12 (the korrduth), T5 (the tezsib is contained in every ovipon collection), T6 (a mornglim is reldhurn exactly when its xilgel is one) and T7 (the xilgel divides the number of mornglims).

T4. For every mornglim x, the collection [x] is ovipon. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under |. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 64 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x lies in the mornkeld then every mornglim of [x] lies in the mornkeld. (1) [T3] The mornkeld is ovipon. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest ovipon collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the mornkeld is one. Checked over 16 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the xilgel of a mornglim. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. The results now available are T4 and T8, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy.

So far the mornglims have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up the korrduth, where some mornglim reaches every other breaks down and the tezsib is contained in every ovipon collection. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 4, 7 and 8, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over mornglims, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.
D12. The korrduth. The korrduth of the system is the collection of mornglims whose xilgel is largest. Running the definition over every mornglim leaves nyrrast and xilwren.

Picture the tezsib as what happens when you start with one mornglim and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 4 mornglims, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R6 rests on D8 (the tezsib of a mornglim) and D11 (the xilgel of a mornglim). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T5 rests on D8 (the tezsib of a mornglim) and T4 (the tezsib of a mornglim is ovipon). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T6 rests on D1 (reldhurn mornglims), D11 (the xilgel of a mornglim) and T4 (the tezsib of a mornglim is ovipon). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D11 (the xilgel of a mornglim) and T4 (the tezsib of a mornglim is ovipon). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (oviazt | nyrrast) | xilwren and work it out one step at a time. oviazt | nyrrast = oviazt (the table for |) oviazt | xilwren = oviazt (the table for |) That leaves oviazt, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, nyrrast | (xilwren | oviazt), to show what the brackets are doing. xilwren | oviazt = oviazt (the table for |) nyrrast | oviazt = oviazt (the table for |) The value is oviazt. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does kapon <~ xilwren hold? Read off what kapon stands over: oviazt, kapon, nyrrast and xilwren. xilwren is among them, so it holds.

R6. It is not the case that: There is a mornglim whose tezsib is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 2, size = 4. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. That is not a rhetorical caution. Take the same 4 objects, the same symbols, and a different table, and T7 stop holding. The notation survives the substitution and the mathematics does not.
The material this chapter borrows from: D1 (reldhurn mornglims), D11 (the xilgel of a mornglim), D8 (the tezsib of a mornglim) and T4 (the tezsib of a mornglim is ovipon).

R6. It is not the case that: There is a mornglim whose tezsib is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 4, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 4 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is ovipon and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 32 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x | x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x | x = x then {x} is already closed under |. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the xilgel is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x | x, which is then x. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every mornglim x, the xilgel of x divides 4. (1) [T4] [x] is a ovipon collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the xilgel of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 4. Checked over 4 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the korrduth. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T5, T6 and T7. Do not carry forward R6. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

documents.text:
The Clomorn system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth
the trouble. It has 6 duthpons, one operation, and one relation, and nothing else.

The duthpons are written nakvint, rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn. The
first operation is written -. The relation is written >>; where it holds between two
duthpons we say the left one yields to the right one. Both operations associate to the
left when written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x - x - x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

The results collected here were not found in this order. The Clomorn signature, the Clomorn combination tables and closure under the first operation came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over duthpons, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for -. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | nakvint rastrast espanyr yuksol vorwren vashtarn ----------------------------------------------------------------------- nakvint | nakvint rastrast espanyr yuksol vorwren vashtarn rastrast | rastrast espanyr yuksol vorwren vashtarn vashtarn espanyr | espanyr yuksol vorwren vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn yuksol | yuksol vorwren vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn vorwren | vorwren vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn | vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn vashtarn Every pair standing in the >> relation, grouped by left argument. nakvint >> nakvint, rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn rastrast >> rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn espanyr >> espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn yuksol >> yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn vorwren >> vorwren and vashtarn vashtarn >> vashtarn

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all duthpons x and y, x - y is again a duthpon. A2. Association of the first operation. For all duthpons x, y, z: (x - y) - z = x - (y - z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all duthpons x and y: x - y = y - x.

A useful mental split: some duthpons are inert under the operation and some are not. nakvint and vashtarn come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and nakvint, rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn commute with everything. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 duthpons the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Clomorn combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Clomorn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take (vashtarn - nakvint) - espanyr and work it out one step at a time. vashtarn - nakvint = vashtarn (the table for -) vashtarn - espanyr = vashtarn (the table for -) The expression comes to vashtarn. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take nakvint - (espanyr - vashtarn). espanyr - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) nakvint - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) The value is vashtarn. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test vorwren >> vorwren. The gelgel of vorwren is vorwren and vashtarn, and vorwren lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R2. It is not the case that: For every duthpon x: x - x = x. The case that settles it: x = rastrast, value = espanyr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all duthpons x, y, z: if x - y = x - z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = rastrast, y = vorwren, z = vashtarn. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (reflexivity of the relation) and A7 (antisymmetry of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every duthpon x: x - x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = rastrast, value = espanyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all duthpons x, y, z: if x - y = x - z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = rastrast, y = vorwren, z = vashtarn, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R2 and R3. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

The practical content of this chapter is a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. It is the part that shows up in use. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 duthpons that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a duthpon nakvint with nakvint - x = x - nakvint = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a duthpon vashtarn with vashtarn - x = x - vashtarn = vashtarn for every x.

The neutral duthpon nakvint is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R1 rests on S2 (the Clomorn combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (espanyr - yuksol) - (vashtarn - rastrast). Each line below is one lookup in a table. espanyr - yuksol = vashtarn (the table for -) vashtarn - rastrast = vashtarn (the table for -) vashtarn - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) That leaves vashtarn, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, yuksol - (vashtarn - espanyr), to show what the brackets are doing. vashtarn - espanyr = vashtarn (the table for -) yuksol - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) That gives vashtarn, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test yuksol >> rastrast. The gelgel of yuksol is yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn, and rastrast lies outside it, so the relation fails.

R1. Some duthpon x admits no duthpon y for which x - y and y - x both land on a neutral object. The case that settles it: x = rastrast. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
Read alongside S2 (the Clomorn combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the nakisk) and T1 (the nakisk is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some duthpon x admits no duthpon y for which x - y and y - x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = rastrast, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R1. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through agreement of the relation with the first operation, reflexivity of the relation and antisymmetry of the relation. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over duthpons, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A10. Agreement of the relation with the first operation. For all duthpons x, y, z: if x >> y then (z - x) >> (z - y) and (x - z) >> (y - z). A6. Reflexivity of the relation. For every duthpon x: x >> x. A7. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all duthpons x and y: if x >> y and y >> x then x = y. A8. Transitivity of the relation. For all duthpons x, y, z: if x >> y and y >> z then x >> z. A9. Comparability of every pair. For all duthpons x and y, at least one of x >> y and y >> x holds. D4. The gelgel of a duthpon. The gelgel of a duthpon x is the collection of duthpons y for which x >> y holds. Worked out for each duthpon: nakvint to nakvint, rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn; rastrast to rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn; espanyr to espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn; yuksol to yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn; vorwren to vorwren and vashtarn; vashtarn to vashtarn.

documents.text: The present chapter develops lornxil duthpons, duthpons that tarnwren and the nakisk. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 duthpons that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

D1. Lornxil duthpons. A duthpon x is called lornxil when x - x = x. Running the definition over every duthpon leaves nakvint and vashtarn. D2. Duthpons that tarnwren. Two duthpons x and y are said to tarnwren when x - y = y - x. D5. The nakisk. The duthpon nakvint is called the nakisk of the system. It is the unique duthpon that leaves every duthpon unchanged under -. Here that is nakvint.

Two questions sort the duthpons quickly. Does combining a duthpon with itself change it? For nakvint and vashtarn it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For nakvint, rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn it does not. The neutral duthpon nakvint is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 duthpons the table is short enough to consult every time.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Move the brackets and the work changes. Take rastrast - (yuksol - vashtarn). yuksol - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) rastrast - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) The value is vashtarn. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does yuksol >> espanyr hold? Read off what yuksol stands over: yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn. espanyr is not among them, so it fails.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of duthpons that come back unchanged from themselves: nakvint and vashtarn. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

documents.text: D13. Falvex pairs. Two distinct duthpons x and y form a falvex pair when x >> y and y >> x both hold, that is, when each lies in the gelgel of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Shenshen collections. A collection S of duthpons is shenshen when x - y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A vintdri. A duthpon f is a vintdri when f >> y holds for every duthpon y, that is, when the gelgel of f is the whole system. Running the definition over every duthpon leaves nakvint.

documents.text: The right picture for nakxil is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one duthpon in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The gelgel of a duthpon is everything downhill of it, and those shadows here have sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. documents.text: The results collected here were not found in this order. Shenwren duthpons, the falazt and the thrahurn came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 2 and 4 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over duthpons, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D10. Shenwren duthpons. A duthpon x is shenwren when x - x equals the nakisk. In this system that picks out nakvint, which is 1 of the 6 duthpons. D6. The falazt. The falazt of the system is the collection of duthpons that tarnwren with every duthpon. In this system that picks out nakvint, rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn, that is, all of them. D7. The thrahurn. The thrahurn is the collection of all lornxil duthpons. In this system that picks out nakvint and vashtarn, which is 2 of the 6 duthpons.

A useful mental split: some duthpons are inert under the operation and some are not. nakvint and vashtarn come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and nakvint, rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single duthpon and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

R8. It is not the case that: e - x equals the nakisk for every duthpon x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = nakvint, x = rastrast, value = rastrast, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one duthpon e with e - x = x - e = x for every duthpon x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every duthpon unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e - f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e - f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 36 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text: T10. No two distinct duthpons can both be vintdris. (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors. (2) [D9] Then f >> h, since h is any object, and h >> f likewise. (3) [A7] Antisymmetry forces f = h. Checked over 36 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T11. Some duthpon vintdris the whole system. (1) [A9] Every pair is comparable, so the relation orders the objects into a line. (2) [D9] The claim is that the line has a bottom. (3) The carrier is finite, so the search over candidates terminates. Checked over 36 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T13. No two distinct duthpons lie in each other's gelgel. (1) [D13] Suppose x and y form a tight pair. (2) [A7] Antisymmetry then identifies x with y. (3) So a tight pair of distinct objects cannot arise. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

R5. It is not the case that: x - x = x for every duthpon x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = rastrast, value = espanyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough.
