The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T14. Every pair of duthpons tarnwrens. (1) [D6] The falazt is defined by tarnwrening with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x - y = y - x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The nakisk tarnwrens with every duthpon. (1) [D5] Let e be the nakisk and x any duthpon. (2) [D5] Then e - x = x and x - e = x. (3) [D2] So e - x = x - e, which is what it means to tarnwren. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the falazt. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both tarnwren with every duthpon, then so does x - y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the falazt and let z be any duthpon. (2) [A2] Then (x - y) - z = x - (y - z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each tarnwrens with everything. (4) [D3] So x - y tarnwrens with z, and the falazt is shenshen. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x and y are both lornxil then so is x - y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be lornxil. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x - y) - (x - y) returns x - y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 duthpons that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

D11. The xilquil of a duthpon. The xilquil of a duthpon x is the number of duthpons in its nakxil [x]. Worked out for each duthpon: nakvint to 1; rastrast to 5; espanyr to 3; yuksol to 2; vorwren to 2; vashtarn to 1.

The right picture for nakxil is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one duthpon in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1, 2, 3 and 5 duthpons depending on where it started. A useful mental split: some duthpons are inert under the operation and some are not. nakvint and vashtarn come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and nakvint, rastrast, espanyr, yuksol, vorwren and vashtarn commute with everything. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. T4 rests on D8 (the nakxil of a duthpon) and D3 (shenshen collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D8 (the nakxil of a duthpon), D6 (the falazt) and T3 (the falazt is shenshen). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is (vorwren - yuksol) - rastrast, reduced without skipping anything. vorwren - yuksol = vashtarn (the table for -) vashtarn - rastrast = vashtarn (the table for -) So (vorwren - yuksol) - rastrast is vashtarn. A companion case, yuksol - (rastrast - vorwren), to show what the brackets are doing. rastrast - vorwren = vashtarn (the table for -) yuksol - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) That gives vashtarn, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does vashtarn >> espanyr hold? Read off what vashtarn stands over: vashtarn. espanyr is not among them, so it fails. Now compute [yuksol]. Fold yuksol against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is yuksol and vashtarn, of size 2.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

Read alongside D3 (shenshen collections), D6 (the falazt), D8 (the nakxil of a duthpon) and T3 (the falazt is shenshen). What is built on it later: D12 (the yukopal), T5 (the nakxil is contained in every shenshen collection), T6 (a duthpon is lornxil exactly when its xilquil is one) and R4 (where the xilquil divides the number of duthpons breaks down).

T4. For every duthpon x, the collection [x] is shenshen. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under -. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 216 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the falazt then every duthpon of [x] lies in the falazt. (1) [T3] The falazt is shenshen. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest shenshen collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the falazt is one. Checked over 36 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Carry forward the xilquil of a duthpon. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T4 and T7.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers the yukopal, where the xilquil divides the number of duthpons breaks down and where some duthpon reaches every other breaks down, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 4, 7 and 9, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over duthpons, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
D12. The yukopal. The yukopal of the system is the collection of duthpons whose xilquil is largest. Running the definition over every duthpon leaves rastrast.

Picture the nakxil as what happens when you start with one duthpon and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 6 duthpons, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2, 3 and 5. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R4 rests on D11 (the xilquil of a duthpon) and T4 (the nakxil of a duthpon is shenshen). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R6 rests on D8 (the nakxil of a duthpon) and D11 (the xilquil of a duthpon). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T5 rests on D8 (the nakxil of a duthpon) and T4 (the nakxil of a duthpon is shenshen). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T6 rests on D1 (lornxil duthpons), D11 (the xilquil of a duthpon) and T4 (the nakxil of a duthpon is shenshen). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate (vashtarn - rastrast) - (yuksol - espanyr). Each line below is one lookup in a table. vashtarn - rastrast = vashtarn (the table for -) yuksol - espanyr = vashtarn (the table for -) vashtarn - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) That leaves vashtarn, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is rastrast - (yuksol - vashtarn) for contrast. yuksol - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) rastrast - vashtarn = vashtarn (the table for -) That gives vashtarn, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test vorwren >> nakvint. The gelgel of vorwren is vorwren and vashtarn, and nakvint lies outside it, so the relation fails.

R4. It is not the case that: For every duthpon x, the xilquil of x divides 6. It fails at x = rastrast, reach = 5, size = 6. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R6. It is not the case that: There is a duthpon whose nakxil is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 5, size = 6. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside D1 (lornxil duthpons), D11 (the xilquil of a duthpon), D8 (the nakxil of a duthpon) and T4 (the nakxil of a duthpon is shenshen).

R4. It is not the case that: For every duthpon x, the xilquil of x divides 6. (1) [S2] Take the case x = rastrast, reach = 5, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R6. It is not the case that: There is a duthpon whose nakxil is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 5, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is shenshen and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 90 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x - x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x - x = x then {x} is already closed under -. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the xilquil is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x - x, which is then x. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the yukopal. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T5 and T6. Explicitly not available: R4 and R6. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

documents.text:
What follows is a complete account of the Nyrazt system. It is complete in a strong
sense: the system has 6 naksols and finitely many facts, and every one of those facts is
settled here by inspection rather than left to argument.

The naksols are written wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil. The first
operation is written %. The second is written <> and binds more tightly, so x % y <> z
means x % (y <> z). The relation is written >-; where it holds between two naksols we
say the left one dominates the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x % x % x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet the Nyrazt signature, the Nyrazt combination tables and closure under the first operation early, whether or not they go looking. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about naksols covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for %. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | wrenpyr vexlorn vexnak glimzam reldxil pyrxil ---------------------------------------------------------------- wrenpyr | wrenpyr wrenpyr wrenpyr wrenpyr wrenpyr wrenpyr vexlorn | wrenpyr vexlorn vexnak glimzam reldxil pyrxil vexnak | wrenpyr vexnak reldxil wrenpyr vexnak reldxil glimzam | wrenpyr glimzam wrenpyr glimzam wrenpyr glimzam reldxil | wrenpyr reldxil vexnak wrenpyr reldxil vexnak pyrxil | wrenpyr pyrxil reldxil glimzam vexnak vexlorn The table for <>. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | wrenpyr vexlorn vexnak glimzam reldxil pyrxil ---------------------------------------------------------------- wrenpyr | wrenpyr wrenpyr wrenpyr wrenpyr wrenpyr wrenpyr vexlorn | wrenpyr vexlorn vexlorn vexlorn vexlorn vexlorn vexnak | wrenpyr vexlorn vexnak vexnak vexnak vexnak glimzam | wrenpyr vexlorn vexnak glimzam glimzam glimzam reldxil | wrenpyr vexlorn vexnak glimzam reldxil reldxil pyrxil | wrenpyr vexlorn vexnak glimzam reldxil pyrxil Every pair standing in the >- relation, grouped by left argument. wrenpyr >- wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil vexlorn >- vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil vexnak >- vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil glimzam >- glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil reldxil >- reldxil and pyrxil pyrxil >- pyrxil

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all naksols x and y, x % y is again a naksol. A2. Association of the first operation. For all naksols x, y, z: (x % y) % z = x % (y % z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all naksols x and y: x % y = y % x.

Two questions sort the naksols quickly. Does combining a naksol with itself change it? For wrenpyr, vexlorn, glimzam and reldxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil it does not. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 naksols the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Nyrazt combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. R3 rests on S2 (the Nyrazt combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take vexlorn % wrenpyr <> reldxil and work it out one step at a time. wrenpyr <> reldxil = wrenpyr (the table for <>) vexlorn % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) The expression comes to wrenpyr. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take wrenpyr % (reldxil % vexlorn). reldxil % vexlorn = reldxil (the table for %) wrenpyr % reldxil = wrenpyr (the table for %) That gives wrenpyr, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does wrenpyr >- wrenpyr hold? Read off what wrenpyr stands over: wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil. wrenpyr is among them, so it holds.

R2. It is not the case that: For every naksol x: x % x = x. The case that settles it: x = vexnak, value = reldxil. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all naksols x, y, z: if x % y = x % z then y = z. It fails at x = wrenpyr, y = wrenpyr, z = vexlorn. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (closure under the second operation) and A7 (association of the second operation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every naksol x: x % x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = vexnak, value = reldxil, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all naksols x, y, z: if x % y = x % z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = wrenpyr, y = wrenpyr, z = vexlorn, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R2 and R3. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

So far the naksols have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about naksols covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a naksol vexlorn with vexlorn % x = x % vexlorn = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a naksol wrenpyr with wrenpyr % x = x % wrenpyr = wrenpyr for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single naksol and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Nyrazt combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take (glimzam % pyrxil) % (vexnak % vexlorn) and work it out one step at a time. glimzam % pyrxil = glimzam (the table for %) vexnak % vexlorn = vexnak (the table for %) glimzam % vexnak = wrenpyr (the table for %) That leaves wrenpyr, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take pyrxil % (vexnak % glimzam). vexnak % glimzam = wrenpyr (the table for %) pyrxil % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) That gives wrenpyr, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does glimzam >- pyrxil hold? Read off what glimzam stands over: glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil. pyrxil is among them, so it holds.

R1. Some naksol x admits no naksol y for which x % y and y % x both land on a neutral object. The case that settles it: x = wrenpyr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
Read alongside S2 (the Nyrazt combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the wrenjen) and T1 (the wrenjen is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some naksol x admits no naksol y for which x % y and y % x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = wrenpyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

We turn to reflexivity of the relation, antisymmetry of the relation and transitivity of the relation. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over naksols, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A11. Reflexivity of the relation. For every naksol x: x >- x. A12. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all naksols x and y: if x >- y and y >- x then x = y. A13. Transitivity of the relation. For all naksols x, y, z: if x >- y and y >- z then x >- z. A14. Comparability of every pair. For all naksols x and y, at least one of x >- y and y >- x holds. A15. Agreement of the relation with the second operation. For all naksols x, y, z: if x >- y then (z <> x) >- (z <> y) and (x <> z) >- (y <> z). D4. The oviwren of a naksol. The oviwren of a naksol x is the collection of naksols y for which x >- y holds. Worked out for each naksol: wrenpyr to wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil; vexlorn to vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil; vexnak to vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil; glimzam to glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil; reldxil to reldxil and pyrxil; pyrxil to pyrxil.

documents.text: Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is self combination under the second operation, closure under the second operation and association of the second operation. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about naksols covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A10. Self combination under the second operation. For every naksol x: x <> x = x. A6. Closure under the second operation. For all naksols x and y, x <> y is again a naksol. A7. Association of the second operation. For all naksols x, y, z: (x <> y) <> z = x <> (y <> z). A8. Commutation of the second operation. For all naksols x and y: x <> y = y <> x. A9. A neutral object for the second operation. There is a naksol pyrxil with pyrxil <> x = x for every x.

documents.text: The interesting content of a two operation system sits in the gap between them: which one distributes over which, and which naksols are fixed by both. Every proof goes through the tables.

documents.text: What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, hobrast naksols, naksols that aztqen and the wrenjen, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over naksols, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

D1. Hobrast naksols. A naksol x is called hobrast when x % x = x. In this system that picks out wrenpyr, vexlorn, glimzam and reldxil, which is 4 of the 6 naksols. D2. Naksols that aztqen. Two naksols x and y are said to aztqen when x % y = y % x. D5. The wrenjen. The naksol vexlorn is called the wrenjen of the system. It is the unique naksol that leaves every naksol unchanged under %. Here that is vexlorn.

A useful mental split: some naksols are inert under the operation and some are not. wrenpyr, vexlorn, glimzam and reldxil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single naksol and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 naksols the table is short enough to consult every time.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Take glimzam % reldxil <> vexnak and work it out one step at a time. reldxil <> vexnak = vexnak (the table for <>) glimzam % vexnak = wrenpyr (the table for %) That leaves wrenpyr, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take reldxil % (vexnak % glimzam). vexnak % glimzam = wrenpyr (the table for %) reldxil % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) That gives wrenpyr, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test pyrxil >- glimzam. The oviwren of pyrxil is pyrxil, and glimzam lies outside it, so the relation fails.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

The material this chapter borrows from: A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). These results are used again in D6 (the iskvash), D7 (the lorngel), D10 (glimvash naksols) and T1 (the wrenjen is the only one of its kind).
No proofs are needed here. Everything asserted is a definition or a table entry.
New vocabulary from this chapter: hobrast naksols, naksols that aztqen and the wrenjen. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

documents.text: D13. Opalrast pairs. Two distinct naksols x and y form a opalrast pair when x >- y and y >- x both hold, that is, when each lies in the oviwren of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Yukgrix collections. A collection S of naksols is yukgrix when x % y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A hurnnak. A naksol f is a hurnnak when f >- y holds for every naksol y, that is, when the oviwren of f is the whole system. In this system that picks out wrenpyr, which is 1 of the 6 naksols.

(2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T10. If y lies in the oviwren of x, then the oviwren of y is contained in the oviwren of x. (1) [D4] Let y satisfy x >- y and let z satisfy y >- z. (2) [A13] Transitivity gives x >- z. (3) [D4] So every member of the oviwren of y is a member of that of x. Checked over 216 cases: every ordered triple. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text: So far the naksols have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up glimvash naksols, the iskvash and the lorngel. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 2 and 5, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over naksols, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

D10. Glimvash naksols. A naksol x is glimvash when x % x equals the wrenjen. In this system that picks out vexlorn and pyrxil, which is 2 of the 6 naksols. D6. The iskvash. The iskvash of the system is the collection of naksols that aztqen with every naksol. Running the definition over every naksol leaves wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil. D7. The lorngel. The lorngel is the collection of all hobrast naksols. Running the definition over every naksol leaves wrenpyr, vexlorn, glimzam and reldxil.

Two questions sort the naksols quickly. Does combining a naksol with itself change it? For wrenpyr, vexlorn, glimzam and reldxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single naksol and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R10 rests on D5 (the wrenjen). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T1 rests on D5 (the wrenjen) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take reldxil % vexnak <> wrenpyr and work it out one step at a time. vexnak <> wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for <>) reldxil % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) So reldxil % vexnak <> wrenpyr is wrenpyr. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take vexnak % (wrenpyr % reldxil). wrenpyr % reldxil = wrenpyr (the table for %) vexnak % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) That gives wrenpyr, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does vexnak >- wrenpyr hold? Read off what vexnak stands over: vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil. wrenpyr is not among them, so it fails.

R10. It is not the case that: e % x equals the wrenjen for every naksol x. The case that settles it: anchor = vexlorn, x = wrenpyr, value = wrenpyr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

Read alongside A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (hobrast naksols), D2 (naksols that aztqen) and D5 (the wrenjen). What is built on it later: T2 (the wrenjen lies in the iskvash), T3 (the iskvash is yukgrix), T8 (the umbglim of a iskvash naksol stays in the iskvash) and T9 (the lorngel is yukgrix).

R10. It is not the case that: e % x equals the wrenjen for every naksol x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = vexlorn, x = wrenpyr, value = wrenpyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one naksol e with e % x = x % e = x for every naksol x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every naksol unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e % f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e % f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 36 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward glimvash naksols, the iskvash and the lorngel. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T1. Do not carry forward R10. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

documents.text: D8. The umbglim of a naksol. The umbglim of a naksol x, written [x], is the smallest yukgrix collection that contains x. Worked out for each naksol: wrenpyr to wrenpyr; vexlorn to vexlorn; vexnak to vexnak and reldxil; glimzam to glimzam; reldxil to reldxil; pyrxil to vexlorn and pyrxil.

documents.text: Picture the umbglim as what happens when you start with one naksol and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. The oviwren of a naksol is everything downhill of it, and those shadows here have sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 naksols the table is short enough to consult every time.

documents.text: T11. No two distinct naksols can both be hurnnaks. (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors. (2) [D9] Then f >- h, since h is any object, and h >- f likewise. (3) [A12] Antisymmetry forces f = h. Checked over 36 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T12. Some naksol hurnnaks the whole system. (1) [A14] Every pair is comparable, so the relation orders the objects into a line. (2) [D9] The claim is that the line has a bottom. (3) The carrier is finite, so the search over candidates terminates. Checked over 36 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T13. No two distinct naksols lie in each other's oviwren. (1) [D13] Suppose x and y form a tight pair. (2) [A12] Antisymmetry then identifies x with y. (3) So a tight pair of distinct objects cannot arise. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text: Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers where every naksol is hobrast breaks down, every naksol lies in the iskvash and the wrenjen lies in the iskvash, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1, 5, 6 and 7, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over naksols, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
Nothing new is named here. The chapter is about consequences of definitions already given.

Two questions sort the naksols quickly. Does combining a naksol with itself change it? For wrenpyr, vexlorn, glimzam and reldxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil it does not. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R7 rests on D7 (the lorngel). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T14 rests on D6 (the iskvash). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T2 rests on D5 (the wrenjen) and D6 (the iskvash). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T3 rests on D6 (the iskvash), D3 (yukgrix collections) and A2 (association of the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T9 rests on D7 (the lorngel) and D3 (yukgrix collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate wrenpyr % vexnak <> glimzam. Each line below is one lookup in a table. vexnak <> glimzam = vexnak (the table for <>) wrenpyr % vexnak = wrenpyr (the table for %) That leaves wrenpyr, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take vexnak % (glimzam % wrenpyr). glimzam % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) vexnak % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) That gives wrenpyr, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does pyrxil >- vexnak hold? Read off what pyrxil stands over: pyrxil. vexnak is not among them, so it fails.
R7. It is not the case that: x % x = x for every naksol x. It fails at x = vexnak, value = reldxil. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

Read alongside A2 (association of the first operation), D3 (yukgrix collections), D5 (the wrenjen) and D6 (the iskvash). What is built on it later: T8 (the umbglim of a iskvash naksol stays in the iskvash) and T15 (the second operation keeps the iskvash intact).

R7. It is not the case that: x % x = x for every naksol x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = vexnak, value = reldxil, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T14. Every pair of naksols aztqens. (1) [D6] The iskvash is defined by aztqening with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x % y = y % x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The wrenjen aztqens with every naksol. (1) [D5] Let e be the wrenjen and x any naksol. (2) [D5] Then e % x = x and x % e = x. (3) [D2] So e % x = x % e, which is what it means to aztqen. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the iskvash. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both aztqen with every naksol, then so does x % y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the iskvash and let z be any naksol. (2) [A2] Then (x % y) % z = x % (y % z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each aztqens with everything. (4) [D3] So x % y aztqens with z, and the iskvash is yukgrix. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. If x and y are both hobrast then so is x % y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be hobrast. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x % y) % (x % y) returns x % y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

The results now available are T14, T2, T3 and T9, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Do not carry forward R7. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

The results collected here were not found in this order. The tumorn of a naksol, the umbglim of a naksol is yukgrix and the umbglim of a iskvash naksol stays in the iskvash came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 6, 7, 8 and 9, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about naksols covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D11. The tumorn of a naksol. The tumorn of a naksol x is the number of naksols in its umbglim [x]. Worked out for each naksol: wrenpyr to 1; vexlorn to 1; vexnak to 2; glimzam to 1; reldxil to 1; pyrxil to 2.

Picture the umbglim as what happens when you start with one naksol and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 6 naksols, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1 and 2. Two questions sort the naksols quickly. Does combining a naksol with itself change it? For wrenpyr, vexlorn, glimzam and reldxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For wrenpyr, vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil it does not. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 naksols the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. T4 rests on D8 (the umbglim of a naksol) and D3 (yukgrix collections). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T8 rests on D8 (the umbglim of a naksol), D6 (the iskvash) and T3 (the iskvash is yukgrix). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (pyrxil % reldxil) % (vexnak % wrenpyr). Each line below is one lookup in a table. pyrxil % reldxil = vexnak (the table for %) vexnak % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) vexnak % wrenpyr = wrenpyr (the table for %) The expression comes to wrenpyr. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is reldxil % (vexnak % pyrxil) for contrast. vexnak % pyrxil = reldxil (the table for %) reldxil % reldxil = reldxil (the table for %) That gives reldxil, against wrenpyr above. Test vexlorn >- reldxil. The oviwren of vexlorn is vexlorn, vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil, and reldxil lies inside it, so the relation holds. Now compute [wrenpyr]. Fold wrenpyr against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is wrenpyr, of size 1.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

Read alongside D3 (yukgrix collections), D6 (the iskvash), D8 (the umbglim of a naksol) and T3 (the iskvash is yukgrix). What is built on it later: D12 (the quilgrix), T5 (the umbglim is contained in every yukgrix collection), T6 (a naksol is hobrast exactly when its tumorn is one) and T7 (the tumorn divides the number of naksols).

T4. For every naksol x, the collection [x] is yukgrix. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under %. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 216 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x lies in the iskvash then every naksol of [x] lies in the iskvash. (1) [T3] The iskvash is yukgrix. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest yukgrix collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the iskvash is one. Checked over 36 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the tumorn of a naksol. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. The results now available are T4 and T8, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy.

The practical content of this chapter is the quilgrix, where some naksol reaches every other breaks down and the umbglim is contained in every yukgrix collection. It is the part that shows up in use. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 5, 8 and 10, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over naksols, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
D12. The quilgrix. The quilgrix of the system is the collection of naksols whose tumorn is largest. Running the definition over every naksol leaves vexnak and pyrxil.

The right picture for umbglim is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one naksol in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1 and 2 naksols depending on where it started. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R8 rests on D8 (the umbglim of a naksol) and D11 (the tumorn of a naksol). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T5 rests on D8 (the umbglim of a naksol) and T4 (the umbglim of a naksol is yukgrix). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T6 rests on D1 (hobrast naksols), D11 (the tumorn of a naksol) and T4 (the umbglim of a naksol is yukgrix). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D11 (the tumorn of a naksol) and T4 (the umbglim of a naksol is yukgrix). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take glimzam % vexlorn <> pyrxil and work it out one step at a time. vexlorn <> pyrxil = vexlorn (the table for <>) glimzam % vexlorn = glimzam (the table for %) That leaves glimzam, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is vexlorn % (pyrxil % glimzam) for contrast. pyrxil % glimzam = glimzam (the table for %) vexlorn % glimzam = glimzam (the table for %) The value is glimzam. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does vexnak >- vexlorn hold? Read off what vexnak stands over: vexnak, glimzam, reldxil and pyrxil. vexlorn is not among them, so it fails.

R8. It is not the case that: There is a naksol whose umbglim is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 2, size = 6. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
The material this chapter borrows from: D1 (hobrast naksols), D11 (the tumorn of a naksol), D8 (the umbglim of a naksol) and T4 (the umbglim of a naksol is yukgrix).

R8. It is not the case that: There is a naksol whose umbglim is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is yukgrix and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 156 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x % x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x % x = x then {x} is already closed under %. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the tumorn is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x % x, which is then x. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every naksol x, the tumorn of x divides 6. (1) [T4] [x] is a yukgrix collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the tumorn of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 6. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

The results now available are T5, T6 and T7, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Do not carry forward R8. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

documents.text:
What follows is a complete account of the Duthsol system. It is complete in a strong
sense: the system has 5 opalmis and finitely many facts, and every one of those facts is
settled here by inspection rather than left to argument.

The opalmis are written keldsib, duthzam, hobfex, iskxil and qenxil. The first operation
is written -. The relation is written <~; where it holds between two opalmis we say the
left one covers the right one. Both operations associate to the left when written
without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is abbreviated: x^3
means x - x - x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through the Duthsol signature, the Duthsol combination tables and closure under the first operation. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about opalmis covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for -. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | keldsib duthzam hobfex iskxil qenxil ------------------------------------------------------- keldsib | keldsib duthzam hobfex iskxil qenxil duthzam | duthzam hobfex iskxil qenxil qenxil hobfex | hobfex iskxil qenxil qenxil qenxil iskxil | iskxil qenxil qenxil qenxil qenxil qenxil | qenxil qenxil qenxil qenxil qenxil Every pair standing in the <~ relation, grouped by left argument. keldsib <~ keldsib duthzam <~ keldsib hobfex <~ keldsib iskxil <~ keldsib qenxil <~ keldsib, duthzam, hobfex, iskxil and qenxil

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all opalmis x and y, x - y is again a opalmi. A2. Association of the first operation. For all opalmis x, y, z: (x - y) - z = x - (y - z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all opalmis x and y: x - y = y - x.

Two questions sort the opalmis quickly. Does combining a opalmi with itself change it? For keldsib and qenxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For keldsib, duthzam, hobfex, iskxil and qenxil it does not. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 opalmis the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Duthsol combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Duthsol combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (iskxil - qenxil) - duthzam, reduced without skipping anything. iskxil - qenxil = qenxil (the table for -) qenxil - duthzam = qenxil (the table for -) That leaves qenxil, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is qenxil - (duthzam - iskxil) for contrast. duthzam - iskxil = qenxil (the table for -) qenxil - qenxil = qenxil (the table for -) That gives qenxil, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. documents.text: The results collected here were not found in this order. D1. Hurnazt opalmis. A opalmi x is called hurnazt when x - x = x. In this system that picks out keldsib and qenxil, which is 2 of the 5 opalmis. D2. Opalmis that hobclo. Two opalmis x and y are said to hobclo when x - y = y - x. D5. The rastfex. The opalmi keldsib is called the rastfex of the system. It is the unique opalmi that leaves every opalmi unchanged under -. Here that is keldsib.

Two questions sort the opalmis quickly. Does combining a opalmi with itself change it? For keldsib and qenxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For keldsib, duthzam, hobfex, iskxil and qenxil it does not. The neutral opalmi keldsib is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. None of these images are load bearing. documents.text: D13. Shenkeld pairs. Two distinct opalmis x and y form a shenkeld pair when x <~ y and y <~ x both hold, that is, when each lies in the muxsib of the other. The muxshen is the collection of all hurnazt opalmis. In this system that picks out keldsib and qenxil, which is 2 of the 5 opalmis.

R11. It is not the case that: e - x equals the rastfex for every opalmi x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = keldsib, x = duthzam, value = duthzam, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one opalmi e with e - x = x - e = x for every opalmi x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every opalmi unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e - f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e - f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 25 cases: every object paired with every object. documents.text: Picture the duthumb as what happens when you start with one opalmi and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 opalmis, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. The relation is easiest to see as a height. Each opalmi casts a muxsib over what it covers, and the sizes of those shadows here are 1 and 5. Sizes repeat, so the objects do not line up in single file. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T11 rests on D13 (shenkeld pairs) and A6 (antisymmetry of the relation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Each line below is one lookup in a table. keldsib - duthzam = duthzam (the table for -) duthzam - iskxil = qenxil (the table for -) The expression comes to qenxil. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is duthzam - (iskxil - keldsib) for contrast. iskxil - keldsib = iskxil (the table for -) duthzam - iskxil = qenxil (the table for -) That gives qenxil, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test keldsib <~ duthzam. The muxsib of keldsib is keldsib, and duthzam lies outside it, so the relation fails. Now compute [hobfex]. Fold hobfex against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is hobfex and qenxil, of size 2.

documents.text: Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of opalmis that come back unchanged from themselves: keldsib and qenxil. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

These results are used again in D11 (the muxbra of a opalmi), T4 (the duthumb of a opalmi is tezmorn), T5 (the duthumb is contained in every tezmorn collection) and T7 (the duthumb of a nakfal opalmi stays in the nakfal).

documents.text: T10. No two distinct opalmis can both be rastzels. (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors. (2) [D9] Then f <~ h, since h is any object, and h <~ f likewise. (3) [A6] Antisymmetry forces f = h. Checked over 25 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T11. No two distinct opalmis lie in each other's muxsib. (1) [D13] Suppose x and y form a tight pair. (2) [A6] Antisymmetry then identifies x with y. (3) So a tight pair of distinct objects cannot arise. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text: Carry forward the duthumb of a opalmi. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. The results now available are T10 and T11, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy.
