documents.text: Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers where every opalmi is hurnazt breaks down, every opalmi lies in the nakfal and the rastfex lies in the nakfal, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1, 4, 5 and 6, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 5 opalmis that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
Nothing new is named here. The chapter is about consequences of definitions already given.

A useful mental split: some opalmis are inert under the operation and some are not. keldsib and qenxil come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and keldsib, duthzam, hobfex, iskxil and qenxil commute with everything. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R8 rests on D7 (the muxshen). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T12 rests on D6 (the nakfal). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T2 rests on D5 (the rastfex) and D6 (the nakfal). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T3 rests on D6 (the nakfal), D3 (tezmorn collections) and A2 (association of the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T8 rests on D7 (the muxshen) and D3 (tezmorn collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (hobfex - keldsib) - (qenxil - duthzam). Each line below is one lookup in a table. hobfex - keldsib = hobfex (the table for -) qenxil - duthzam = qenxil (the table for -) hobfex - qenxil = qenxil (the table for -) That leaves qenxil, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, keldsib - (qenxil - hobfex), to show what the brackets are doing. qenxil - hobfex = qenxil (the table for -) keldsib - qenxil = qenxil (the table for -) The value is qenxil. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test iskxil <~ duthzam. The muxsib of iskxil is keldsib, and duthzam lies outside it, so the relation fails.
R8. It is not the case that: x - x = x for every opalmi x. It fails at x = duthzam, value = hobfex. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation, association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

The material this chapter borrows from: A2 (association of the first operation), D3 (tezmorn collections), D5 (the rastfex) and D6 (the nakfal). What is built on it later: T7 (the duthumb of a nakfal opalmi stays in the nakfal).

R8. It is not the case that: x - x = x for every opalmi x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = duthzam, value = hobfex, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T12. Every pair of opalmis hobclos. (1) [D6] The nakfal is defined by hobcloing with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x - y = y - x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The rastfex hobclos with every opalmi. (1) [D5] Let e be the rastfex and x any opalmi. (2) [D5] Then e - x = x and x - e = x. (3) [D2] So e - x = x - e, which is what it means to hobclo. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the nakfal. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both hobclo with every opalmi, then so does x - y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the nakfal and let z be any opalmi. (2) [A2] Then (x - y) - z = x - (y - z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each hobclos with everything. (4) [D3] So x - y hobclos with z, and the nakfal is tezmorn. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x and y are both hurnazt then so is x - y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be hurnazt. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x - y) - (x - y) returns x - y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

The results now available are T12, T2, T3 and T8, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Explicitly not available: R8. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, the muxbra of a opalmi, the duthumb of a opalmi is tezmorn and the duthumb of a nakfal opalmi stays in the nakfal, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 5, 6, 7 and 8 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over opalmis, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.
D11. The muxbra of a opalmi. The muxbra of a opalmi x is the number of opalmis in its duthumb [x]. Worked out for each opalmi: keldsib to 1; duthzam to 4; hobfex to 2; iskxil to 2; qenxil to 1.

Picture the duthumb as what happens when you start with one opalmi and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 opalmis, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. Two questions sort the opalmis quickly. Does combining a opalmi with itself change it? For keldsib and qenxil it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For keldsib, duthzam, hobfex, iskxil and qenxil it does not. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 opalmis the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. T4 rests on D8 (the duthumb of a opalmi) and D3 (tezmorn collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D8 (the duthumb of a opalmi), D6 (the nakfal) and T3 (the nakfal is tezmorn). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Here is (keldsib - qenxil) - duthzam, reduced without skipping anything. keldsib - qenxil = qenxil (the table for -) qenxil - duthzam = qenxil (the table for -) So (keldsib - qenxil) - duthzam is qenxil. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is qenxil - (duthzam - keldsib) for contrast. duthzam - keldsib = duthzam (the table for -) qenxil - duthzam = qenxil (the table for -) The value is qenxil. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does duthzam <~ iskxil hold? Read off what duthzam stands over: keldsib. iskxil is not among them, so it fails. Now compute [hobfex]. Fold hobfex against itself, then fold whatever appeared against everything present, and stop when a round adds nothing. The result is hobfex and qenxil, of size 2.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by association of the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

Read alongside D3 (tezmorn collections), D6 (the nakfal), D8 (the duthumb of a opalmi) and T3 (the nakfal is tezmorn). What is built on it later: D12 (the tezopal), T5 (the duthumb is contained in every tezmorn collection), T6 (a opalmi is hurnazt exactly when its muxbra is one) and R7 (where the muxbra divides the number of opalmis breaks down).

T4. For every opalmi x, the collection [x] is tezmorn. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under -. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 125 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the nakfal then every opalmi of [x] lies in the nakfal. (1) [T3] The nakfal is tezmorn. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest tezmorn collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the nakfal is one. Checked over 25 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
New vocabulary from this chapter: the muxbra of a opalmi. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T4 and T7.

The practical content of this chapter is the tezopal, where the muxbra divides the number of opalmis breaks down and where some opalmi reaches every other breaks down. It is the part that shows up in use. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 4, 7 and 9 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about opalmis covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.
D12. The tezopal. The tezopal of the system is the collection of opalmis whose muxbra is largest. Running the definition over every opalmi leaves duthzam.

Picture the duthumb as what happens when you start with one opalmi and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 opalmis, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 opalmis the table is short enough to consult every time.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R7 rests on D11 (the muxbra of a opalmi) and T4 (the duthumb of a opalmi is tezmorn). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R9 rests on D8 (the duthumb of a opalmi) and D11 (the muxbra of a opalmi). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T5 rests on D8 (the duthumb of a opalmi) and T4 (the duthumb of a opalmi is tezmorn). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T6 rests on D1 (hurnazt opalmis), D11 (the muxbra of a opalmi) and T4 (the duthumb of a opalmi is tezmorn). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (hobfex - keldsib) - (qenxil - iskxil), reduced without skipping anything. hobfex - keldsib = hobfex (the table for -) qenxil - iskxil = qenxil (the table for -) hobfex - qenxil = qenxil (the table for -) The expression comes to qenxil. A companion case, keldsib - (qenxil - hobfex), to show what the brackets are doing. qenxil - hobfex = qenxil (the table for -) keldsib - qenxil = qenxil (the table for -) That gives qenxil, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test keldsib <~ hobfex. The muxsib of keldsib is keldsib, and hobfex lies outside it, so the relation fails.

R7. It is not the case that: For every opalmi x, the muxbra of x divides 5. It fails at x = duthzam, reach = 4, size = 5. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R9. It is not the case that: There is a opalmi whose duthumb is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 4, size = 5. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
The material this chapter borrows from: D1 (hurnazt opalmis), D11 (the muxbra of a opalmi), D8 (the duthumb of a opalmi) and T4 (the duthumb of a opalmi is tezmorn).

R7. It is not the case that: For every opalmi x, the muxbra of x divides 5. (1) [S2] Take the case x = duthzam, reach = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R9. It is not the case that: There is a opalmi whose duthumb is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is tezmorn and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 55 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x - x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x - x = x then {x} is already closed under -. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the muxbra is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x - x, which is then x. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: the tezopal. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T5 and T6. Explicitly not available: R7 and R9. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

documents.text:
The Vintfex system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth
the trouble. It has 5 shenopals, two operations, and one relation, and nothing else.

The shenopals are written opallorn, qenthra, grixlum, vorpon and pontu. The first
operation is written %. The second is written & and binds more tightly, so x % y & z
means x % (y & z). The relation is written ::; where it holds between two shenopals we
say the left one yields to the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x % x % x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

The present chapter develops the Vintfex signature, the Vintfex combination tables and closure under the first operation. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 5 shenopals that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for %. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | opallorn qenthra grixlum vorpon pontu ------------------------------------------------------------- opallorn | opallorn opallorn opallorn opallorn opallorn qenthra | opallorn qenthra grixlum vorpon pontu grixlum | opallorn grixlum pontu qenthra vorpon vorpon | opallorn vorpon qenthra pontu grixlum pontu | opallorn pontu vorpon grixlum qenthra The table for &. These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all shenopals x and y, x % y is again a shenopal. A2. documents.text: D13. Falreld pairs. Two distinct shenopals x and y form a falreld pair when x :: y and y :: x both hold, that is, when each lies in the mornclo of the other. documents.text: Everything in this chapter is checkable by inspection. The subject is muxnak shenopals, the opalopal and the kadri. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 2 and 5 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about shenopals covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D10. Muxnak shenopals. A shenopal x is muxnak when x % x equals the kazam. Running the definition over every shenopal leaves qenthra and pontu. D6. The opalopal. The opalopal of the system is the collection of shenopals that tezshen with every shenopal. Running the definition over every shenopal leaves opallorn, qenthra, grixlum, vorpon and pontu. D7. The kadri. The kadri is the collection of all sollum shenopals. Running the definition over every shenopal leaves opallorn and qenthra.

A useful mental split: some shenopals are inert under the operation and some are not. opallorn and qenthra come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and opallorn, qenthra, grixlum, vorpon and pontu commute with everything. The neutral shenopal qenthra is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R14 rests on D5 (the kazam). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T1 rests on D5 (the kazam) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take grixlum % opallorn & qenthra and work it out one step at a time. opallorn & qenthra = qenthra (the table for &) grixlum % qenthra = grixlum (the table for %) That leaves grixlum, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take opallorn % (qenthra % grixlum). qenthra % grixlum = grixlum (the table for %) opallorn % grixlum = opallorn (the table for %) That gives opallorn, against grixlum above. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does grixlum :: grixlum hold? Read off what grixlum stands over: nothing at all. grixlum is not among them, so it fails.

R14. It is not the case that: e % x equals the kazam for every shenopal x. The case that settles it: anchor = qenthra, x = opallorn, value = opallorn. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (sollum shenopals), D2 (shenopals that tezshen) and D5 (the kazam). These results are used again in T2 (the kazam lies in the opalopal), T3 (the opalopal is tutez), T7 (the lumsib of a opalopal shenopal stays in the opalopal) and T8 (the kadri is tutez).

R14. It is not the case that: e % x equals the kazam for every shenopal x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = qenthra, x = opallorn, value = opallorn, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one shenopal e with e % x = x % e = x for every shenopal x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every shenopal unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e % f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e % f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 25 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: muxnak shenopals, the opalopal and the kadri. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. The results now available are T1, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Explicitly not available: R14. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The results collected here were not found in this order. The lumsib of a shenopal, there is at most one zelhurn and no falreld pairs exist came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 3 and 6, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over shenopals, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

documents.text: D8. The lumsib of a shenopal. The lumsib of a shenopal x, written [x], is the smallest tutez collection that contains x. Worked out for each shenopal: opallorn to opallorn; qenthra to qenthra; grixlum to qenthra, grixlum, vorpon and pontu; vorpon to qenthra, grixlum, vorpon and pontu; pontu to qenthra and pontu.

documents.text: T10. No two distinct shenopals can both be zelhurns. (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors. (2) [D9] Then f :: h, since h is any object, and h :: f likewise. (3) [A10] Antisymmetry forces f = h. Checked over 25 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T12. No two distinct shenopals lie in each other's mornclo. (1) [D13] Suppose x and y form a tight pair. (2) [A10] Antisymmetry then identifies x with y. (3) So a tight pair of distinct objects cannot arise. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text: The practical content of this chapter is where every shenopal is sollum breaks down, every shenopal lies in the opalopal and the kazam lies in the opalopal. It is the part that shows up in use. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1, 5, 6 and 7, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over shenopals, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.
Nothing new is named here. The chapter is about consequences of definitions already given.

Two questions sort the shenopals quickly. Does combining a shenopal with itself change it? For opallorn and qenthra it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For opallorn, qenthra, grixlum, vorpon and pontu it does not. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T13 rests on D6 (the opalopal). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T2 rests on D5 (the kazam) and D6 (the opalopal). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T3 rests on D6 (the opalopal), D3 (tutez collections) and A2 (association of the first operation). Each line below is one lookup in a table. grixlum & pontu = qenthra (the table for &) vorpon % qenthra = vorpon (the table for %) So vorpon % grixlum & pontu is vorpon. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is grixlum % (pontu % vorpon) for contrast. pontu % vorpon = grixlum (the table for %) grixlum % grixlum = pontu (the table for %) That gives pontu, against vorpon above. Test pontu :: vorpon. The mornclo of pontu is empty, and vorpon lies outside it, so the relation fails.
R11. It is not the case that: x % x = x for every shenopal x. It fails at x = grixlum, value = pontu. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

R11. It is not the case that: x % x = x for every shenopal x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = grixlum, value = pontu, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T13. Every pair of shenopals tezshens. (1) [D6] The opalopal is defined by tezshening with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x % y = y % x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The kazam tezshens with every shenopal. (1) [D5] Let e be the kazam and x any shenopal. (2) [D5] Then e % x = x and x % e = x. (3) [D2] So e % x = x % e, which is what it means to tezshen. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the opalopal. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both tezshen with every shenopal, then so does x % y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the opalopal and let z be any shenopal. (2) [A2] Then (x % y) % z = x % (y % z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each tezshens with everything. (4) [D3] So x % y tezshens with z, and the opalopal is tutez. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x and y are both sollum then so is x % y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be sollum. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x % y) % (x % y) returns x % y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Established here and safe to use: T13, T2, T3 and T8. Do not carry forward R11. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

So far the shenopals have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up the solmux of a shenopal, the lumsib of a shenopal is tutez and the lumsib of a opalopal shenopal stays in the opalopal. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 6, 7, 8 and 9, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over shenopals, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

D11. The solmux of a shenopal. The solmux of a shenopal x is the number of shenopals in its lumsib [x]. Worked out for each shenopal: opallorn to 1; qenthra to 1; grixlum to 4; vorpon to 4; pontu to 2.

Picture the lumsib as what happens when you start with one shenopal and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 shenopals, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. A useful mental split: some shenopals are inert under the operation and some are not. opallorn and qenthra come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and opallorn, qenthra, grixlum, vorpon and pontu commute with everything. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. T4 rests on D8 (the lumsib of a shenopal) and D3 (tutez collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T7 rests on D8 (the lumsib of a shenopal), D6 (the opalopal) and T3 (the opalopal is tutez). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (qenthra % pontu) % (opallorn % grixlum) and work it out one step at a time. qenthra % pontu = pontu (the table for %) opallorn % grixlum = opallorn (the table for %) pontu % opallorn = opallorn (the table for %) So (qenthra % pontu) % (opallorn % grixlum) is opallorn. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take pontu % (opallorn % qenthra). opallorn % qenthra = opallorn (the table for %) pontu % opallorn = opallorn (the table for %) That gives opallorn, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does pontu :: qenthra hold? Read off what pontu stands over: nothing at all. qenthra is not among them, so it fails. A second case, this time a lumsib. Start from vorpon. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is qenthra, grixlum, vorpon and pontu, so the solmux of vorpon is 4.

These results are used again in D12 (the sibglim), T5 (the lumsib is contained in every tutez collection), T6 (a shenopal is sollum exactly when its solmux is one) and R10 (where the solmux divides the number of shenopals breaks down).

T4. For every shenopal x, the collection [x] is tutez. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under %. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 125 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the opalopal then every shenopal of [x] lies in the opalopal. (1) [T3] The opalopal is tutez. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest tutez collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the opalopal is one. Checked over 25 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
New vocabulary from this chapter: the solmux of a shenopal. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. Established here and safe to use: T4 and T7.

We turn to the sibglim, where the solmux divides the number of shenopals breaks down and where some shenopal reaches every other breaks down. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 5, 8 and 10 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.
D12. The sibglim. The sibglim of the system is the collection of shenopals whose solmux is largest. In this system that picks out grixlum and vorpon, which is 2 of the 5 shenopals.

The right picture for lumsib is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one shenopal in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1, 2 and 4 shenopals depending on where it started. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 shenopals the table is short enough to consult every time.

It fails at largest_span = 4, size = 5. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

R10. It is not the case that: For every shenopal x, the solmux of x divides 5. (1) [S2] Take the case x = grixlum, reach = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is tutez and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 35 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x % x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x % x = x then {x} is already closed under %. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the solmux is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x % x, which is then x. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text:
The Quilpon system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth
the trouble. It has 6 lumpons, one operation, and one relation, and nothing else.

The lumpons are written glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob. The
first operation is written -. The relation is written >-; where it holds between two
lumpons we say the left one precedes the right one. Both operations associate to the
left when written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x - x - x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers the Quilpon signature, the Quilpon combination tables and closure under the first operation, and each claim can be checked by hand. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about lumpons covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The table for -. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | glimtez glimkorr nakkorr duthwren kaka mornhob ----------------------------------------------------------------------- glimtez | glimtez glimkorr nakkorr duthwren kaka mornhob glimkorr | glimkorr nakkorr duthwren kaka mornhob mornhob nakkorr | nakkorr duthwren kaka mornhob mornhob mornhob duthwren | duthwren kaka mornhob mornhob mornhob mornhob kaka | kaka mornhob mornhob mornhob mornhob mornhob mornhob | mornhob mornhob mornhob mornhob mornhob mornhob Every pair standing in the >- relation, grouped by left argument. glimtez >- glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob glimkorr >- glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob nakkorr >- nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob duthwren >- duthwren, kaka and mornhob kaka >- kaka and mornhob mornhob >- mornhob

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all lumpons x and y, x - y is again a lumpon. A2. Association of the first operation. For all lumpons x, y, z: (x - y) - z = x - (y - z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all lumpons x and y: x - y = y - x.

A useful mental split: some lumpons are inert under the operation and some are not. glimtez and mornhob come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob commute with everything. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Quilpon combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Quilpon combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take (glimtez - kaka) - mornhob and work it out one step at a time. glimtez - kaka = kaka (the table for -) kaka - mornhob = mornhob (the table for -) That leaves mornhob, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is kaka - (mornhob - glimtez) for contrast. mornhob - glimtez = mornhob (the table for -) kaka - mornhob = mornhob (the table for -) That gives mornhob, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does kaka >- glimkorr hold? Read off what kaka stands over: kaka and mornhob. glimkorr is not among them, so it fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every lumpon x: x - x = x. The case that settles it: x = glimkorr, value = nakkorr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all lumpons x, y, z: if x - y = x - z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = glimkorr, y = kaka, z = mornhob. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (reflexivity of the relation) and A7 (antisymmetry of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every lumpon x: x - x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimkorr, value = nakkorr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all lumpons x, y, z: if x - y = x - z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimkorr, y = kaka, z = mornhob, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The results collected here were not found in this order. A neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation came first, and the rest was assembled around that once the pattern was visible. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 lumpons that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a lumpon glimtez with glimtez - x = x - glimtez = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a lumpon mornhob with mornhob - x = x - mornhob = mornhob for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single lumpon and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R1 rests on S2 (the Quilpon combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Take (duthwren - glimkorr) - (glimtez - kaka) and work it out one step at a time. duthwren - glimkorr = kaka (the table for -) glimtez - kaka = kaka (the table for -) kaka - kaka = mornhob (the table for -) The expression comes to mornhob. A companion case, glimkorr - (glimtez - duthwren), to show what the brackets are doing. glimtez - duthwren = duthwren (the table for -) glimkorr - duthwren = kaka (the table for -) That gives kaka, against mornhob above. Test nakkorr >- kaka. The jenmorn of nakkorr is nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob, and kaka lies inside it, so the relation holds.
R1. Some lumpon x admits no lumpon y for which x - y and y - x both land on a neutral object. It fails at x = glimkorr. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside S2 (the Quilpon combination tables). What is built on it later: D5 (the gelmi) and T1 (the gelmi is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some lumpon x admits no lumpon y for which x - y and y - x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimkorr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R1. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

The practical content of this chapter is agreement of the relation with the first operation, reflexivity of the relation and antisymmetry of the relation. It is the part that shows up in use. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about lumpons covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A10. Agreement of the relation with the first operation. For all lumpons x, y, z: if x >- y then (z - x) >- (z - y) and (x - z) >- (y - z). A6. Reflexivity of the relation. For every lumpon x: x >- x. A7. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all lumpons x and y: if x >- y and y >- x then x = y. A8. Transitivity of the relation. For all lumpons x, y, z: if x >- y and y >- z then x >- z. A9. Comparability of every pair. For all lumpons x and y, at least one of x >- y and y >- x holds. D4. The jenmorn of a lumpon. The jenmorn of a lumpon x is the collection of lumpons y for which x >- y holds. Worked out for each lumpon: glimtez to glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob; glimkorr to glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob; nakkorr to nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob; duthwren to duthwren, kaka and mornhob; kaka to kaka and mornhob; mornhob to mornhob.

documents.text: So far the lumpons have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up zelespa lumpons, lumpons that miquil and the gelmi. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 lumpons that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent.

D1. Zelespa lumpons. A lumpon x is called zelespa when x - x = x. In this system that picks out glimtez and mornhob, which is 2 of the 6 lumpons. D2. Lumpons that miquil. Two lumpons x and y are said to miquil when x - y = y - x. D5. The gelmi. The lumpon glimtez is called the gelmi of the system. It is the unique lumpon that leaves every lumpon unchanged under -. Here that is glimtez.

A useful mental split: some lumpons are inert under the operation and some are not. glimtez and mornhob come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single lumpon and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Take (duthwren - nakkorr) - (kaka - glimtez) and work it out one step at a time. duthwren - nakkorr = mornhob (the table for -) kaka - glimtez = kaka (the table for -) mornhob - kaka = mornhob (the table for -) The expression comes to mornhob. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take nakkorr - (kaka - duthwren). kaka - duthwren = mornhob (the table for -) nakkorr - mornhob = mornhob (the table for -) The value is mornhob. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test glimtez >- glimtez. The jenmorn of glimtez is glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob, and glimtez lies inside it, so the relation holds.
No counterexample exists to anything asserted here. That is a fact about this system and not a general one, and the next chapter is where it stops being true.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). What is built on it later: D6 (the nyrhurn), D7 (the tezduth), D10 (naklorn lumpons) and T1 (the gelmi is the only one of its kind).
No proofs are needed here. Everything asserted is a definition or a table entry.
New vocabulary from this chapter: zelespa lumpons, lumpons that miquil and the gelmi. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up.

The present chapter develops nakkeld pairs, muxovi collections and a grixfex. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1 and 3 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over lumpons, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

documents.text: D13. Nakkeld pairs. Two distinct lumpons x and y form a nakkeld pair when x >- y and y >- x both hold, that is, when each lies in the jenmorn of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Muxovi collections. A collection S of lumpons is muxovi when x - y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A grixfex. A lumpon f is a grixfex when f >- y holds for every lumpon y, that is, when the jenmorn of f is the whole system. In this system that picks out glimtez, which is 1 of the 6 lumpons.

The stain here reaches 1, 2, 3 and 5 lumpons depending on where it started. Think of >- as pointing downhill. The jenmorn of a lumpon is everything downhill of it, and those shadows here have sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Treat the above as scaffolding. documents.text: Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers naklorn lumpons, the nyrhurn and the tezduth, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 2 and 4, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 lumpons that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D10. Naklorn lumpons. A lumpon x is naklorn when x - x equals the gelmi. Running the definition over every lumpon leaves glimtez. D6. The nyrhurn. The nyrhurn of the system is the collection of lumpons that miquil with every lumpon. Running the definition over every lumpon leaves glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob. D7. The tezduth. The tezduth is the collection of all zelespa lumpons. Running the definition over every lumpon leaves glimtez and mornhob.

A useful mental split: some lumpons are inert under the operation and some are not. glimtez and mornhob come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob commute with everything. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single lumpon and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R8 rests on D5 (the gelmi). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T1 rests on D5 (the gelmi) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take duthwren - (glimtez - glimkorr). glimtez - glimkorr = glimkorr (the table for -) duthwren - glimkorr = kaka (the table for -) The value is kaka, not mornhob. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does glimtez >- nakkorr hold? Read off what glimtez stands over: glimtez, glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob. nakkorr is among them, so it holds.

R8. It is not the case that: e - x equals the gelmi for every lumpon x. The case that settles it: anchor = glimtez, x = glimkorr, value = glimkorr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (zelespa lumpons), D2 (lumpons that miquil) and D5 (the gelmi). What is built on it later: T2 (the gelmi lies in the nyrhurn), T3 (the nyrhurn is muxovi), T7 (the xilhob of a nyrhurn lumpon stays in the nyrhurn) and T8 (the tezduth is muxovi).

R8. It is not the case that: e - x equals the gelmi for every lumpon x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = glimtez, x = glimkorr, value = glimkorr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one lumpon e with e - x = x - e = x for every lumpon x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every lumpon unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e - f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e - f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 36 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

New vocabulary from this chapter: naklorn lumpons, the nyrhurn and the tezduth. Each of these is used by name later, so the names are worth learning rather than looking up. The results now available are T1, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Explicitly not available: R8. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, the xilhob of a lumpon, there is at most one grixfex and the system has a grixfex, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 3 and 5 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over lumpons, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

documents.text: T10. No two distinct lumpons can both be grixfexs. (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors. (2) [D9] Then f >- h, since h is any object, and h >- f likewise. (3) [A7] Antisymmetry forces f = h. Checked over 36 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T11. Some lumpon grixfexs the whole system. (1) [A9] Every pair is comparable, so the relation orders the objects into a line. (2) [D9] The claim is that the line has a bottom. (3) The carrier is finite, so the search over candidates terminates. Checked over 36 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T13. No two distinct lumpons lie in each other's jenmorn. (1) [D13] Suppose x and y form a tight pair. (2) [A7] Antisymmetry then identifies x with y. (3) So a tight pair of distinct objects cannot arise. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

(2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. (2) [D2] The claim is that x - y = y - x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair. (2) [D5] Then e - x = x and x - e = x. (3) [D2] So e - x = x - e, which is what it means to miquil. (4)

[D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the nyrhurn. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both miquil with every lumpon, then so does x - y. (1) [D6] Let x and y lie in the nyrhurn and let z be any lumpon. (2) [A2] Then (x - y) - z = x - (y - z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each miquils with everything. (4) [D3] So x - y miquils with z, and the nyrhurn is muxovi. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x and y are both zelespa then so is x - y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be zelespa. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x - y) - (x - y) returns x - y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 36 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Established here and safe to use: T14, T2, T3 and T8. Do not carry forward R5. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

D12. The keldglim. The keldglim of the system is the collection of lumpons whose zelgrix is largest. Running the definition over every lumpon leaves glimkorr.

Picture the xilhob as what happens when you start with one lumpon and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 6 lumpons, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2, 3 and 5. Treat the above as scaffolding. Read off what glimkorr stands over: glimkorr, nakkorr, duthwren, kaka and mornhob. mornhob is among them, so it holds.

R4. It is not the case that: For every lumpon x, the zelgrix of x divides 6. It fails at x = glimkorr, reach = 5, size = 6. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R6. It is not the case that: There is a lumpon whose xilhob is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 5, size = 6. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
Read alongside D1 (zelespa lumpons), D11 (the zelgrix of a lumpon), D8 (the xilhob of a lumpon) and T4 (the xilhob of a lumpon is muxovi).

R4. It is not the case that: For every lumpon x, the zelgrix of x divides 6. (1) [S2] Take the case x = glimkorr, reach = 5, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R6. It is not the case that: There is a lumpon whose xilhob is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 5, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is muxovi and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 90 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x - x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x - x = x then {x} is already closed under -. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the zelgrix is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x - x, which is then x. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the keldglim. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. The results now available are T5 and T6, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Do not carry forward R4 and R6. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

documents.text:
The Vorjen system is small enough to hold in the hand and strange enough to be worth the
trouble. It has 6 driwrens, one operation, and one relation, and nothing else.

The driwrens are written nakquil, soltarn, muxsib, braovi, yukzel and thraisk. The first
operation is written *. The relation is written <<; where it holds between two driwrens
we say the left one precedes the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x * x * x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, the Vorjen signature, the Vorjen combination tables and closure under the first operation, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about driwrens covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The table for *. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | nakquil soltarn muxsib braovi yukzel thraisk ---------------------------------------------------------------- nakquil | nakquil nakquil nakquil nakquil nakquil nakquil soltarn | nakquil soltarn muxsib braovi yukzel thraisk muxsib | nakquil muxsib yukzel nakquil muxsib yukzel braovi | nakquil braovi nakquil braovi nakquil braovi yukzel | nakquil yukzel muxsib nakquil yukzel muxsib thraisk | nakquil thraisk yukzel braovi muxsib soltarn Every pair standing in the << relation, grouped by left argument. nakquil << nakquil, soltarn, muxsib, braovi, yukzel and thraisk soltarn << soltarn muxsib << soltarn and yukzel braovi << soltarn, braovi and thraisk yukzel << soltarn and yukzel thraisk << soltarn

These are the laws this system obeys. Each was checked against every case before it was written down. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all driwrens x and y, x * y is again a driwren. A2. Association of the first operation. For all driwrens x, y, z: (x * y) * z = x * (y * z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all driwrens x and y: x * y = y * x.

A useful mental split: some driwrens are inert under the operation and some are not. nakquil, soltarn, braovi and yukzel come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and nakquil, soltarn, muxsib, braovi, yukzel and thraisk commute with everything. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Vorjen combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Vorjen combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (soltarn * muxsib) * nakquil. Each line below is one lookup in a table. soltarn * muxsib = muxsib (the table for *) muxsib * nakquil = nakquil (the table for *) So (soltarn * muxsib) * nakquil is nakquil. A companion case, muxsib * (nakquil * soltarn), to show what the brackets are doing. nakquil * soltarn = nakquil (the table for *) muxsib * nakquil = nakquil (the table for *) That gives nakquil, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test soltarn << braovi. The hobvint of soltarn is soltarn, and braovi lies outside it, so the relation fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every driwren x: x * x = x. The case that settles it: x = muxsib, value = yukzel. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all driwrens x, y, z: if x * y = x * z then y = z. It fails at x = nakquil, y = nakquil, z = soltarn. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (antisymmetry of the relation) and A7 (transitivity of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every driwren x: x * x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = muxsib, value = yukzel, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all driwrens x, y, z: if x * y = x * z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = nakquil, y = nakquil, z = soltarn, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The practical content of this chapter is a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. It is the part that shows up in use. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 driwrens that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a driwren soltarn with soltarn * x = x * soltarn = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a driwren nakquil with nakquil * x = x * nakquil = nakquil for every x.

The neutral driwren soltarn is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Vorjen combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Take (braovi * soltarn) * (yukzel * muxsib) and work it out one step at a time. braovi * soltarn = braovi (the table for *) yukzel * muxsib = muxsib (the table for *) braovi * muxsib = nakquil (the table for *) That leaves nakquil, and no other reading of the notation gives anything else. A companion case, soltarn * (yukzel * braovi), to show what the brackets are doing. yukzel * braovi = nakquil (the table for *) soltarn * nakquil = nakquil (the table for *) The value is nakquil. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test thraisk << soltarn. The hobvint of thraisk is soltarn, and soltarn lies inside it, so the relation holds.

R1. Some driwren x admits no driwren y for which x * y and y * x both land on a neutral object. The case that settles it: x = nakquil. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
Read alongside S2 (the Vorjen combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the duthgrix) and T1 (the duthgrix is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some driwren x admits no driwren y for which x * y and y * x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = nakquil, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through antisymmetry of the relation, transitivity of the relation and the hobvint of a driwren. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 driwrens that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A6. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all driwrens x and y: if x << y and y << x then x = y. A7. Transitivity of the relation. For all driwrens x, y, z: if x << y and y << z then x << z. D4. The hobvint of a driwren. The hobvint of a driwren x is the collection of driwrens y for which x << y holds. Worked out for each driwren: nakquil to nakquil, soltarn, muxsib, braovi, yukzel and thraisk; soltarn to soltarn; muxsib to soltarn and yukzel; braovi to soltarn, braovi and thraisk; yukzel to soltarn and yukzel; thraisk to soltarn.
