documents.text: The present chapter develops shenka driwrens, driwrens that shentu and the duthgrix. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1 and 2 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over driwrens, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other.

D1. Shenka driwrens. A driwren x is called shenka when x * x = x. In this system that picks out nakquil, soltarn, braovi and yukzel, which is 4 of the 6 driwrens. D2. Driwrens that shentu. Two driwrens x and y are said to shentu when x * y = y * x. D5. The duthgrix. The driwren soltarn is called the duthgrix of the system. It is the unique driwren that leaves every driwren unchanged under *. Here that is soltarn.

Two questions sort the driwrens quickly. Does combining a driwren with itself change it? For nakquil, soltarn, braovi and yukzel it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For nakquil, soltarn, muxsib, braovi, yukzel and thraisk it does not. The neutral driwren soltarn is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.
Nothing is derived in this chapter. It lays down material that later chapters draw on.

Here is (thraisk * braovi) * (yukzel * nakquil), reduced without skipping anything. thraisk * braovi = braovi (the table for *) yukzel * nakquil = nakquil (the table for *) braovi * nakquil = nakquil (the table for *) So (thraisk * braovi) * (yukzel * nakquil) is nakquil. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take braovi * (yukzel * thraisk). yukzel * thraisk = muxsib (the table for *) braovi * muxsib = nakquil (the table for *) That gives nakquil, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test thraisk << yukzel. The hobvint of thraisk is soltarn, and yukzel lies outside it, so the relation fails.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of driwrens that come back unchanged from themselves: nakquil, soltarn, braovi and yukzel. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.

documents.text: D13. Pyrfex pairs. Two distinct driwrens x and y form a pyrfex pair when x << y and y << x both hold, that is, when each lies in the hobvint of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Driglim collections. A collection S of driwrens is driglim when x * y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A zelpyr. A driwren f is a zelpyr when f << y holds for every driwren y, that is, when the hobvint of f is the whole system. In this system that picks out nakquil, which is 1 of the 6 driwrens.

documents.text: What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, rastjen driwrens, the vintnak and the duthsib, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 2 and 4 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over driwrens, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

D10. Rastjen driwrens. A driwren x is rastjen when x * x equals the duthgrix. Running the definition over every driwren leaves soltarn and thraisk. D6. The vintnak. The vintnak of the system is the collection of driwrens that shentu with every driwren. Running the definition over every driwren leaves nakquil, soltarn, muxsib, braovi, yukzel and thraisk. D7. The duthsib. The duthsib is the collection of all shenka driwrens. In this system that picks out nakquil, soltarn, braovi and yukzel, which is 4 of the 6 driwrens.

Two questions sort the driwrens quickly. Does combining a driwren with itself change it? For nakquil, soltarn, braovi and yukzel it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For nakquil, soltarn, muxsib, braovi, yukzel and thraisk it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single driwren and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 6 driwrens the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R10 rests on D5 (the duthgrix). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T1 rests on D5 (the duthgrix) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Move the brackets and the work changes. Take yukzel * (thraisk * muxsib). thraisk * muxsib = yukzel (the table for *) yukzel * yukzel = yukzel (the table for *) The value is yukzel, not nakquil. Test braovi << muxsib. The hobvint of braovi is soltarn, braovi and thraisk, and muxsib lies outside it, so the relation fails.
R10. It is not the case that: e * x equals the duthgrix for every driwren x. It fails at anchor = soltarn, x = nakquil, value = nakquil. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

(2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one driwren e with e * x = x * e = x for every driwren x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every driwren unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e * f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e * f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. documents.text: T11. No two distinct driwrens can both be zelpyrs. (1) [D9] Let f and h both be floors. (2) [D9] Then f << h, since h is any object, and h << f likewise. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take soltarn * (thraisk * muxsib). thraisk * muxsib = yukzel (the table for *) soltarn * yukzel = yukzel (the table for *) The value is yukzel. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does nakquil << muxsib hold? Read off what nakquil stands over: nakquil, soltarn, muxsib, braovi, yukzel and thraisk. muxsib is among them, so it holds.

R8. It is not the case that: There is a driwren whose pyrumb is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 2, size = 6. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. That is not a rhetorical caution. Take the same 6 objects, the same symbols, and a different table, and T7 stop holding. The notation survives the substitution and the mathematics does not.
Read alongside D1 (shenka driwrens), D11 (the thrakeld of a driwren), D8 (the pyrumb of a driwren) and T4 (the pyrumb of a driwren is driglim).

R8. It is not the case that: There is a driwren whose pyrumb is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is driglim and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 156 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x * x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x * x = x then {x} is already closed under *. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the thrakeld is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x * x, which is then x. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every driwren x, the thrakeld of x divides 6. (1) [T4] [x] is a driglim collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the thrakeld of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 6. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the ovisib. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. The results now available are T5, T6 and T7, each settled by exhaustive check rather than by argument from analogy. Explicitly not available: R8. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

documents.text:
This book is about vintzams. A vintzam is not a number and not a set; it is one of
exactly 6 objects, and everything said here is said about how those 6 objects combine.

The vintzams are written hurnvash, duthsib, drishen, pyryuk, aztka and ovijen. The first
operation is written :. The relation is written ::; where it holds between two vintzams
we say the left one yields to the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x : x : x.

Readers arriving from arithmetic should put it down at the door. The operations below
are defined by their tables and by nothing else. Several arithmetic habits survive the
crossing and several do not, and the text is careful to say which is which.

Anyone using this system to keep track of something will meet the Bravor signature, the Bravor combination tables and closure under the first operation early, whether or not they go looking. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 6 vintzams that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for :. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | hurnvash duthsib drishen pyryuk aztka ovijen ----------------------------------------------------------------------- hurnvash | hurnvash hurnvash hurnvash hurnvash hurnvash hurnvash duthsib | hurnvash duthsib drishen pyryuk aztka ovijen drishen | hurnvash drishen aztka hurnvash drishen aztka pyryuk | hurnvash pyryuk hurnvash pyryuk hurnvash pyryuk aztka | hurnvash aztka drishen hurnvash aztka drishen ovijen | hurnvash ovijen aztka pyryuk drishen duthsib Every pair standing in the :: relation, grouped by left argument. hurnvash :: hurnvash, duthsib, drishen, pyryuk, aztka and ovijen duthsib :: duthsib drishen :: duthsib and aztka pyryuk :: duthsib, pyryuk and ovijen aztka :: duthsib and aztka ovijen :: duthsib

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all vintzams x and y, x : y is again a vintzam. A2. Association of the first operation. For all vintzams x, y, z: (x : y) : z = x : (y : z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all vintzams x and y: x : y = y : x.

Two questions sort the vintzams quickly. Does combining a vintzam with itself change it? For hurnvash, duthsib, pyryuk and aztka it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For hurnvash, duthsib, drishen, pyryuk, aztka and ovijen it does not. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R2 rests on S2 (the Bravor combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. R3 rests on S2 (the Bravor combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (drishen : pyryuk) : hurnvash, reduced without skipping anything. drishen : pyryuk = hurnvash (the table for :) hurnvash : hurnvash = hurnvash (the table for :) The expression comes to hurnvash. A companion case, pyryuk : (hurnvash : drishen), to show what the brackets are doing. hurnvash : drishen = hurnvash (the table for :) pyryuk : hurnvash = hurnvash (the table for :) That gives hurnvash, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test pyryuk :: drishen. The kazam of pyryuk is duthsib, pyryuk and ovijen, and drishen lies outside it, so the relation fails.

R2. It is not the case that: For every vintzam x: x : x = x. It fails at x = drishen, value = aztka. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one. R3. It is not the case that: For all vintzams x, y, z: if x : y = x : z then y = z. It fails at x = hurnvash, y = hurnvash, z = duthsib. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

These results are used again in A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (antisymmetry of the relation) and A7 (transitivity of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every vintzam x: x : x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = drishen, value = aztka, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all vintzams x, y, z: if x : y = x : z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = hurnvash, y = hurnvash, z = duthsib, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

Here is the question this chapter answers: once the combining is settled, what can be said about the objects themselves? The route runs through a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about vintzams covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a vintzam duthsib with duthsib : x = x : duthsib = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a vintzam hurnvash with hurnvash : x = x : hurnvash = hurnvash for every x.

Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single vintzam and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R1 rests on S2 (the Bravor combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (duthsib : hurnvash) : (pyryuk : ovijen). Each line below is one lookup in a table. duthsib : hurnvash = hurnvash (the table for :) pyryuk : ovijen = pyryuk (the table for :) hurnvash : pyryuk = hurnvash (the table for :) So (duthsib : hurnvash) : (pyryuk : ovijen) is hurnvash. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is hurnvash : (pyryuk : duthsib) for contrast. pyryuk : duthsib = pyryuk (the table for :) hurnvash : pyryuk = hurnvash (the table for :) That gives hurnvash, the same value the first reading gave, which is a fact about these particular arguments and not a law. Test duthsib :: aztka. The kazam of duthsib is duthsib, and aztka lies outside it, so the relation fails.
R1. Some vintzam x admits no vintzam y for which x : y and y : x both land on a neutral object. It fails at x = hurnvash. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. These particular results happen to survive rebuilding the system over different tables with the same names, which makes them weaker tests of understanding than the chapters around them.
The material this chapter borrows from: S2 (the Bravor combination tables). What is built on it later: D5 (the espavex) and T1 (the espavex is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some vintzam x admits no vintzam y for which x : y and y : x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = hurnvash, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 216 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R1. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

We turn to antisymmetry of the relation, transitivity of the relation and the kazam of a vintzam. The treatment is self contained given the material already established. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over vintzams, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A6. Antisymmetry of the relation. For all vintzams x and y: if x :: y and y :: x then x = y. A7. Transitivity of the relation. For all vintzams x, y, z: if x :: y and y :: z then x :: z. D4. The kazam of a vintzam. The kazam of a vintzam x is the collection of vintzams y for which x :: y holds. Worked out for each vintzam: hurnvash to hurnvash, duthsib, drishen, pyryuk, aztka and ovijen; duthsib to duthsib; drishen to duthsib and aztka; pyryuk to duthsib, pyryuk and ovijen; aztka to duthsib and aztka; ovijen to duthsib.

documents.text: Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers hobdri vintzams, vintzams that zamsib and the espavex, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about vintzams covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D1. Hobdri vintzams. A vintzam x is called hobdri when x : x = x. Running the definition over every vintzam leaves hurnvash, duthsib, pyryuk and aztka. D2. Vintzams that zamsib. Two vintzams x and y are said to zamsib when x : y = y : x. D5. The espavex. The vintzam duthsib is called the espavex of the system. It is the unique vintzam that leaves every vintzam unchanged under :. Here that is duthsib.

A useful mental split: some vintzams are inert under the operation and some are not. hurnvash, duthsib, pyryuk and aztka come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and hurnvash, duthsib, drishen, pyryuk, aztka and ovijen commute with everything. The neutral vintzam duthsib is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Take (hurnvash : duthsib) : (aztka : pyryuk) and work it out one step at a time. hurnvash : duthsib = hurnvash (the table for :) aztka : pyryuk = hurnvash (the table for :) hurnvash : hurnvash = hurnvash (the table for :) So (hurnvash : duthsib) : (aztka : pyryuk) is hurnvash. A companion case, duthsib : (aztka : hurnvash), to show what the brackets are doing. aztka : hurnvash = hurnvash (the table for :) duthsib : hurnvash = hurnvash (the table for :) The value is hurnvash. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test pyryuk :: duthsib. The kazam of pyryuk is duthsib, pyryuk and ovijen, and duthsib lies inside it, so the relation holds.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of vintzams that come back unchanged from themselves: hurnvash, duthsib, pyryuk and aztka. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

documents.text: D13. Brareld pairs. Two distinct vintzams x and y form a brareld pair when x :: y and y :: x both hold, that is, when each lies in the kazam of the other. In this system nothing satisfies it, which is itself a fact worth carrying forward. D3. Nakkeld collections. A collection S of vintzams is nakkeld when x : y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A rastshen. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over vintzams, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. D10. Umbgrix vintzams. A vintzam x is umbgrix when x : x equals the espavex. In this system that picks out duthsib and ovijen, which is 2 of the 6 vintzams. D6. The lumisk. The lumisk of the system is the collection of vintzams that zamsib with every vintzam. In this system that picks out hurnvash, duthsib, drishen, pyryuk, aztka and ovijen, that is, all of them. D7. The lumvash. The lumvash is the collection of all hobdri vintzams. Running the definition over every vintzam leaves hurnvash, duthsib, pyryuk and aztka.

Two questions sort the vintzams quickly. Does combining a vintzam with itself change it? For hurnvash, duthsib, pyryuk and aztka it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For hurnvash, duthsib, drishen, pyryuk, aztka and ovijen it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single vintzam and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The kazam of duthsib is duthsib, and drishen lies outside it, so the relation fails.

(1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every vintzam unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e : f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e : f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. R8. It is not the case that: There is a vintzam whose vashpon is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 2, size = 6. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Every result in this chapter is downstream of closure under the first operation. Those are properties of this system, not of systems in general. That is not a rhetorical caution. Take the same 6 objects, the same symbols, and a different table, and T7 stop holding. R8. It is not the case that: There is a vintzam whose vashpon is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 2, size = 6, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 6 cases: every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is nakkeld and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number

of applications. Checked over 156 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x : x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x : x = x then {x} is already closed under :. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the zamrast is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x : x, which is then x. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. For every vintzam x, the zamrast of x divides 6. (1) [T4] [x] is a nakkeld collection. (2) [D11] Its size is the zamrast of x. (3) The claim is that this size always divides 6. Checked over 6 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Carry forward the thrakeld. Later chapters state their results in these terms and do not restate the definitions. Established here and safe to use: T5, T6 and T7. Explicitly not available: R8. documents.text:
What follows is a complete account of the Hobnak system. It is complete in a strong
sense: the system has 5 rastvashs and finitely many facts, and every one of those facts
is settled here by inspection rather than left to argument.

The rastvashs are written lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast. The first
operation is written ?. The relation is written >>; where it holds between two rastvashs
we say the left one supports the right one. Both operations associate to the left when
written without brackets, and brackets override that. Repeated combination is
abbreviated: x^3 means x ? x ? x.

A warning that will be repeated because it is the one readers ignore: nothing here is
inherited from arithmetic. Familiar names have been avoided on purpose. Where a law of
arithmetic happens to hold it is stated and checked, and where it fails a counterexample
is given.

So far the rastvashs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up the Hobnak signature, the Hobnak combination tables and closure under the first operation. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over rastvashs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The table for ?. Read the left argument down the side and the right argument across the top. | lumpyr lumnyr opalbra rastumb fexrast ------------------------------------------------------- lumpyr | lumpyr lumpyr lumpyr lumpyr lumpyr lumnyr | lumpyr lumnyr opalbra rastumb fexrast opalbra | lumpyr opalbra fexrast lumnyr rastumb rastumb | lumpyr rastumb lumnyr fexrast opalbra fexrast | lumpyr fexrast rastumb opalbra lumnyr Every pair standing in the >> relation, grouped by left argument. lumpyr >> lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast lumnyr >> lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast opalbra >> lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast rastumb >> lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast fexrast >> lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A1. Closure under the first operation. For all rastvashs x and y, x ? y is again a rastvash. A2. Association of the first operation. For all rastvashs x, y, z: (x ? y) ? z = x ? (y ? z). A3. Commutation of the first operation. For all rastvashs x and y: x ? y = y ? x.

Two questions sort the rastvashs quickly. Does combining a rastvash with itself change it? For lumpyr and lumnyr it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast it does not. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. R2 rests on S2 (the Hobnak combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. R3 rests on S2 (the Hobnak combination tables). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Here is (fexrast ? lumnyr) ? rastumb, reduced without skipping anything. fexrast ? lumnyr = fexrast (the table for ?) fexrast ? rastumb = opalbra (the table for ?) The expression comes to opalbra. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take lumnyr ? (rastumb ? fexrast). rastumb ? fexrast = opalbra (the table for ?) lumnyr ? opalbra = opalbra (the table for ?) The value is opalbra. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. One decision about the relation, since deciding is as much a skill as computing. Does rastumb >> lumpyr hold? Read off what rastumb stands over: lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast. lumpyr is among them, so it holds.

R2. It is not the case that: For every rastvash x: x ? x = x. The case that settles it: x = opalbra, value = fexrast. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R3. It is not the case that: For all rastvashs x, y, z: if x ? y = x ? z then y = z. The case that settles it: x = lumpyr, y = lumpyr, z = lumnyr. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
What is built on it later: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), A5 (an absorbing object for the first operation), A6 (reflexivity of the relation) and A7 (transitivity of the relation).

R2. It is not the case that: For every rastvash x: x ? x = x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = opalbra, value = fexrast, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R3. It is not the case that: For all rastvashs x, y, z: if x ? y = x ? z then y = z. (1) [S2] Take the case x = lumpyr, y = lumpyr, z = lumnyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Explicitly not available: R2 and R3. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The present chapter develops a neutral object for the first operation, an absorbing object for the first operation and the system does not have reversal under the first operation. Prerequisites are real here: chapter 1 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about rastvashs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Some of what follows is negative. A claim that fails is set out with the case that breaks it, because knowing which habits do not carry over is worth as much as knowing which do.

The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A4. A neutral object for the first operation. There is a rastvash lumnyr with lumnyr ? x = x ? lumnyr = x for every x. A5. An absorbing object for the first operation. There is a rastvash lumpyr with lumpyr ? x = x ? lumpyr = lumpyr for every x.

The neutral rastvash lumnyr is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 rastvashs the table is short enough to consult every time.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R1 rests on S2 (the Hobnak combination tables). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

Evaluate (opalbra ? rastumb) ? (fexrast ? lumnyr). Each line below is one lookup in a table. opalbra ? rastumb = lumnyr (the table for ?) fexrast ? lumnyr = fexrast (the table for ?) lumnyr ? fexrast = fexrast (the table for ?) So (opalbra ? rastumb) ? (fexrast ? lumnyr) is fexrast. Move the brackets and the work changes. Take rastumb ? (fexrast ? opalbra). fexrast ? opalbra = rastumb (the table for ?) rastumb ? rastumb = fexrast (the table for ?) The value is fexrast. It agrees with the first case here, and a reader should resist reading anything general into that. Test opalbra >> lumpyr. The jennak of opalbra is lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast, and lumpyr lies inside it, so the relation holds.
R1. Some rastvash x admits no rastvash y for which x ? y and y ? x both land on a neutral object. It fails at x = lumpyr. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.
Read alongside S2 (the Hobnak combination tables). These results are used again in D5 (the thraclo) and T1 (the thraclo is the only one of its kind).

R1. Some rastvash x admits no rastvash y for which x ? y and y ? x both land on a neutral object. (1) [S2] Take the case x = lumpyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 125 cases: every tuple of the carrier the axiom quantifies over. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
Do not carry forward R1. These were tested and failed, and the failing cases are recorded above.

Work through this chapter with the tables in front of you. It covers reflexivity of the relation, transitivity of the relation and comparability of every pair, and each claim can be checked by hand. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapter 1, and a reader who has skipped it will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about rastvashs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

documents.text: The following hold in this system, without exception, and each was verified by running through the tables in full. A6. Reflexivity of the relation. For every rastvash x: x >> x. A7. Transitivity of the relation. For all rastvashs x, y, z: if x >> y and y >> z then x >> z. A8. Comparability of every pair. For all rastvashs x and y, at least one of x >> y and y >> x holds. A9. Agreement of the relation with the first operation. For all rastvashs x, y, z: if x >> y then (z ? x) >> (z ? y) and (x ? z) >> (y ? z). D4. The jennak of a rastvash. The jennak of a rastvash x is the collection of rastvashs y for which x >> y holds. Worked out for each rastvash: lumpyr to lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast; lumnyr to lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast; opalbra to lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast; rastumb to lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast; fexrast to lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast.

documents.text: What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, opalsol rastvashs, rastvashs that drifal and the thraclo, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 1 and 2, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about rastvashs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows.

D1. Opalsol rastvashs. A rastvash x is called opalsol when x ? x = x. Running the definition over every rastvash leaves lumpyr and lumnyr. D2. Rastvashs that drifal. Two rastvashs x and y are said to drifal when x ? y = y ? x. D5. The thraclo. The rastvash lumnyr is called the thraclo of the system. It is the unique rastvash that leaves every rastvash unchanged under ?. Here that is lumnyr.

Two questions sort the rastvashs quickly. Does combining a rastvash with itself change it? For lumpyr and lumnyr it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast it does not. Neutrality is a strong condition disguised as a weak one. It fixes a single rastvash and, through that, constrains everything that can combine with it. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.
This chapter is groundwork. The derivations that use it start in the next one.

Take (fexrast ? opalbra) ? (rastumb ? lumpyr) and work it out one step at a time. fexrast ? opalbra = rastumb (the table for ?) rastumb ? lumpyr = lumpyr (the table for ?) rastumb ? lumpyr = lumpyr (the table for ?) The expression comes to lumpyr. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is opalbra ? (rastumb ? fexrast) for contrast. rastumb ? fexrast = opalbra (the table for ?) opalbra ? opalbra = fexrast (the table for ?) That gives fexrast, against lumpyr above. Test rastumb >> fexrast. The jennak of rastumb is lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast, and fexrast lies inside it, so the relation holds.

Every claim in this chapter survives every case, which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly. The nearest thing to a trap is the set of rastvashs that come back unchanged from themselves: lumpyr and lumnyr. Assuming more of them than that is the mistake to avoid.

It is worth being exact about what has been shown and what has not. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A1 (closure under the first operation) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). What is built on it later: D6 (the nakzel), D7 (the oviwren), D10 (grixxil rastvashs) and T1 (the thraclo is the only one of its kind).

The practical content of this chapter is braespa pairs, zelduth collections and a bragrix. It is the part that shows up in use. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1 and 3 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. documents.text: D13. Braespa pairs. Two distinct rastvashs x and y form a braespa pair when x >> y and y >> x both hold, that is, when each lies in the jennak of the other. In this system that picks out lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast, that is, all of them. D3. Zelduth collections. A collection S of rastvashs is zelduth when x ? y belongs to S for every pair x, y drawn from S. D9. A bragrix. A rastvash f is a bragrix when f >> y holds for every rastvash y, that is, when the jennak of f is the whole system. Running the definition over every rastvash leaves lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast.

documents.text: T11. If x >> y then (x ? z) >> (y ? z) for every rastvash z. (1) [D4] Let y lie in the jennak of x. (2) [A9] Compatibility applies the operation to both sides at once. (3) Nothing else is needed, since z was arbitrary. Checked over 125 cases: every ordered triple. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T13. If x >> y then y >> x. (1) [D4] Symmetry would mean y lies in the jennak of x exactly when x lies in that of y. (2) The listed pairs settle it directly. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T9. If y lies in the jennak of x, then the jennak of y is contained in the jennak of x. (1) [D4] Let y satisfy x >> y and let z satisfy y >> z. (2) [A7] Transitivity gives x >> z. (3) [D4] So every member of the jennak of y is a member of that of x. Checked over 125 cases: every ordered triple. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

documents.text: So far the rastvashs have been objects to be pushed around. This chapter starts asking what they are like. We take up grixxil rastvashs, the nakzel and the oviwren. Nothing here stands on its own. The arguments lean on chapters 2 and 4, and a reader who has skipped them will find the derivations opaque rather than difficult. A note on method before starting. Everything asserted below was checked against every case the statement quantifies over, not argued from a pattern in a few examples. With 5 rastvashs that is cheap, and it means a claim in this book is either settled or absent. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D10. Grixxil rastvashs. A rastvash x is grixxil when x ? x equals the thraclo. In this system that picks out lumnyr and fexrast, which is 2 of the 5 rastvashs. D6. The nakzel. The nakzel of the system is the collection of rastvashs that drifal with every rastvash. Running the definition over every rastvash leaves lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast. D7. The oviwren. The oviwren is the collection of all opalsol rastvashs. Running the definition over every rastvash leaves lumpyr and lumnyr.

A useful mental split: some rastvashs are inert under the operation and some are not. lumpyr and lumnyr come back unchanged when combined with themselves, and lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast commute with everything. The neutral rastvash lumnyr is the one that does nothing. That sounds trivial and is not: almost every result in this chapter is an argument about what doing nothing forces. Treat the above as scaffolding. It is the fastest route into a system nobody has intuitions about yet, and it should be discarded the moment it disagrees with a computation.

The order matters. Each of these leans on what came before it, and the chain is short enough to hold in mind. R8 rests on D5 (the thraclo). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T1 rests on D5 (the thraclo) and A4 (a neutral object for the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary.

Evaluate (opalbra ? lumnyr) ? (fexrast ? lumpyr). Each line below is one lookup in a table. opalbra ? lumnyr = opalbra (the table for ?) fexrast ? lumpyr = lumpyr (the table for ?) opalbra ? lumpyr = lumpyr (the table for ?) The expression comes to lumpyr. Bracketing is not cosmetic, so here is lumnyr ? (fexrast ? opalbra) for contrast. fexrast ? opalbra = rastumb (the table for ?) lumnyr ? rastumb = rastumb (the table for ?) The value is rastumb, not lumpyr. Test fexrast >> lumnyr. The jennak of fexrast is lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast, and lumnyr lies inside it, so the relation holds.
R8. It is not the case that: e ? x equals the thraclo for every rastvash x. It fails at anchor = lumnyr, x = lumpyr, value = lumpyr. One case is enough, and this is the earliest one.

The limits of these results are sharper than they look. The load is carried by a neutral object for the first operation and closure under the first operation. A system without them is not a system where these results are harder to prove; it is a system where they are false. Unusually, nothing in this chapter distinguishes this system from its near neighbours. Take that as a warning about how much a familiar looking statement can be worth.

The material this chapter borrows from: A4 (a neutral object for the first operation), D1 (opalsol rastvashs), D2 (rastvashs that drifal) and D5 (the thraclo). These results are used again in T2 (the thraclo lies in the nakzel), T3 (the nakzel is zelduth), T7 (the umbvash of a nakzel rastvash stays in the nakzel) and T8 (the oviwren is zelduth).

R8. It is not the case that: e ? x equals the thraclo for every rastvash x. (1) [S2] Take the case anchor = lumnyr, x = lumpyr, value = lumpyr, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T1. There is exactly one rastvash e with e ? x = x ? e = x for every rastvash x. (1) [D5] Suppose e and f both leave every rastvash unchanged. (2) [A4] Then e ? f = f, reading e as neutral on the left. (3) [A4] And e ? f = e, reading f as neutral on the right. (4) So e = f, and the two suppositions describe the same object. Checked over 25 cases: every object paired with every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

Explicitly not available: R8. A later argument that quietly assumes one of these is wrong, and the counterexamples above say exactly where.

The present chapter develops the umbvash of a rastvash, the system has a bragrix and where every rastvash is opalsol breaks down. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. The standard of proof here is exhaustion. A universal claim about rastvashs covers at most a few hundred cases, so it is run over all of them. Nothing below rests on an argument from analogy with a system the reader already knows. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.

D8. The umbvash of a rastvash. The umbvash of a rastvash x, written [x], is the smallest zelduth collection that contains x. Worked out for each rastvash: lumpyr to lumpyr; lumnyr to lumnyr; opalbra to lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast; rastumb to lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast; fexrast to lumnyr and fexrast.

Picture the umbvash as what happens when you start with one rastvash and keep folding it against itself and against whatever appears, until nothing new appears. Because there are only 5 rastvashs, that stops. In this system the sizes it stops at are 1, 2 and 4. Think of >> as pointing downhill. The jennak of a rastvash is everything downhill of it, and those shadows here have sizes 5. Two questions sort the rastvashs quickly. Does combining a rastvash with itself change it? For lumpyr and lumnyr it does not. Does it matter which side it goes on? For lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast it does not. None of these images are load bearing. They are here because a reader who can see the shape makes fewer lookups, not because any argument below depends on seeing it. Every proof goes through the tables.

Each result below is reached from earlier material, and the route is worth reading before the statement. T10 rests on D9 (a bragrix) and A8 (comparability of every pair). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. R6 rests on D7 (the oviwren). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T12 rests on D6 (the nakzel). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable. T2 rests on D5 (the thraclo) and D6 (the nakzel). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T3 rests on D6 (the nakzel), D3 (zelduth collections) and A2 (association of the first operation). The dependence is on the content of those results, not only on their vocabulary. T8 rests on D7 (the oviwren) and D3 (zelduth collections). Remove any one of them and the statement stops making sense, not merely stops being provable.

The jennak of lumpyr is lumpyr, lumnyr, opalbra, rastumb and fexrast, and fexrast lies inside it, so the relation holds. A second case, this time a umbvash. Start from fexrast. Combine it with itself, add whatever is new, and repeat until nothing is added. What survives is lumnyr and fexrast, so the espalum of fexrast is 2.

T10. Some rastvash bragrixs the whole system. (1) [A8] Every pair is comparable, so the relation orders the objects into a line. (2) [D9] The claim is that the line has a bottom. (3) The carrier is finite, so the search over candidates terminates. Checked over 25 cases: every candidate against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R6. It is not the case that: x ? x = x for every rastvash x. (1) [S2] Take the case x = opalbra, value = fexrast, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: every object. pair of rastvashs drifals. (1) [D6] The nakzel is defined by drifaling with everything. (2) [D2] The claim is that x ? y = y ? x for every pair. (3) That is settled by scanning the table for a pair that disagrees. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T2. The thraclo drifals with every rastvash. (1) [D5] Let e be the thraclo and x any rastvash. (2) [D5] Then e ? x = x and x ? e = x. (3) [D2] So e ? x = x ? e, which is what it means to drifal. (4) [D6] Since x was arbitrary, e belongs to the nakzel. Checked over 5 cases: the anchor against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T3. If x and y both drifal with every rastvash, then so does x ? y. (1)

[D6] Let x and y lie in the nakzel and let z be any rastvash. (2) [A2] Then (x ? y) ? z = x ? (y ? z). (3) [D6] Move z past y, then past x, using that each drifals with everything. (4) [D3] So x ? y drifals with z, and the nakzel is zelduth. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the core. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T8. If x and y are both opalsol then so is x ? y. (1) [D7] Let x and y be opalsol. (2) [D1] The claim asks whether (x ? y) ? (x ? y) returns x ? y. (3) Whether it does is settled by running the operation table on every such pair. Checked over 25 cases: every ordered pair drawn from the ridge. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

T4. For every rastvash x, the collection [x] is zelduth. (1) [D8] [x] is built by taking x and closing under ?. (2) [D3] Closing under an operation is exactly the sealing condition. (3) The carrier is finite, so the closure stops after finitely many rounds. Checked over 125 cases: every object, then every pair inside its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T7. If x lies in the nakzel then every rastvash of [x] lies in the nakzel. (1) [T3] The nakzel is zelduth. (2) [D8] [x] is the smallest zelduth collection containing x. (3) A smallest such collection sits inside any other, and the nakzel is one. Checked over 25 cases: every object of the core, then its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.

What follows was pieced together backwards. The last item of it, the umbhurn, where the espalum divides the number of rastvashs breaks down and where some rastvash reaches every other breaks down, was noticed before anyone had a reason to expect it. Prerequisites are real here: chapters 4, 7 and 8 supply the notions the statements below are phrased in. One habit to adopt: when a statement below quantifies over rastvashs, check two or three cases by hand before reading on. The tables are short and the checking is fast, and it is the only way to build the intuition this system does not share with any other. Not every claim in this chapter survives. The ones that do not are kept, with their counterexamples, rather than quietly dropped.
D12. The umbhurn. The umbhurn of the system is the collection of rastvashs whose espalum is largest. Running the definition over every rastvash leaves opalbra and rastumb.

The right picture for umbvash is a spreading stain rather than a list. Drop one rastvash in, apply the operation to whatever is wet, repeat. The stain here reaches 1, 2 and 4 rastvashs depending on where it started. The honest caveat on all of this: a picture is a way of remembering a table, not a substitute for one. Where the picture and the table disagree the table wins, and in a system with 5 rastvashs the table is short enough to consult every time.

Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates. R7. It is not the case that: There is a rastvash whose umbvash is the whole system. The case that settles it: largest_span = 4, size = 5. Anyone carrying this claim over from a more familiar system will be wrong here, and wrong in a way that propagates.

R5. It is not the case that: For every rastvash x, the espalum of x divides 5. (1) [S2] Take the case x = opalbra, reach = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. R7. It is not the case that: There is a rastvash whose umbvash is the whole system. (1) [S2] Take the case largest_span = 4, size = 5, read straight from the tables. (2) [S2] The two sides of the claim come apart on that case, so the claim cannot hold for every case. (3) One counterexample is enough. Note that the claim may still hold for many particular objects; what fails is the universal reading. Checked over 5 cases:

every object and its span. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T5. If S is zelduth and contains x, then S contains all of [x]. (1) [D8] Every member of [x] is reached from x by finitely many applications of the operation. (2) [D3] A sealed S containing x is closed under each of those applications. (3) So each member of [x] is in S, by induction on the number of applications. Checked over 35 cases: every sealed collection against every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported. T6. x ? x = x holds if and only if [x] contains x alone. (1) [D1] If x ? x = x then {x} is already closed under ?. (2) [T4] So [x] = {x} and the espalum is one. (3) [D11] Conversely a span of one object must contain x ? x, which is then x. Checked over 5 cases: every object. The check is exhaustive, so the statement is settled rather than supported.
